title: Safe Chain Solutions to settle alleged counterfeit HIV drug claims
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Safe Chain Solutions to settle alleged counterfeit HIV drug claims

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Local News 
 
 754
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Over two years of civil litigation against Cambridge-based pharmaceutical distributor Safe Chain Solutions relating to its alleged implication in a counterfeit HIV drug scheme has reached a settlement, according to federal court documents.A consent judgment and permanent injunction filed Feb. 20 in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York is awaiting a signature from a federal judge, which will formally settle Gilead Sciences Inc's complex lawsuit against the local pharmaceutical distributor and its founders, brothers Charlie and Patrick Boyd.
Gilead is a biopharmaceutical company that develops and markets a variety of medications, including drugs that treat or prevent HIV.
The complaint, originally filed in 2021 and amended in 2022, alleged Safe Chain's involvement in the distribution of authentic-looking bottles of two of Gilead's HIV medications, Biktarvy and Descovy, to pharmacies across the country.
Gilead's deeper investigation into the alleged scheme revealed that some of the bottles contained completely different drugs not used to treat HIV. Some of the bottles reportedly contained quetiapine, or Seroquel XR — an antipsychotic used to treat schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder, according to the amended complaint.
The complaint alleged that some of the counterfeit bottles purchased from Safe Chain, which were received by pharmacies and later reported to the pharmacies by customers, came with falsified pedigrees, or documentation, that claimed to trace the drugs back to an authentic source.
The consent judgment and permanent injunction will prohibit Safe Chain from selling any Gilead product in the United States, including a number of Gilead's HIV medications.
Under the terms of the agreement, Gilead will have the right to have an independent firm audit Safe Chain's purchase and sales records for all products bought and sold after the consent judgment is entered, according to the document.
The firm will not provide information to Gilead unless it relates to Gilead-branded products or non-compliance with the order.
Additionally, Safe Chain will be required to relinquish its rights to over $2.7 million in frozen assets, which includes over $1.9 million of Safe Chain's funds in an equitable trust account and money in the brothers' personal investment and life insurance accounts.
If a court finds that Safe Chain violated any terms of the consent judgment and injunction, the company would be required to pay Gilead 100 times the wholesale acquisition cost of the Gilead product sold, according to the document.
The wholesale acquisition cost for Biktarvy is over $3,000. Descovy is over $2,000.
Despite the lawsuit's allegations, Safe Chain believes that the drugs "were actually legitimate Gilead products that had been diverted into the stream of commerce," said August Matteis, an attorney for the the company.
In counterclaims against Gilead, Safe Chain alleged that Gilead's accusations were "false and defamatory" and that Gilead was "motivated by trying to destroy the secondary market for its drugs," he said.
According to Matteis, Safe Chain believes Gilead sued the company in "an attempt to cover up the fact that thousands of bottles of Gilead HIV drugs entered the stream of commerce due to poor oversight of Gilead's free drug access program in Florida."
"There has been no judicial ruling on Gilead's claims against Safe Chain or on Safe Chain's counterclaims against Gilead," he said. "Safe Chain agreed to settle this case to end the legal costs associated with this litigation and to get back to running its business."
Gilead's lawsuit was not the only documentation explaining concerns with Safe Chain.
A June 2023 warning letter issued by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration detailed the company's violations of the Drug Supply Chain Security Act. It followed the FDA's monthlong inspection of Safe Chain's Cambridge facility from April to May 2022.
Specifically, it called the company out for not having adequate verification systems required under law that "may have resulted in suspect product entering the supply chain" rather than being quarantined, according to the letter.
The letter also confirmed that Safe Chain purchased products from other drug wholesalers that were not authorized, failed to maintain records of suspect product investigations and failed to respond to notifications of illegitimate products.
The Feb. 20 injunction prohibiting Safe Chain from selling Gilead products ensures that Safe Chain "will never again be a source of counterfeit versions of our medicines," according to a Gilead spokesperson.
"This is the latest result of years of work reflecting our longstanding commitment to protect patients and the public from bad actors selling counterfeit and illicit versions of Gilead's medicines," the spokesperson said in an email. "This includes working closely with the FDA, FBI and prosecutors to dismantle this counterfeiting network, deter bad actors, and thwart illegal pharmaceutical distribution."

title: Department of Aging funding anticipated to remain flat, secretary says
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Department of Aging funding anticipated to remain flat, secretary says

 January 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: General Assembly 
 
 443
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Funding for the Maryland Department of Aging is expected to remain flat over the coming year, according to Maryland Secretary of Aging Carmel Roques.The secretary's comment came after Del. Chris Adams (R-Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) asked if there were concerns about the department's budget outcome during an Eastern Shore Delegation meeting Friday morning.
Concerns are not with losing funding, but with an anticipated inability to grow funding.
"The okay news is we don't anticipate our funding to be cut, but we're not going to have additional funding," Roques said. "And the way we're going to try and make that a better situation is the way we engage with, in a collaborative fashion, … our health and our housing agencies."
The majority of the department's funding comes from the federal government. State funding comprises a smaller portion of the dollars the department has to distribute.
In fiscal year 2024, Upper Shore Aging, the designated area agency on aging for Talbot, Caroline and Kent counties, received almost $782,000 from the state Department of Aging.
Queen Anne's County received about $333,000, and Cecil County received roughly $554,000.
MAC Inc., which is the area agency for Dorchester, Somerset, Wicomico and Worcester counties, received just over $1.3 million.
Knowing the funding was unlikely to grow, the department took steps early on to maximize the funding available to direct it more effectively at the local level, Roques said.
Those steps included working with stakeholder groups to look at three state programs — subsidized assisted living, congregate living and senior care money — to think about redesigning the long-term services and supports system in place from the state funding.
According to Roques, the work being done now will not "dramatically" change anything about fiscal year 2025, but it will in the coming years.
The Administration on Community Living, a federal agency that increases access to community supports for older adults and those with disabilities, also recently changed regulations to include guidance that will impact equity, she said.
Roques said the update to the regulations is "good news" for the rural elderly population, their families and care providers.
The state's rural communities have the highest populations of adults age 50 and older, according to data shared during her presentation.
The rural counties on the Eastern Shore have some of the highest numbers. In 2020, 50.8% of Talbot County's population was over age 50.
Maryland's overall population is rapidly growing older. In the next six years, the state will see more residents over 60 than under 18 — a first, Roques said.
"...What's being baked into that guidance is that rural communities need to be more heavily weighted in the formula for distribution of funds to recognize that their challenges are very different," she said.

title: Common sense degrees needed
author: Staff Writer
content:
Common sense degrees needed

 March 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 391
 Words 

 Read News Document

 This past weekend, I was enjoying my morning tea when I got a curious phone call. The gentleman knew me by my nickname, and I quickly became a good listener. Trying to place the voice it took me a few minutes to realize who it was a long-time multigenerational family friend. Let's call him Mike. I would later reflect on what an honor it was for me.For the better part of an hour, he regaled me with stories of yesteryear (none, surprisingly, set in the famed bygone watering hole of that name), featuring my father, grandfather and great-grandfather. My eyes swelled as he began to bring the good old days back to life, first in black and white, then in color. Some stories I had had a taste of, but most were new to me. What gentlemen they were.
I share that story to preface this one. While enjoying the company of "The Thursday Brotherhood" the topic of today's social climate came up. All of our comments were true and valid in their own way; I can only imagine that each generation feels the same, that in any moment in history, there are good times and not-so-good times.
The conversation brought back memories of my great-grandfather Walter Wood; he was the chief of police for then little old Easton. He called it "my town," and used his platform to serve with understanding as only he could. One quality of old Walter I heard about more than a few times was his sensible approach to life. My dad called it his C.S. (common sense) degree.
As it goes, he would leave home after supper, head to the firehouse, and open the door to the locals who needed shelter for the night. Today, we call them homeless. He would lock the door and call it a night. In the morning, the routine played out in reverse. What a novel solution.
Today, we share the same challenges as our predecessors, updated for the 21st century. How we approach them and resolve them is up to us, let's call it perspective. Sometimes what is old is what's new again. Having a bit more compassion and understanding for our neighbors can't be all wrong. Just maybe if we all use our C.S. degrees a bit more, we can all wake up and go to sleep with a smile.
ROO WOOD
Wittman

title: Not sure what the problem is
author: Staff Writer
content:
Not sure what the problem is

 April 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 178
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In a 2015 article from the Star Democrat titled "Parking Problems — Perception or Reality," statistics were quoted citing 900 available parking spaces in Easton.True not every space puts you right in front of your intended destination, but compared to dealing with parking garages and exorbitant hourly rates, Easton has a sweet deal.
I'm not sure what the problem with the farmers market is. Steve Mangasarian was quoted as saying trash was a problem. Is he saying it is the vendors or the patrons?
He also states the impact on merchants, but most stores are not open when the market opens at 8, and downtown Easton is not hopping in those early morning hours.
We, my spouse and I, are farmers market aficionados. When we go on extended vacations our first stop is a farmers market. It's where we learn about local specialties and food customs.
Over the years we have developed relationships with vendors at the Easton market, and I am grateful to have a vegetable on my plate that has not traveled 1,200 miles to grace my table.
SHARON HARRINGTON
Easton

title: TODAY IN HISTORY/May 21
author: Staff Writer
content:
TODAY IN HISTORY/May 21

 May 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Columns 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Today's Highlight in History:On May 21, 1881, Clara Barton founded the American Red Cross.
On this date:
In 1471, King Henry VI of England died in the Tower of London at age 49.
In 1542, Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto died while searching for gold along the Mississippi River.
In 1924, in a case that drew much notoriety, 14-year-old Bobby Franks was murdered in a "thrill killing" carried out by University of Chicago students Nathan Leopold Jr. and Richard Loeb (Bobby's cousin).
In 1927, Charles A. Lindbergh landed his Spirit of St. Louis monoplane near Paris, completing the first solo airplane flight across the Atlantic Ocean in 33½ hours.
In 1932, Amelia Earhart became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean as she landed in Northern Ireland, about 15 hours after leaving Newfoundland.
In 1941, a German U-boat sank the American merchant steamship SS Robin Moor in the South Atlantic after the ship's passengers and crew were allowed to board lifeboats.
In 1955, Chuck Berry recorded his first single, "Maybellene," for Chess Records in Chicago.
In 1972, Michelangelo's Pieta, on display at the Vatican, was damaged by a hammer-wielding man who shouted he was Jesus Christ.
In 1979, former San Francisco City Supervisor Dan White was convicted of voluntary manslaughter in the slayings of Mayor George Moscone and openly gay Supervisor Harvey Milk; outrage over the verdict sparked rioting. (White was sentenced to seven years and eight months in prison; he ended up serving five years and took his own life in 1985.)
In 1991, former Indian Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated during national elections by a suicide bomber.
In 2000, death claimed actor Sir John Gielgud at age 96 and author Dame Barbara Cartland at age 98.
In 2017, the Ringling Bros. and Barnum & Bailey Circus received its final standing ovation as it performed its last show, at the Nassau County Coliseum in Uniondale, New York, ending its 146-year existence.
In 2020, President Donald Trump visited a Ford Motor Co. plant outside Detroit that had been repurposed to manufacture ventilators; he did not publicly wear a face mask but said he had worn one while out of public view.
In 2021, thousands of Palestinians rallied after a cease-fire took effect in the latest Gaza war; the 11 days of fighting left more than 250 people dead, the vast majority Palestinians, and brought widespread destruction to the Gaza Strip.

title: Teen shot at Delaware car meet at industrial park
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Teen shot at Delaware car meet at industrial park

 August 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 195
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A 17-year-old boy is recovering after being shot during an unsanctioned car meet in an industrial park near Newark.The incident happened just before 1:30 a.m. Sunday on Tyler Way in the Delaware Industrial Park, located off South Chapel Street between Scottfield and Interstate 95.
According to Delaware State Police, the teen was part of a large crowd that had gathered for the car meet. At some point during the event, he got into an argument with another attendee, and that attendee threatened to shoot him.
A few minutes later, a second person approached the teen and fired a handgun at him. The teen suffered multiple gunshot wounds to his legs and was treated and released at a hospital, police said.
The man who argued with the teen was described as a Middle-Eastern man wearing a white hooded sweatshirt. The shooter was described as a light-skinned Black male with dreadlocks wearing a black hooded sweatshirt and a mask covering his face.
Both suspects drove away in a silver sedan.
Detectives are asking anyone who has information regarding this incident to contact Det. M. Conway at 302-365-8411. Information can also be provided by contacting Delaware Crime Stoppers at 1-800-847-3333 or delaware.crimestoppers.com.

title: Kerns, Queen Anne's thinking they have the goods for another long postseason run.
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Kerns, Queen Anne's thinking they have the goods for another long postseason run.

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 2164
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It wasn't a prediction.It was just something Mike Kern believed.
"If we can get out of the region, I think we have a good shot at states," Kern said of Queen Anne's County High's girls soccer team.
That was at the outset of the season. The Lions did get out of the region, then went on to become the first Bayside Conference school ever to win a girls state soccer championship.
Now, as the girls basketball season approaches tip-off, Kern again strongly believes if Queen Anne's can get out of its region, it has a chance to do well at the state level.
"We're very multi-dimensional," Kern said. "All of our guards can penetrate and shoot. And then our post players are very dangerous inside. They move well. They're very athletic. So I think the sky's the limit for them. The biggest thing is play as a team. We learned that in soccer. If we play as a team and aren't selfish, and do the little things, I think we can do really well."
Getting out of the Class 2A East Region II could prove more difficult than in soccer. Kent Island still has Sydney Riska and Lacey Dauses. Wicomico returns the bulk of the team that handed the Lions their only three losses last season, including bouts for the Bayside Conference and 2A East Region II championships. And Parkside has improved.
But this Queen Anne's team is different.
Not only does Kern return the majority of a team that went 20-3 and won the North Bayside championship, he welcomes two additions who have the potential to be impact players in juniors Damya Henry, a transfer from Cambridge-South Dorchester, and Cheyanne Hollis — daughter of Queen Anne's boys head coach Jeff Hollis — who has been sidelined by injury the past two seasons.
"With our core coming back, plus those additions, I think we stand a good chance of challenging them this year," Kern said of Wicomico. "Damya gives us that defensive pressure. She reads well. Anticipates well. And she's quick. So she definitely helps on the defensive end.
"And Chayenne, she's a true post player; and that will free up Bea (Holthaus) and Lucy (Taylor) a little bit having her in there," Kern continued.
Then there's the core group. Seniors RJ Ensor and Lucy Taylor return along with sophomores Laila Coles, Kariana Hickson, and Holthaus, the 2023 North Bayside Player of the Year.
"The thing about our team right now, I feel like we can score so many different ways," Kern said. "We have pretty good shooters. We can get the ball inside. We can drive. We're a very multi-dimensional team. And Bea herself is very multi-dimensional. She can play outside, go inside. She can drive.
"I'm not worried about us being able to score this year," Kern added. "My biggest focus so far is making sure we play good defense. One of the things that we've done well over the years is we've been a really good defensive team. And I feel like we have so much energy on the offense, that we kind of rest on the defense. And we can't do that with good teams. So we have to play up-tempo defense the entire game."
Kent Island remains Queen Anne's biggest challenger, though Cambridge-SD, with the senior core of Le'Asia Todd, Destiny Johnson and Tejanae Ballin have the potential to give Queen Anne's a battle.
Here's a look at this season's teams.
CAMBRIDGE-SD
Head Coach: Shamya Johnson.
Who's Where: Le'Asia Todd (Sr., C); Destiny Johnson (Sr., G); Tejanae Ballin (Sr., PG); AzEyera Johnson (Sr., F); Skyla Ali (So., F); Jade Ballin (So., F); JaNaya Stanley (Jr., G); Tonyia Brooks (Sr., G); Aamiyah Wilcox (Sr., C); Neveah Adams (Fr., G); Montiasha Jackson (So., G); Amari Winters (Fr., F/C); Kennedy Bourne (So., F); Kamryn Bourne (So., F); D'Asia Mack (So., G).
Outlook: Todd can reach 1,000 career points in Thursday's opener against Crisfield, and together with Destiny Johnson and Tejanae Ballin makes the Vikings a favorite in 1A East Region II.
And though Coach Johnson thinks Cambridge-SD can again reach the 1A state quarterfinals, one of her biggest challenges is keeping her team's intensity and discipline up from start to finish.
"That was the conversation we had tonight,' Coach Johnson said Tuesday in a phone interview. "'You all got it. You've got the pieces. But you all don't have the discipline. And that's the difference.'"
Johnson also knows her team needs to play great transition defense and create points off turnovers if it hopes to challenge Queen Anne's and Kent Island.
COL. RICHARDSON
Head Coach: Tom Corsey.
Who's Where: Jaz Jackson (Jr., G); Monae Ross (Sr., C); Selina Austriville (So., F); Tybria Williams (Sr., G); Ella Downie (So., F); Angelina Algre (Fr., C).
Outlook: Corsey thinks the 6-foot-5 Algre can develop into an inside force.
"She's a work in progress," Corsey said. "She's a presence. She's learning, but I'm going to get her there."
This is one of the younger teams Corsey's coached, but the goal is another 10-win season with eyes on upsetting a 2A school.
EASTON
Head Coach: Lesley Staehli.
Who's Where: Sam Murphy (Sr., G); Serenity Velez (Jr., G); Maia Bailey (Fr., G); Ki'Mauri Lewis (So., G); Jordyn Wilson-Colbert (So., F/C); Myles Booker (Sr., F/C); Dakota Dietrich (Sr., G); Addison Knox (So., G/F); Stella Kabler (Jr., G); Taylor Bowen (Fr., F/C); Addison Chandler (Sr., G/F).
Outlook: The Warriors are an interesting mix.
Velez returns as one of the team's top scorers, and Murphy has transferred from Saints Peter and Paul.
"She is one of the scrappiest people I have ever played against the last four years that I've been coaching defense wise," Staehli said of Murphy. "Now it's awesome to have her with us because she barely comes out."
Bailey, daughter of Marty Bailey, who has come over from the boys team to be an assistant, could be one of the Bayside's top newcomers. And then there is a list of talent that includes Knox, Kabler and Bowen, who helped the Warriors reach the state field hockey semifinals this past season, and Chandler, a force on the Easton soccer team.
"We're going to be fast," Staehli said. "Everybody has talent. I think we're going to shock a lot of people this year with the fact (they're) not expecting a lot of athletic people to come back into the program with us having no jayvee last year. There's certain teams we'll struggle with, but I think we're going to be pretty good."
KENT COUNTY
Head Coach: Tyray Johnson.
Who's Where: Kate Cannon (Sr., C); Talicia Wright (So., PG); Jane Cleary (So., F); Love Jackson (Jr., SF); Kaliyah Smith (Sr., SF); Ariyana Green (So., SF); Saniyah Jones (So., C); Tameeia Savage (Jr., SF); Juliette Camilli (Jr., SG); Sanorra Parker (Fr., SG); Abigael Lachance (Sr., SF); Emerence Boutaud (Jr., PF).
Outlook: Johnson begins his fourth season with the biggest roster he's ever had at Kent with 12. Though still young, experience was gained last year, especially with Wright, who returns at point guard.
"We turned the ball over a lot last year," Johnson said. "She (Wright) stepped up toward the end of the season. So a lot of the mistakes she made early on we won't really have them this year. So it's going to be less turnovers for us."
Speed and defense will be critical if the undersized Trojans are to improve on last season's five-win mark.
KENT ISLAND
Head Coach: Dave Plumer.
Who's Where: Sydney Riska (Sr., F); Lacey Dauses (Jr., G); Abigail Staton (Sr., PG); Ellie Burnside (Sr., G); Machaela Thomas (So., C); Avery Eaton (Sr., G)
Outlook: Lilli Dauses graduated and Makayla Kropfelder transferred to Broadneck. But don't expect the Bucs to fall far from the top.
The smooth-playing Riska was a double-double machine last season, and Lacey Dauses gained confidence with her ability to attack the rim and draw contact. Add Thomas, a 6-foot-2 center, who could create problems for opponents, and Burnside, the first player off the bench from last season.
"I think Lacey had grown as a player and in size," Plumer said. "Obviously Sydney had a big year last year, and now adding another 6-2 center to play along side of her is going to benefit her as well. Who are you going to guard? Machaela's got great footwork. She just needs playing time to get better.
"I think we got to run," Plumer continued. "I mean we're guard heavy. We do have a big player inside but I think we're going to be a running team. We just got to play. There's talent there. It's going to take them a month or two to get them up to speed. But they can play."
NORTH CAROLINE
Head Coach: AJ Jackson.

title: Federalsburg unveils sign to recognize historic 2023 election, people who made it possible
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Federalsburg unveils sign to recognize historic 2023 election, people who made it possible

 November 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 744
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — The Rev. Jeffrey Butler, a Federalsburg resident, remembers when Brooklyn Avenue went from being a dirt road to a paved one in the late 1970s. He also remembers the more than 40 years it took for the town to get that road repaved."It was so bad," he said. "I mean, just tearing cars up. And we went to the town to complain. They still didn't do nothing."
"Finally, along with this lawsuit, came them also fixing this road up after 40 years," Butler said.
Since a lawsuit led to the election of the town's first two Black council members last year, the road — which is situated in a historically Black area in town — has been repaved.
On Saturday, with the newly paved Brooklyn Avenue in view, Federalsburg Mayor Kim Abner and the Federalsburg Town Council unveiled a new sign that commemorates the town's historic election and the new election system that made it possible.
The sign recognizes the individuals and groups who helped make it possible for Black Councilwomen Darlene Pitt Hammond and Brandy James to be elected to the Town Council in September 2023.
A MARKER OF PROGRESSAfter the unveiling, Hammond looked at the sign, tears forming in her eyes.
"It's a lot," she said, taking a pause, "to think that this small little town was able to stand for the rights of all people, not some people."
Hammond, who was a plaintiff in the lawsuit against the town, said the progress that has been made in the town is "heartwarming" and "breathtaking."
"It's a dream come true for me and for others that (came) before me, that we have established that everybody should be represented no matter what the color of your skin is," she said.
Although Black residents now make up nearly half of the town's population, the town had never had a minority representative on the council in its 200-year history. In June 2023 — through charter amendments, legislation and federal court rulings — the town's at-large election system was changed to a two-district system to ensure more representation of Federalsburg's Black residents.
In April, a $260,000 settlement was reached in the lawsuit filed against the town by the Caroline County branch of the NAACP, the Caucus of African American Leaders and Federalsburg residents regarding its discriminatory election system.
The settlement included a sweeping array of measures aimed at providing reconciliation after the town's previous election system was determined to have prevented Black residents from electing their chosen representatives. This includes the town apologizing to those who brought on the lawsuit, affixing a plaque to its town hall building, proclaiming Sept. 26 as Voting Rights Day and erecting the historical marker in the town's Black community.
Hammond said this sign unveiling and the first annual Voting Rights Day celebration, which was held in September, point to "a new era" in Federalsburg.
"It is a new era where everybody has a voice and everybody will be heard," she said.
After years of Butler speaking out about the need for Brooklyn Avenue to be repaved, Hammond said the new council was able to get the project done in about a year.
Before the sign was unveiled, Mayor Kim Abner said she and the council are excited about the direction that Federalsburg is going in.
"We have great things to come," she said. "We are making great progress in the town, and we are super excited that you're all here to celebrate."
Butler said he is hopeful more positive changes are coming with the current council in place.
"It's coming," he said. "We know Rome wasn't built in a day, so it's coming."
Sherone Lewis, a Federalsburg native and first vice president for the Caroline County branch of the NAACP who was a plaintiff on the lawsuit, called it surreal to be celebrating the changes that have been made.
"But I must say, the struggle continues," she said. "We still have a lot of work to do for diversity, equity and inclusion. I know those are buzz words these days. But I do believe that because I want this for my children, my grandchildren."
Willie Woods, president of the Caroline County branch of the NAACP, said the new sign is something that will be seen and read for generations.
"I hate to talk about it from this standpoint, but in the future, we will be passed on and there will be other generations," she said. "And this signage will remind them of the stance that was taken and of the progress that Federalsburg has embraced as we are moving forward."

title: Unwelcome lecture from a neighbor
content:
Unwelcome lecture from a neighbor

 October 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 22 | Section: News

 Words 

 Read News Document

 DEAR HARRIETTE: I'm 28, and I live in a small apartment complex where everyone knows each other. My neighbor, a gentleman in his 50s, saw me smoking a cigarette the other day and decided to take it upon himself to lecture me on the dangers of smoking.Although I appreciated his concern, his lecture was unwelcome. I intend to quit smoking at some point, but I don't need my neighbor to intervene. I fear that the next time I bump into him, he will give me another lecture. What can I do to make him understand that his unsolicited advice is not helping? I'm a grown adult, and I don't need lectures. - Good IntentionsDEAR GOOD INTENTIONS: As you know, your neighbor expressed his concerns out of genuine care for you. Remember that when you speak to him. It is your right to do whatever you want with your life and your body. Provided that the cigarette smoke is not contaminating your neighbors' air, you should be able to smoke in peace.That said, it is likely that this man will either say something or scowl at you the next time he sees a cigarette in your hand. Can you say something?Yes, but be careful. You can thank him for his concern, but put up a guardrail. Tell him you know what you are doing. When you decide to quit, you will. Politely ask him to refrain from giving you advice on this topic in the future.Harriette Cole is a lifestylist andfounder of Dream Leapers, an initiative to help people access and activate their dreams. title: Caps fill void, acquire Thompson
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Caps fill void, acquire Thompson

 June 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: News 
 
 751
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Tampa Bay Lightning and Washington Capitals were active Saturday during rounds 2-7 of the NHL draft, each making multiple moves to shake up their rosters for next season and beyond.Tampa Bay sent two-time Stanley Cup-winning defenseman Mikhail Sergachev to Utah and depth forward Tanner Jeannot to Los Angeles in moves that cleared more than $11 million in salary cap space. That could be enough money to keep captain and face of the franchise Steven Stamkos or make a significant free agent signing, and it will go a long way to providing room to lock up cornerstone defenseman Victor Hedman with a long-term contract extension.
The Lightning got younger on the blue line by receiving 24-year-old defenseman J.J. Moser, along with forward prospect Conor Geekie and two draft picks for Sergachev, who was signed through 2031 making $8.5 million annually. A 2025 second-rounder and a fourth this year allows Tampa Bay to restock its prospect pool after making eight consecutive playoff appearances, winning two titles and reaching the final three times.
That contending window remains wide open, and general manage Julien BriseBois now has flexibility to retool on the fly with free agency opening Monday. Stamkos staying is a possibility, and now the Lightning have the opportunity to pursue one or more of the top wingers available, a group that includes Jake Guentzel, Patrick Kane and Jonathan Marchessault.
The Capitals already did their big-name hunting last week by acquiring highly paid center Pierre-Luc Dubois from the Kings for goaltender Darcy Kuemper. On Saturday, they filled that void in net by acquiring Logan Thompson from host Vegas for a pair of third-round picks.
Thompson figures to split time with Charlie Lindgren in a tandem costing less than $2 million total next season, with a year left on each goalie's contract. Thompson, 27, was an All-Star and played 37 games for the Golden Knights during their 2022-23 championship run before getting injured before the playoffs.
"I got a lot more that I can prove in this league and I'm hoping that I get that opportunity with Washington," said Thompson, who was in bed when he was informed of the trade and hurried to the Sphere for a previously scheduled autograph signing. "Actually, it was a good alarm clock. I woke up to that and then obviously get ready and come down, and I knew it was going to be an interesting day."
Long before getting his name engraved on the Stanley Cup, Thompson got his first foray into the NHL Capitals development camp in the summer of 2018. He played for Washington at back-to-back prospect showcases, went to training camp with the American Hockey League's Hershey Bears in 2019, starred for the ECHL's South Carolina and earned his first contract as a result.
"I'm thankful for the Washington goalie department every day," Thompson told The Associated Press at 2023 All-Star Weekend. "They're the reason why I'm here. They're the only team that gave me a chance three years ago. If it wasn't for them, I wouldn't be here today."
Washington also traded fourth-line winger Beck Malenstyn to Buffalo for the 43rd pick, taking U.S.-born defenseman Cole Hutson, and traded up in the third round to select Ilya Protas, the younger brother of Capitals forward Aliaksei Protas. Malenstyn, 26, is a restricted free agent with arbitration rights who had 21 points in 81 games during his first full NHL season and gives the Sabres Buffalo valuable forward depth as they try to end the league's longest playoff drought.
Looking to end the longest Stanley Cup drought, the Toronto Maple Leafs took a step toward upgrading their defense by acquiring the rights to pending free agent Chris Tanev from Dallas for a 2026 seventh-round pick. The trade gives Toronto the first crack at signing the valuable 24-year-old top-four defenseman.
Vegas moved quickly to replenish goalie depth by acquiring Akira Schmid from New Jersey along with young forward Alexander Holtz in a trade that sent Paul Cotter and a third-rounder to the Devils. Among the other moves, St. Louis traded Kevin Hayes and a '25 second-rounder to Pittsburgh for future considerations to shed the remainder of the his contract, and Boston sent Jakob Lauko to Minnesota for Vinni Lettieri in a swap of centers that also involved draft picks.
The Sabres after getting Malenstyn began the process of buying out the contract of forward Jeff Skinner, GM Kevyn Adams confirmed at the conclusion of the draft. The buyout saves Buffalo $7.5 million next season while spreading out money owed to Skinner against the cap through 2030.

title: CWDI responds to Cambridge commissioners' lawsuit
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
CWDI responds to Cambridge commissioners' lawsuit

 May 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 865
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Cambridge Waterfront Development Inc. Executive Director Matt Leonard sees the lawsuit filed earlier this month against CWDI by the Commissioners of Cambridge as a threat to the progress of the Cambridge Harbor project."We had no choice but to respond," Leonard said in a press release May 14. "The city's lawsuit has its facts wrong and threatens the significant progress CWDI is making on behalf of the community to finally realize the 30-year vision for Cambridge's waterfront."
On May 14, CWDI and CWDI Holdings filed a response to the lawsuit filed against them and Yacht Maintenance Company in Dorchester County Circuit Court on May 1.
The lawsuit, which was amended May 3, alleges CWDI is in violation of a transfer agreement it entered into with the city in June 2021. It seeks $75,000 in damages and requests temporary, preliminary and permanent injunctions stopping defendants from transferring any portion of the property in violation of the covenants of the 2021 transfer agreement.
According to court documents, CWDI's May 14 response to the suit argues that the city's complaint "is the product of the well-publicized frustrations of the recently departed city manager," Tom Carroll. The response alleges Carroll has "sought to undermine CWDI" for the past eight months.
CWDI's response replies to the commissioners' claims about the property transfer agreement and the right of CWDI Holdings to be in possession of the property.
In the lawsuit filed May 1, the commissioners mention Section 6E of the transfer agreement, which states, "no portion of the property may be transferred unless the proposed use of the subject parcel(s) is 'shovel ready' (with permits, financing and groundbreaking within 90-days of closing)..."
The May 1 suit also mentions Exhibit C of the agreement that "CWDI will not transfer, subdivide or encumber all or any portion of the property" until reaching a definitive agreement with a developer or developers. That developer must come from a developer request for proposal process, which is outlined in the transfer agreement.
The commissioners argue in the May 1 lawsuit that CWDI violated this in March 2022 by transferring city-donated property to CWDI Holdings, a limited liability company.
CWDI states in its response that the city and CWDI agreed to CWDI creating CWDI Holdings to hold title to property named in the property transfer agreement. CWDI also states this was agreed to in a 2022 amendment to a 2014 state transfer agreement.
In response to city allegations that CWDI has not gone through the request for proposal process to choose a developer, CWDI alleges in court documents that Exhibit C of the transfer agreement gives leeway to seek a master developer or combination of individual project developers for all or parts of the Cambridge Harbor project. CWDI states it issued a request for proposals, called "Request for Expressions of Interest for Redevelopment," on July 15 and issued a press release Nov. 22 summarizing proposals it had received.
In its response, CWDI discusses its plans to sell a piece of property from the 2021 transfer agreement to Yacht Maintenance. In the court document, CWDI states that it has been transparent with its intentions regarding Yacht Maintenance. It says CWDI would "routinely" update the city on the status of negotiations to convey the property to Yacht Maintenance.
CWDI's response states that the lot line revision needed for the sale of the property had been finalized and executed by both parties and delivered to Cambridge's Planning and Zoning Department on April 29.
"CWDI cannot conceive of any legitimate explanation why, more than two weeks later, the document has not yet been signed and recorded," the court document says.
The press release — sent out the same day as the response was filed — states CWDI is tasked with developing the waterfront using a "community-first approach consistent with the community's long-term vision. It says the realization of that vision is threatened by the city's actions.
The press release says the city eliminated "baseless claims" that CWDI illegally transferred property from its amended lawsuit on May 3.
"Someone advising the city commissioners must have finally read all the transfer documents, and not just the one the city used in their original filing," CWDI Board President Angie Hengst said. "So they pulled that claim in their amended filing."
The press release also states that the amended lawsuit does not contain language asserting there could not be an imminent hotel deal.
The lawsuit filed May 1 mentions CWDI's "imminent" agreement with a boutique hotel developer, which Hengst said was nearing signing at a CWDI Board of Directors meeting March 20. The lawsuit states it is "highly unlikely" that the deal is imminent because "any established hotelier would conduct significant due diligence," which includes inquiring the city about various aspects of the project. The lawsuit says the city has not received any inquiries.
"Whoever advised the city commissioners that there was no way CWDI could have a hotel deal ready to sign clearly has no idea how property development works or community development or economic development," Leonard said in the press release.
Hengst said that with CWDI's response to the lawsuit filed May 14, the board hopes the city commissioners have all of the facts to withdraw the lawsuit "and return to a more collaborative path with us and the other partners."

title: Cambridge woman pleads guilty to altering evidence in Sidetracked Saloon shooting
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge woman pleads guilty to altering evidence in Sidetracked Saloon shooting

 May 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Crime 
 
 370
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A Cambridge woman was handed a three-year sentence after pleading guilty to altering physical evidence in the shooting death of 23-year-old Antonio Smith.Judge Broughton Earnest handed down the sentence following a plea hearing on May 22. Chadnee Harris, 33, will serve 236 days followed by one year of probation, with the remainder of the sentence suspended.
Harris originally faced charges of of acting as an accessory after the fact of first- and second-degree murder and acting as an accessory after a felony for the same incident. The charges were amended to one count of altering physical evidence.
The charge stems from a shooting in the parking lot of Sidetracked Saloon in Easton on Sept. 30. Officers who responded to the incident just before 2 a.m. found Smith in the parking lot suffering from a gunshot wound to the head. Smith was transported to the University of Maryland Shore Medical Center at Easton, where he was pronounced dead.
On May 20, Kevron Chase, 35, of Cambridge, pled guilty to first-degree murder for Smith's death. A sentencing hearing for Chase is set for July 19.
According to previous Star Democrat reporting, in charging documents, police said the bar's security camera footage showed Chase and Harris standing between two cars near the entrance of the bar and Smith approaching the two.
According to the documents, Chase pulled a handgun from his waistband area and pointed it at Smith. Chase put the handgun back toward his waistband area and then appeared to hand the gun to Harris, police said.
After a fight broke out, Harris reportedly walked toward the men. A crowd that had gathered quickly dispersed. According to the charging documents, Smith appeared to duck behind a car and Chase walked toward Smith, pointing a handgun at him. The officer who reviewed the footage wrote in charging documents that they saw a muzzle flash from the gun and Smith collapse in between two cars.
At Chase's plea hearing on May 20, Talbot County State's Attorney Joseph Coale said Chase then left the scene and drove to Cambridge, where he disposed of the handgun in the Choptank River.
Chase and Harris were later found during a traffic stop on Race Street in Cambridge. They were both detained by police.

title: Moore says budget will balance, protect school funding
author: KIERSTEN HACKER Capital News Service
content:
Moore says budget will balance, protect school funding

 January 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KIERSTEN HACKER Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 930
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Gov. Wes Moore unveiled a budget proposal on Wednesday that would balance the books and protect the state's ambitious reform plan for Maryland public schools, without raising taxes in the fiscal year that begins in July.The $63.1 billion plan would balance the books where officials had projected a shortfall, in part by returning some programs to spending levels closer to those of the pre-pandemic era. The plan proposes leveraging state debt and dipping into rainy day funds.
The Blueprint for Maryland's Future, the state's sweeping education plan of 2021, will be fully funded, state budget officials said Wednesday. Moore, a Democrat, said his administration crafted the budget plan in partnership with lawmakers, community leaders and other "village elders."
"We wanted to make sure that this proposed budget had everyone's fingerprints on it," Moore said in his public announcement of the new plan. "Because this budget is not just a reflection of an administration. This budget is a reflection of our shared aspiration."
Those aspirations will now go to the Maryland General Assembly for debate. Lawmakers have set a target of early April for passing a budget, and the state Constitution requires that it be balanced.
But the joint Republican Caucus will look closely at where funding transfers in the proposed budget are coming from, House Minority Leader Jason Buckel, R-Allegany, told Capital News Service.
While he said he is pleased that the Moore administration kept total spending similar to that of years past, he expressed concerns about the possibility of fees for certain businesses or tax hikes down the road. Buckel said he'll keep worrying about that possibility until the legislature adjourns.
"All in all, it's a mixed bag, I think, and we'll look forward to working with the governor and working with the Democratic leadership here to try to make the budget as good as possible," Buckel said.
Senate Minority Leader Stephen Hershey suggested he worries about the possibility of fee increases down the road.
"While it is a relief that the governor's budget spends less than last year and does not raise taxes, the number of fee increases proposed by his administration through legislation and the regulatory process is concerning," said Hershey, a Republican representing Kent, Cecil, Queen Anne's and Caroline, in an email release. He and other Republicans contend fee hikes are coming through the administrative pipeline.
"Taxes aren't the only way to raise revenue," Hershey said, "and state government should not be in the business of nickel and diming Maryland's families and small businesses."
The only fee increases currently in the budget plan are in the Department of the Environment, and those would generate roughly $3.5 million in revenue, according to a spokesman for the governor's office.
Working together to approve a balanced budget had been shaping up as no easy task. The state's spending had been projected to outpace revenues starting in the coming fiscal year, according to a recent report from the Department of Legislative Services.
But Moore has now proposed a plan that would instead balance the 2025 budget, saying it is a step in the right direction toward addressing the state's structural deficit in the years beyond that.
His budget flips the expected cash shortfall of $1.1 billion to a positive cash balance of $103 million in fiscal 2025, according to Helene Grady, Maryland's secretary of budget and management.
Moore said his budget prioritizes public safety, affordable housing, child care, education and public service. It also raises pay for state employees.
"We know that budgets, they're moral documents," Moore said. "Where we choose to invest actually defines our values. And it dictates the course of our future."
State budget officials said they avoided wide-ranging cuts across the board, hiring freezes or salary freezes. Rather, state agency heads went through an intense process and found areas to trim, and several agency budgets will be lower this year than they were the year before.
Moore said he proposed a record $127 million for local police agencies, citing the importance of supporting law enforcement and getting "more boots on the ground" to solve crimes and keep repeat offenders off the streets. Other investments would go toward the prevention of gun violence and support for crime victims.
While addressing public safety, Moore acknowledged the debates about juvenile justice likely to come during the legislative session, announcing an increase in funding to the Department of Juvenile Services. He didn't specifically discuss any cuts made to juvenile services programs.
Affordable housing and child care would receive significant funding under the proposal. Those are two areas Moore claimed are the biggest strains on Maryland residents. Access to housing and child care allow for increased participation in the workforce as Maryland tries to grow its economy, he argued.
"Access to child care doesn't just affect your child and your family," Moore said. "It changes the trajectory of our state's fiscal health."
Options for job training in innovative industries and public service were a priority. Through Moore's budget, the state is on track to increase the number of Service Year Option and Maryland Corps participants to 500, as required by law.
The Blueprint for Maryland's Future will be fully funded in the coming fiscal year, budget officials said, but its money problems are far from resolved. Prior to the beginning of the legislative session, the Department of Legislative Services report projected the state would exhaust the Blueprint balance in fiscal 2027.
"It's not inaccurate to say, 'Hey, we funded the Blueprint, or at least the state's portion of the Blueprint, for today,'" Buckel said. "But I also think it's completely honest to say the blueprint looming large over the next four or five years, blows billion-dollar holes into our state budget."

title: Candy hearts and other Valentine's treats
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Candy hearts and other Valentine's treats

 February 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1552
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The big day is here, and the traditions of flowers and chocolates still holds their spots as number one favorites for all ages.My favorite Valentine's Day memories are of the elementary school parties — the cute cards and little candy hearts. The girls would gather and compare the message candies from the boys.
What fun that was. Then came high school, and the stakes were higher. The cute juvenile cards turned into single rose buds and candy.
No matter how you celebrate this special day — with or without candy — just tell that special person (or persons) "happy Valentine's Day."
HEART SHAPED PIZZA
1 pound store-bought pizza dough, 1 tbsp olive oil (plus more for brushing), 16 slices pepperoni, All-purpose flour (for dusting), 1/2 cup prepared pizza sauce, 1 cup shredded low-moisture mozzarella. Put the pizza dough in a medium bowl and coat well with the olive oil. Cover with plastic wrap and allow to sit at room temperature for 1 hour. Meanwhile, put a large inverted baking sheet on the lowest oven rack and preheat the oven to 500 degrees. Fold a pepperoni slice in half and use a pair of kitchen shears to trim the edges into the shape of half of a heart. When you unfold the pepperoni slice, it will be a whole heart. Repeat this process with the remaining pepperoni, then set aside.
Divide the pizza dough into 2 balls. On a lightly floured surface, stretch 1 ball of dough into a 10-inch round. Transfer the dough to a piece of parchment paper, then slide the parchment and dough onto a second inverted baking sheet. Use a pair of kitchen shears or a paring knife to cut the pizza dough into the shape of a large heart, discarding the dough scraps. Spread half of the sauce on the dough in a thin layer and scatter half of the mozzarella on top. Top with half of the pepperoni slices. Use a pastry brush to brush the exposed edges of the dough with olive oil. Carefully slide the parchment onto the preheated baking sheet and bake until the crust is golden brown and the cheese is bubbling, 6 to 8 minutes. Let cool for 1 to 2 minutes before slicing. Repeat to make a second pizza.
SURF AND TURF
1/4 cup chopped fresh parsley, 2 tbsps chopped fresh chives, 2 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil, Kosher salt and freshly ground pepper, 6 jumbo shrimp (peeled and deveined, tails intact), 2 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil, juice of 1/2 lemon, 2 tsps chopped fresh thyme (plus 2 to 3 sprigs), freshly ground pepper, 6 slices pancetta (about 2 ounces), 1 10-ounce piece beef tenderloin (trimmed), sea salt, 8 asparagus spears, 1 tbsp unsalted butter. Pulse the parsley, chives and olive oil in a mini food processor until smooth. Thin with water, if necessary, and add 1/4 tsp each salt and pepper. Transfer to a small bowl, cover and set aside. (This can be done up to 2 hours ahead.)
Toss the shrimp, olive oil, lemon juice, chopped thyme and pepper to taste in a bowl. Wrap each shrimp with a piece of pancetta. Preheat the broiler. Arrange the shrimp on a foil-lined broiler pan. Season the beef with sea salt and pepper, press the thyme sprigs into the meat and set aside. Snap off the tough ends of the asparagus. Put the asparagus in a microwave-safe dish with 1/4 cup water and a pinch of sea salt. Heat a medium ovenproof skillet over high heat and add the butter. When the foam subsides, sear the beef until golden brown, about 3 minutes per side. Using tongs, hold the meat and brown the sides. Transfer the skillet to the broiler and cook until a thermometer inserted into the beef registers 125 degrees for medium rare, about 4 more minutes. Transfer to a cutting board to rest while you cook the shrimp. Broil the shrimp until the pancetta is crisp, about 2 minutes per side. Meanwhile, microwave the asparagus until tender, about 2 minutes. Slice the beef into 4 pieces. Serve with the shrimp, herb oil and asparagus.
CLASSIC SPAGHETTI AND MEATBALLS
1 pound spaghetti, 1 pound ground beef, 1/3 cup breadcrumbs, 1/4 cup finely chopped parsley, 1/4 cup freshly grated parmesan (plus more for serving), 1 large egg, 2 garlic cloves (minced), Kosher salt, 1/2 tsp. red pepper flakes, 2 tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 1/2 cup onion (finely chopped), 1 (28-oz.) can crushed tomatoes, 1 bay leaf, freshly ground black pepper.
In a large pot of salted boiling water, cook pasta until al dente. Drain. In a large bowl, combine beef with breadcrumbs, parsley, parmesan, egg, garlic, 1 tsp salt and red pepper flakes. Mix until just combined, then form into 16 balls. In a large pot over medium heat, heat oil. Add meatballs and cook, turning occasionally, until browned on all sides, about 10 minutes. Transfer meatballs to a plate. Add onion to pot and cook until soft, 5 minutes. Add crushed tomatoes and bay leaf. Season with salt and pepper and bring to a simmer. Return meatballs to pot and cover. Simmer until the sauce has thickened, 8 to 10 minutes. Serve pasta with a healthy scoop of meatballs and sauce.
VALENTINES DAY SUGAR COOKIES
2 1/2 cups all-purpose flour (plus more for dusting), 1/2 tsp baking powder, 1/2 tsp kosher salt, 1 1/2 sticks unsalted butter (at room temperature), 3/4 cup granulated sugar, 1 tsp pure vanilla extract, 1 large egg. For Icing: 3 cups confectioners' sugar, 1/4 cup plus 2 tbsps milk, 1 1/2 tsps pure vanilla extract, red gel food coloring, pink gel food coloring, sprinkles (optional). Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Line two baking sheets with parchment paper.
For the cookies: Combine the flour, baking powder and salt in a medium bowl and set aside. In a stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment, beat the butter, sugar and vanilla on medium-high speed until light and fluffy, about 3 minutes. Add the egg and mix until fully incorporated, about 1 minute. Reduce the speed to low, add the flour mixture and mix until well combined, scraping down sides of the bowl with a rubber spatula as needed, about 2 minutes.
Divide the dough into 2 equal pieces. Working with 1 piece at a time, roll the dough on a lightly floured piece of parchment paper until it's about 1/8-inch thick. Using heart-shaped cookie cutters, cut the dough and place the cookies on the prepared baking sheets about 1 inch apart (a small off-set spatula is really helpful when transferring the cookies). After both pieces of dough have been rolled out and cut, combine the dough scraps and re-roll and cut to utilize as much of the dough as possible. Bake until the cookies are just barely golden around the edges, rotating halfway through, 12 to 14 minutes. Transfer the cookies to wire racks to cool completely.
For the icing: Whisk the confectioners' sugar, milk and vanilla in a medium bowl until smooth. The consistency should be similar to that of slightly thinned yogurt and should coat the back of a spoon. Adjust with additional confectioners' sugar or milk, if needed. Place 2 tbsps of icing into each of 2 small bowls. Add 4 drops of red gel food coloring to one bowl and 2 drops of pink gel food coloring to the other and stir until fully incorporated. Using a small spoon, drizzle a small amount of each color over the white icing and then repeatedly drag a toothpick through the icing until you create a marbled effect.
Working with one cooled cookie at a time, carefully dip it face-side down into the icing and allow any excess to drip off before placing the cooking back on the cooling rack. Add additional red and pink icing to the bigger bowl of icing as needed to maintain the marbling effect.
HOMEMADE CANDY HEARTS
1 1/4-ounce packet unflavored gelatin powder, 1 tbsp light corn syrup, 1/2 tsp vanilla extract, 1/8 tsp salt, 2 1-pound boxes confectioners' sugar (plus more for kneading), assorted food coloring (for tinting), assorted extracts (such as peppermint, strawberry or almond) for flavoring, cooking spray. Whisk the gelatin, corn syrup, vanilla, salt and 1/2 cup boiling water in a stand mixer bowl until the gelatin dissolves. Using the paddle attachment, beat in the confectioners' sugar on medium-low speed, 1 cup at a time, to make a stiff, sticky dough.
Transfer the dough to a clean surface and knead, adding more confectioners' sugar as needed (up to 1 cup), until the dough is smooth, pliable and slightly tacky, about 5 minutes. Divide the dough into 4 pieces. Flatten 1 piece into a disk. (Cover the rest with plastic wrap.) Add a few drops each of food coloring and extract to the center of the dough; fold in the sides and pinch closed, then knead until the color is distributed.
Lightly coat a large piece of parchment paper with cooking spray. Roll out the colored dough on the parchment until 1/8 to 1/4 inch thick. Cut into hearts using 1-inch cookie cutters; transfer to a parchment-lined baking sheet. Repeat with the remaining dough, using different colors and extracts. Let the hearts sit at room temperature, uncovered, until dry and hard, about 24 hours, flipping them halfway through. Write messages on the hearts using food decorating pens. Store in an airtight container for up to 1 week.

title: Easton Town Council passes cannabis ordinance
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Easton Town Council passes cannabis ordinance

 April 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 532
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Nearly two months since opening a public hearing on the topic, the Easton Town Council has passed an ordinance revising the Town Code to regulate zoning for cannabis-related uses.At its meeting Monday, the council voted to pass Ordinance 809 with amendments.
The amended ordinance permits the use of dispensaries through special exception in the central business commercial zoning district and the general commercial district. It also permits, through special exception, cannabis growing and processing facilities in the industrial zoning district and the business commercial zoning district.
On-site cannabis consumption establishments are prohibited in all of Easton's zoning districts under the ordinance.
The passing of the ordinance comes about nine months after the state's approval of various recreational cannabis uses took effect. In November, the council passed a six-month moratorium on businesses looking to produce or sell cannabis within the town limits, which expires May 9.
"If we don't vote today, we must at the next meeting in order to be handled before our moratorium expires," Council President Frank Gunsallus said at the meeting Monday.
The council waited to vote on the topic while the General Assembly discussed the topic in Annapolis. At the council meeting April 1, Easton Town Planner Lynn Thomas said the Maryland Senate had passed a bill that is different from the House of Delegates. He said said that, considering the General Assembly would be adjourning, the town should have the information it needs to vote at April 15's Town Council meeting.
At the meeting Monday, Easton Director of Planning and Zoning Miguel Salinas said that House Bill 805, which deals with cannabis restrictions, had gone through the Senate and House of Delegates and is now awaiting Gov. Wes Moore's signature.
Salinas listed the amendments to Easton's ordinance, including a separation requirement of a half mile between dispensaries. Salinas said that is in House Bill 805.
Salinas said other amendments to the ordinance include the addition of parking standards for dispensaries and the addition of a requirement that a professional engineer or equivalent qualified professional certify that that the proposed odor measures established effectively eliminate outdoor odors.
Before voting on the ordinance, Ward 2 Council Member Don Abbatiello asked that they change the ordinance to permit cannabis growing and processing facilities in the industrial zoning district through special exception, rather than just permitting it.
"There's one industrial area in particular that is off of Dover Road that backs right up to an entire neighborhood," Abbatiello said. "I'm sure that those individuals would at least like the opportunity to share their concerns or joy that a growing facility is going in that area."
Abbatiello said this change would not prohibit growing and processing facilities from the industrial zoning district, it would just give residents "an extra opportunity" to voice their thoughts.
Gunsallus made a motion at the meeting to approve the ordinance with the amendments from the town and the amendment requested by Abbatiello, which passed.
At the end of the meeting, Abbatiello thanked Thomas, Salinas and Town Attorney Sharon VanEmburgh for their work on the ordinance.
"This has been a long process," he said. "It's been a difficult process. And I really do appreciate all their effort to give us the best information so that we can make a decision."

title: Caroline’s in Denton making strides in new owners tenure
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Caroline’s in Denton making strides in new owners tenure

 July 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline 
 
 512
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Caroline's in Denton has been open for just about nine months under new owners and in that time has seen increased following on social media and increase revenues.Owner and Executive Chef Ken Zellers and his wife, Robin Zellers, have ideas to take Caroline's in Denton to the next level. They will be putting a permanent food truck at a new brewery in Denton called Eden Town Brewing Company.
"We purchased the food trailer out back, so we're going to be doing the food at the brewery, putting the trailer over there, next step of expansion," Zellers said.
This next step in expansion brings hopes for Caroline's in Denton to keep growing.
"That's a scary part of getting in the restaurant industry," Zellers said. "You never know how the community is going to take to you, how they're going to like your food, your drinks and what you're doing, but it seems to be working out pretty well."
Zeller took over ownership from previous owner Nancy Minahan, Zeller interviewed multiple times for the chef position at Caroline's in Denton but was never granted the opportunity, until Minahan called him about buying the restaurant.
Zeller started working at a restaurant at just 14 years old and began cooking at 16 years old and running a kitchen at 18 years old. He is an award-winning chef in Anna Arundel County including best chef of the year just last year.
One thing Zellers has done since taking ownership of Caroline's in Denton is tweaking the menu away from fine dinning to more affordable menu with high quality ingredients.
Zellers keeps the high quality ingredients by serving fresh farm to table items on the menu, fresh farm items that come from Caroline County and other counties across the Mid-Shore.
"Ingredients is always the No. 1 thing," Zellers said.
Starting with a good ingredient is important, he said, plus it supports the local economy and the community, not to mention local farms.
"I think that's the biggest thing like just the quality of the ingredient. You just put that on the plate and let it shine, and you don't have to do much to it," Zellers said. "I think it's a big part of why people have taken to our food so so much because we really can't mess it up because the flavor's there."
The Zellers have added an enclosure onto the porch for extra seating for the winter and summer days. Next to the restaurant is Caroline's side bar which features outside and inside seating with a different menu than Caroline's in Denton. Zellers called the outdoor seating "beautiful."
With plans of more expansion, Zellers says the love and growth Caroline's in Denton has seen still hasn't hit home for him yet.
"This is always going to be the baby, we're always going to make sure this is taken care of, but it's just like I said, I don't think it's hit me," Zellers said. "I could have never imagined especially a restaurant that's this beautiful that I would be the owner of it, but I fell in love with when I first interviewed with Nancy."
