title: How much growth is too much for Easton? Balance between housing needs, infrastructure unsettled
author: Konner Metz
content:
How much growth is too much for Easton? Balance between housing needs, infrastructure unsettled

 August 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 1988
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The predicament on the minds of many Easton residents and leaders continues to be just how much the town can afford to grow.Easton is under a period of significant residential growth with multiple large-scale housing projects under construction. In 2000, the town's population was 11,708, according to census data. Ten years later, it rose to 15,945, and since, it's grown at a slower pace to 17,101 in 2020.
The boom has raised a litany of concerns, from increased traffic to a change in the town's small-town complexion.
Some residents, and a few officials, think Easton should press the brake pedal. But local real estate agents contend that a halt to growth could box out lower- and middle-class buyers and renters.
Martha Witte Suss, an associate broker for Coldwell Banker Realty and Easton resident, said the housing market has been in a crunch since the pandemic. She said there's not enough reasonably priced homes or rentals to satisfy employees who commute from outside Talbot County.
"We have plenty of housing that they can't afford," Suss said. Residential growth, if it focuses on affordability, could cure that dry spell, she added.
Michael Ports, vice chair of the Easton Planning Commission, poses the town's conundrum like this: "What are the housing needs of the people currently, and can we achieve that in a way that doesn't compromise everyone's needs for services?"
It's a question town leaders are taking on, even if there's no easy answer.
This fall, 136 apartments on Elliott Road will begin opening. Two large communities are under construction east of Route 50, combining for over 450 projected single-family homes. Near Easton's downtown, a developer plans to transform two former Perdue AgriBusiness sites into housing projects, totaling 144 units.
In all, roughly 1,127 units are recently finished, under construction or approved by the town's public bodies, according to information from town planners and developers of the 17 listed projects.
The pipeline of projects has yielded varying opinions from town leaders. Some don't want any new large housing projects approved in the next few years. Others prefer a case-by-case approach.
Mayor Megan Cook said the right answer is "probably somewhere in between." The town should focus on the current projects but not be too quick to disregard new ones, she said.
The mayor said growth is a charged topic and especially complicated due to affordable housing needs. No solution is a "silver bullet," Cook and others have repeatedly said.
"It is a balancing act," Town Council President Don Abbatiello said. "There would have to be a project come along that would fit that need, that workforce housing, that affordable housing piece."
In interviews with The Star Democrat, Easton officials weighed in on the town's current list of housing developments. When asked about infrastructure, the most recognized concerns included roads, fire and police services and schools.
They offered thoughts on where the town should focus its residential growth. Most leaned toward building from the inside-out. Planning Commission Chairperson Phil Toussaint is of that opinion. He hopes the sprawling, single-family developments are coming to an end.
"We wouldn't really want to support any development on the outskirts at all," Toussaint said.
And broadly, the 1,127-unit mark can be misleading since some units aren't under construction and may not be for years, Toussaint and others said.
"(People) think they're gonna appear tomorrow," Toussaint said. "They're not."
Single-family home neighborhoods typically take years to build out, such as Easton Village off of St. Michaels Road, a project of around 250 homes first approved in 2003 and just now reaching completion. So far, the 200-home Gannon Range and 252-home Four Seasons projects only have 18 and 11 building permits, respectively, according to Easton planning and zoning director Miguel Salinas.
"It's a daunting number. It's hard to hear," said Cook, who as mayor doesn't have a vote on housing applications. "But at the same time, you look at some of the examples as a community, the neighborhoods that we've had. They're built out over 20 years."
THE PIPELINE
Since town planners prepared a list of Easton housing projects this winter, chatter of "the pipeline" has been frequent at Town Council and Planning Commission meetings. Those two bodies are responsible for approving most of the projects.
The commission is made up of volunteer members and often can only make a recommendation to the council, whose members are elected. But sometimes, the commission holds final say, such as when it approved the 116-apartment Easton Crossing complex on Brookletts Avenue this year.
The five members of the council and six members of the commission offer a range of opinions when it comes to the town's growth.
Town Council Ward 3 representative David Montgomery provided perhaps the most rigid perspective.
"I want to stop for at least five years before we add anything more to this backlog," Montgomery said. "I want to see how fast it actually grows, it's actually built out."
Others were less firm on completely stopping growth, though all council members interviewed for this story said, at the very least, the town needs to be mindful. Some prefer a project-by-project approach, such as Abbatiello, who said future housing proposals need to be the "right fit" for Easton.
"I think right now, there's enough in the pipeline for us to say, 'Let's see how the projects impact the town's resources before we go adding a lot more to that list,'" Abbatiello said.
Planning Commission members have mixed thoughts, too.
Ports, the commission's vice chair, said Easton is "missing a good bit" even with the current project inventory. He said the missing units largely fall between expensive single-family homes and for-rent apartments — a sphere urban planners call "the missing middle."
"The reality is that the median sale price of a home right now is almost twice what a family of four making the absolute average income here in Easton can afford," Ports said. According to Maryland Realtors, the July 2025 median sales price in Talbot County was $545,000, the third highest in the state.
Tom Klein was the commission's lone vote against the Easton Crossing project, citing traffic and parking concerns. He said the need for more affordable housing is clear. But Klein would prefer to have a target number. At times, it feels like Easton is "chasing something" it doesn't know, he said.
"How many more do we need? Do we just keep assuming we keep needing more?" Klein asked. "That, to me, is something I don't really know the answer to. I think it would be helpful to know that so we don't just blindly build."
'MORE AND MORE CROWDED'
Town planners and engineers have processes to gauge the impacts residential projects will have on the town, such as traffic and environmental studies or reviews by the town's nonprofit utility, sewer and water company, Easton Utilities.
Even with project-specific studies, many town leaders believe traffic is a top-of-list concern, along with other infrastructure matters.
Montgomery said town staff should be "much more skeptical about the traffic impact studies" submitted alongside housing proposals. Ward 4 representative the Rev. Elmer Davis said the traffic issue is obvious to the human eye.
"I don't need a traffic study to tell me that the traffic in Easton, periodically, is a problem at best," Davis said.
Handling traffic backups is a tricky matter, Cook said, since some roads are state-run, others are under county purview and many downtown are maintained by town engineers and public works employees.
Off of Route 328, or Matthewstown Road, 136 apartments are opening soon, while 200 single-family homes will be built just down the road. It's an area residents have flagged during council and state transportation meetings.
"(Route) 328 is going to become busier and busier, and folks, I fear, are going to have more and more challenges getting out to (Route) 50," said Councilmember Robert Rankin, who represents residents in the Route 328 area.
A State Highway Administration planning and environmental study is underway to assess pedestrian and traffic needs on the busy state road that funnels onto Ocean Gateway. Previously proposed concepts by the state include adding left-turn lanes on Matthewstown Road and adding a second through lane on Goldsborough Road as drivers cross Route 50.
Traffic has consistently been brought up as a reason to lean away from annexing land for residential growth outside of Easton's core. Nearly all commission and council members interviewed for this story said they prefer to keep growth within the area encircled by Route 50 and Easton Parkway (322).
The Planning Commission has especially expressed that preference during workshops updating the town's comprehensive plan, which lays out the town's vision for handling growth in the next decade.
In July, the commission rejected the Fox Chase Estates, a 365-unit, mixed-use development proposed near a warehouse and industrial park north of Easton Airport and near the under-construction Shore Regional Health hospital. Town Council members maintain final voting power on the project, though it's unclear when or if it will come before them.
The Planning Commission voted unanimously to recommend against the development, citing a lack of connectivity as a main reason. The vote lines up with the commission's recent direction as they draft the new comprehensive plan: build from the inside-out.
"We'd rather see infill," Klein said. "We want to see connected neighborhoods."
That line of thinking, shared by many Town Council members, still leaves Easton with infrastructure challenges, such as downtown streets, utilities and safety. The latter was emphasized by Cook and council members as a chief priority.
Funding for the Easton Police Department and Easton Volunteer Fire Department makes up around 40% of the town's general fund budget. Abbatiello, who volunteers for the fire company, wants to hold off a massive increase in the cost for fire services by maintaining the department's volunteer status for "as (long) as possible."
"The biggest tax increase residents of Easton are ever going to see is if the Town of Easton needs to go to a paid (fire) department," Abbatiello said.
Easton Utilities evaluates water demands annually. According to a statement from Doug Abbott, director of engineering and water/wastewater departments, the utility is using 60% of its water and wastewater capabilities, leaving 40% "to accommodate future growth."
And as for downtown traffic, some town leaders are worried infill will do more harm than good.
"Our streets are becoming more and more crowded, and I am concerned the more that we have infill development, the harder it is to maneuver around this town," Ward 1 Councilmember Maureen Curry said at a comprehensive plan workshop Aug. 25.
"I just don't accept that assumption," Toussaint, the commission chair, later said. He argued that concentrating growth downtown will take cars off town streets and improve walkability.
Overall, the Aug. 25 meeting yielded a key takeaway: the new comprehensive plan is likely to include a preferred annual population growth rate around 1.75%. Planners initially proposed not to mark an annual growth rate in the plan, a change from the 2010 version, which stamped the rate at 1%.
Town Planner Lynn Thomas said at the meeting that without a growth rate, the plan would use historic projections to determine if the town should consider adopting policies to remedy growth trends either "significantly lower or significantly higher" than expected.
But Town Council members said a rate should be clearly stated to keep the town honest.
"I do think it would be helpful to have at least something to point toward," Rankin said. The Planning Commission will adjust the drafted plan later this fall, likely reinstating an annual growth rate, before hosting a public hearing.
The town's Affordable Housing Board and Attainable Housing Task Force are other bodies taking cracks at addressing the housing-growth debate. The task force is currently producing a list of recommended housing policies for the Town Council to consider.
Cook acknowledged that while town boards and discussions are great, "actionable items" — such as the comprehensive plan and policies — are on the way and will bring true benefits to residents. But nevertheless, she's happy Easton is addressing its growth problem head-on.
"No one else around here is having these conversations, but the Town of Easton is," Cook said. "They're difficult conversations. They're polarizing conversations, they're very emotional conversations. But we're having them."

title: Removal of Safe Space stickers draws criticism
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com
content:
Removal of Safe Space stickers draws criticism

 May 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 396
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Calvert County School Board member Melissa Goshorn's comment at the panel's April meeting proved to be prophetic."I recognize it's going to make a lot of people unhappy," Goshorn said just prior to requesting that Superintendent of Schools Andraé Townsel to remove "Safe Space" stickers from school buildings.
Goshorn based her request on anecdotal information she received at a National School Boards Association conference during what she described as a "bone-chilling session" presented by the Beau Biden Foundation.
The story relayed to session attendees dealt with a principal who was arrested on child sex abuse charges and may have gained children's confidence by having a "Safe Space" sticker on the office door.
The sticker is widely used as a sign that LGBTQ students will not be discriminated in that space.
"I think we need to have them removed," Goshorn said.
School maintenance staff removed the stickers and the predicted unhappiness manifested itself during the board's May 8 meeting when 19 of the 20 speakers addressed the issue during the public comment segment. While a handful of the speakers indicated support for the sticker removal, many expressed opposition.
Sheri Tardio of Prince Frederick called the issue "manufactured outrage. Safe space stickers do not promote ideology. Diversity is a fact."
"You are not hiding your biases very well," said Stacy Tayman, president of the Calvert Association for Educational Support Staff.
"Removing stickers is not a violation of First Amendment rights," said school board President Jana Post in her closing comments, adding that the April discussion "was twisted" into an LGBTQ issue.
"Real safety comes from a culture of trust," Post said.
At the conclusion of public comments, board member Paul Harrison made a motion to discuss "a flag policy" at a future meeting. That policy would likely be aimed at setting parameters for displays of flags, posters and decals in school buildings. The motion passed unanimously.
Supervisor's post
The school board unanimously approved the appointment of Marc Watson as supervisor of health, physical education and athletics. The Indiana University of Pennsylvania graduate is a familiar face in Calvert County where he has previously served as a teacher, coach and principal.
Most recently, Watson served as principal of King George High School in Virginia.
Watson told the board he was looking forward to "continuing to create this wonderful environment of learning and athletics" in Calvert County.
In recommending Watson for the appointment, Townsel said the returning administrator will provide "training and mentorship for coaches."

title: Delaware city evaluating ‘Pallet Village’ for homeless people
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
Delaware city evaluating ‘Pallet Village’ for homeless people

 July 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 976
 Words 

 Read News Document

 City officials in Newark, Delaware are in the early stages of evaluating whether a transitional housing village of small cabins could be a solution to local homelessness.Council members John Suchanec and Corinth Ford visited such a village in Georgetown, Delaware and suggested that a similar idea could be implemented here.
"We truly felt the experience was transformative," Suchanec said. "The approach that Georgetown has taken is starting to shape up to be a model for how you would deal with homeless sheltering."
Georgetown's Pallet Village was built in 2023 by the nonprofit Springboard Delaware. It consists of 40 small one-bedroom cabins, as well as shared bathhouses. It's become known as the Pallet Village because the cabins are produced by a company called Pallet.
"Our goal is to get unsheltered people out of the woods, get the help they need and move on to permanent housing or some form of self-independence," said Judson Malone, executive director of Springboard Delaware.
Malone said there are many reasons that people stay in the woods rather than go into traditional homeless shelters. Maybe they don't feel safe in a group shelter, they can't be with their partner, they can't bring their pet or they can't bring all their possessions.
"The most impactful thing you will do for them immediately is a lockable door with heat and air conditioning in a secure community, and that's exactly what we provided," Malone said. "Within two weeks, you'll see a difference in their demeanor simply because of the trauma that they experienced in the woods."
The Pallet Village does not require residents to be sober.
"We do not allow substance use on site, but best practices have shown that when people are in a safe space where they're accepted as they are, they can then begin to process the other issues in their life, including deciding whether or not to get treatment," Malone said. "We have a very high success rate of people voluntarily choosing to go to treatment."
Within a week of opening, the Georgetown shelter was 100 percent occupied and has remained so.
"People see a value in being there," Malone said. "They want to be there, and they want to get help and support."
Springboard Delaware works with 30 different support organizations to provide medical, mental heath, banking, employment and other services to people living at the Pallet Village.
"While people are unsheltered and in the woods, they almost never want those services," Malone said. "They really don't care about getting clean or sober, because getting high is how they survive a traumatic life."
The average length of stay is approximately three months, and then many residents of the Pallet Village move on to more permanent housing.
The Pallet Village cost approximately $1.5 million to build, money that came from the American Rescue Plan Act. Ongoing funds for operation has been harder to come by, however. Last year, Springboard Delaware had to lay off staff when a grant fell through and leaders were scrambling to piece together state money and private grants to keep the village open, according to reporting from Spotlight Delaware.
Malone said he is still working with the state to develop sustainable longterm funding.
Springboard Delaware has another $1.4 million in ARPA money to build a second Pallet Village somewhere else in the state.
"We've got the money in hand to do it," Malone said. "We just need a location."
If a Pallet Village were built in Newark, it would not require funding from the city, Malone said.
Ultimately, Springboard Delaware envisions building five to seven Pallet Villages around the state by the end of the decade.
"We have a vision, and we believe that homelessness is solvable," Malone said. "This is not the whole solution, but it's a huge part of it."
During a city council meeting last month, several council members expressed skepticism.
"Obviously, we all want to be compassionate, we all want to be empathetic, and we all want to help solve this problem," Mayor Travis McDermott said. "But we have realistic hurdles that we would have to overcome, and even with our best intentions, we can't escape it."
One big question, he said, is where would a Pallet Village be located.
"People are not going to want you to use the land behind their house to build this," McDermott said. "That's just a simple fact."
Councilman Jay Bancroft expressed similar thoughts.
"I hope we'll be very sensitive to local opposition that is likely to be an issue," Bancroft said. "I think this idea of making it look suitable to the neighbors is important for this education campaign, for us to take steps that we've been talking about for a long time"
Councilman Jason Lawhorn noted that the Georgetown Pallet Village was built near where there was already a large established homeless encampment. He said it's important to understand the scale of homelessness in Newark to better understand whether a Pallet Village would be utilized here.
He added that city staffers are already overworked and questioned whether the city should have a role in creating a Pallet Village.
"I love the program," he said. "I have reservations about how we execute it in Newark."
Suchanec asked his colleagues to direct City Manager Tom Coleman to prepare a report on whether there are any city-owned properties that could potentially be used for a Pallet Village. He suggested looking at underutilized parks as well as a piece of land the city recently purchased off Paper Mill Road, between the city's electric substation and White Clay Creek.
Ultimately, the council decided that in order to not burden city employees, each council member will compile of list of possible locations in their district for further study.
"You can find so many reasons to say no for something," Suchanec said. "The easy thing is to say no or to convince yourself this is something not worth doing. All I'm saying is take a baby step. Find out if we have any locations in this city where something like this could happen."

 Maryland small business owners will get help with legal, accounting and financial services under a new $10 million grant from the federal government, officials announced last week.The Treasury Department is awarding the money this fall as part of the American Small Business Opportunity Program.
The award came as good news to Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, who used to run his own small business helping underserved students navigate college.

The money is meant to fuel local growth and provide innovative resources to disadvantaged start up businesses in the state, according to a Treasury press release.
This federal funding will go to the Maryland Technology Development Corporation, an independent instrument of the state that provides funding, insight, resources and connections to early stage companies.
"There are three 'T's' that every entrepreneur faces: they face a challenge of time, a challenge of talent, and a challenge of treasure," said Troy A. LeMaile-Stovall, CEO of TEDCO.
The program, he said, will "give them access to talent that they need to grow and scale their enterprises."

title: Preston man sentenced to 15 years for stabbing
author: Natalie Jones
content:
Preston man sentenced to 15 years for stabbing

 February 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Natalie Jones | Section: Crime 
 
 415
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — A Preston man was sentenced Thursday to 15 years in prison for the February 2022 stabbing of a then 25-year-old woman.Agreeing with a recommendation from the prosecution, Caroline County Circuit Judge Heather Price handed Mark William Thompkins a 30-year sentence with all but 15 years suspended. He will receive credit for 714 days, or nearly two years, already served, according to court records.
Thompkins, 26, pleaded guilty last October to one count of attempted second-degree murder.
Price also referred Thompkins to the Patuxent Institution, a treatment-oriented, maximum security correctional facility.
"I believe that it was an appropriate sentence," said Caroline County State's Attorney Sloane Franklin, who prosecuted the case. "Unfortunately, the mental health system is broken and failed both the victim and Mr. Thompkins."
Thompkins' defense attorney, Jesse Hicks, could not be reached for comment.
Thursday's sentence comes nearly two years after the young woman was stabbed near Holly Park Drive and Gilpin Point Road in Preston shortly before 3 p.m. on Feb. 17, 2022.
During the Oct. 30 plea hearing, Franklin said trash collection workers near the scene first saw the woman sitting in the driver's seat of her vehicle with a man, later identified as Thompkins, seated behind her.
Thompkins began striking the woman with his fists, then brandished a knife to stab her neck.
The woman ran from her vehicle and collapsed in the front yard of a nearby house. Thompkins cradled her while holding the knife to his own throat, Franklin said.
A witness attempted to help the victim, but Thompkins threatened them, pointing the knife at them and yelling for them to get back.
Multiple law enforcement agencies, including the Caroline County Sheriff's Office, Maryland State Police and Maryland Natural Resources Police, responded to the stabbing.
Franklin said Thompkins punctured his own neck with a knife while running to the woods to evade officers.
After 15 minutes and the use of multiple non-lethal methods, including a taser, a state trooper was able to knock the knife out of Thompkins' hand to detain him, police said.
Both Thompkins and the woman were flown to the University of Maryland Shock Trauma Center in Baltimore for treatment of their injuries.
After his arrest, a judge found Thompkins incompetent to stand trial in April 2022. He was committed to the Maryland Department of Health until August 2023, then transferred back to a local detention center upon being found competent, according to court filings.
Following his release, Thompkins will be placed on five years of supervised probation. He will also be required to complete mental health treatment.

title: Cambridge nursing facility faces complaints about care
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Cambridge nursing facility faces complaints about care

 May 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 1614
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — When Dorchester County native Danny Frazier lived at Mallard Bay Nursing and Rehab in Cambridge, he loved having visitors.From high school buddies to family members, Frazier — who moved into Mallard Bay in his mid-60s after receiving an ALS diagnosis — treasured those visits, his sister Debbie Linthicum said.
Those visits were among the only reasons Frazier stayed at Mallard Bay from June 2023 until his death in May 2024.
"We talked a few times about moving him to another facility because we were so dissatisfied," Linthicum said. "And his biggest concern was, he said, 'I really love when people come to see me, and I'm afraid if I'm in Easton, it's a little bit of a further drive, they may not come.'"
Linthicum said when Frazier lived at Mallard Bay, he experienced inadequate care from staff, particularly when it came to food. She said when Frazier was no longer able to feed himself, there were instances when staff would bring his food but not feed it to him.
They are not alone in their experience with Mallard Bay.
From a lack of care for residents to staffing problems, residents, their family members and former staff members say they have tried to advocate for the residents of Mallard Bay but have not seen change. On top of that, it has been 2½ years since the last federal inspection of the facility, and the state agency responsible for overseeing nursing homes faces a lawsuit alleging it has failed to inspect nursing facilities and allowed complaints against facilities to pile up.
Former Mallard Bay geriatric nursing assistant Deanna States-Meninger said she spoke with Dorchester County State's Attorney Amanda Leonard about the facility and filed a complaint against the facility with the Maryland Office of Health Care Quality.
States-Meninger said that when she worked at Mallard Bay, management wouldn't do anything in response to her complaints.
"I would go down the chain, and it seemed like it just got pushed off," she said.
In an April interview with The Star Democrat, Del. Tom Hutchinson (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) confirmed Mallard Bay had been reported to the state. He said the Office of Health Care Quality, which is within the Maryland Department of Health, was looking into the complaint.
Key Health, which manages Mallard Bay, originally agreed to an interview and was sent a list of questions from The Star Democrat. However, the company later canceled the interview and sent a statement sharing its goals.
"Since Key Health began managing the facility in November 2022, we've worked hard to build a warm, supportive environment where residents feel valued and staff feel proud," the statement said. "... Like in any healthcare setting, we may occasionally hear concerns, but we always take them seriously. However, the voices of those with positive experiences — of recovery, comfort, and dignity are vast."
The statement said Key Health remains "fully transparent with regulators," accountable to its standards and committed to "every person who calls Mallard Bay home."
According to the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, reviews for Mallard Bay are middling.
STEPHEN'S STORY
After a swimming accident this past summer left Stephen Nowlan, 54, paralyzed from the torso down, he spent three months in Mallard Bay's rehabilitation program.
Although he was excited to go there after hearing about "how incredible it was," he said it ended up being nothing like he expected.
Nowlan said there were not enough staff for the number of residents, and he would often wait a long time to receive help or care.
On his first day at the facility, Nowlan spent a long time waiting for his medication in pain. He said when he finally received his medication, the staff member who brought it didn't administer it.
"She put my pills on my table," he said. "But I can't move. … She put them on the table and left."
Nowlan said that when he shared his concerns with the higher-ups at Mallard Bay, they gave him "all kinds of excuses."
"I mean there's no excuse," Nowlan said.
Although Nowlan said he had good physical therapists and a few good aides, he often found himself waiting for care or simply not getting enough of it.
Nowlan said there were occasions when he spent physical therapy sessions getting a shower from the physical therapists because the care staff hadn't given him a shower.
He left Mallard Bay in December after three months because his insurance stopped covering his stay.
About eight months after his accident, Nowlan said he is able to move again but is considered quadriplegic because he has altered sensation in every part of his body. He attends physical therapy three times a week and expects to walk again one day.
BRITTANY'S STORY
Brittany Fletcher's father Michael Prager, 76, has lived at Mallard Bay since September.
Fletcher said her father had brain surgery for normal pressure hydrocephalus in early April and his doctors asked him to go on the Mediterranean diet for his brain health. According to the Cleveland Clinic, the Mediterranean diet "emphasizes plant-based foods and healthy fats."
That is not what Prager is being served at Mallard Bay, Fletcher said.
"They are giving him sugar drinks and cake, and the meals are very starchy," she said.
Fletcher said her father is learning to walk again. She said Mallard Bay left him alone in the shower, even though he is a fall risk.
And Fletcher said she has not had a great experience when it comes to communicating her concerns to Mallard Bay and its management.
Fletcher said she has thought about moving her father to a different nursing home, but funds are limited, which makes that harder to do.
"And I'm assuming anywhere is better than this at this point," she said. "But I don't know."
DEANNA'S STORY
Deanna States-Meninger said that after six weeks working as a geriatric nursing assistant at Mallard Bay early this year, she quit her job.
States-Meninger said she made the decision due to a culture of neglect and lack of care, consistent understaffing, overworking and unresponsive management.
According to the Code of Maryland Regulations, the ratio of nursing service personnel on duty providing care to residents of a nursing home may not be less than one to 15. States-Meninger said there was one night when she was left to care for an entire floor of 45 patients by herself for four hours.
"It made me feel like I was a failure," she said, "like I couldn't answer all the bells and help the people when they needed it."
According to the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, the nursing staff turnover in a given year at Mallard Bay averages 71.2% compared to the 41.6% state average and the 47.5% national average.
States-Meninger called her job at Mallard Bay an "awful" one.
"I can't tell you how many nights I left in tears," she said.
DEFICIENCIES FOUND
According to the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, Mallard Bay has an overall three-star rating, scoring "above average" (four stars) for health inspections, "much below average" (one star) for staffing and "below average" (two stars) for quality measures.
Concerns with the 160-bed facility pre-date Key Health taking over in November 2022.
In August 2022, seven deficiencies were found during a federal inspection, including failure to report incidents of alleged abuse to law enforcement, failure to serve meals as requested by residents and failure to provide treatment or services to prevent or heal pressure ulcers.
In an email April 30, Maryland Department of Health Director of Communications Chase Cook confirmed the 2022 federal inspection report is the most recent inspection report. This means there have not been any federal inspections since Key Health took over management.
In Maryland, the Office of Health Care Quality within the state's Department of Health is responsible for the oversight of nursing homes, which includes licensure, certification and investigation of complaints.
Last year, a lawsuit was filed against the Maryland Department of Health alleging the department has allowed more than 100 nursing facilities to go without an annual inspection for more than four years and allowed thousands of un-investigated complaints against nursing facilities to pile up.
According to the class action complaint, the plaintiffs argue that when the department fails to complete its oversight responsibilities, "dangerously poor-quality care within nursing facilities goes undetected and uncorrected."
The Department of Health has not responded to questions from The Star Democrat about Mallard Bay, the department's process for addressing complaints against nursing homes and how it ensures nursing homes in Maryland are safe for its residents.
In 2018, the Maryland General Assembly passed the Maryland Nursing Home Resident Protection Act to ensure complaints are addressed in a timely manner.
Specifically, the bill requires the Maryland Department of Health conduct a full inspection of each licensed nursing home in the state at least once a year and initiate investigations into complaints alleging actual harm within 10 business days of receiving the complaint.
The bill states the department shall receive 50 new full-time positions within the Office of Health Care Quality over a five-year period. These hirings were supposed to begin in fiscal year 2020, months before the COVID-19 pandemic shut down the country.
Sen. Stephen Hershey (R-Kent, Queen Anne's, Cecil, and Caroline), who was a sponsor of the 2018 bill, said in an email that this is an issue he still has concerns about. He mentioned a bill passed by the Maryland Senate this year — which he also sponsored — that requires the Department of Health to report inspection data to General Assembly committees.
"We've been extremely concerned with the lack of responsiveness from the Department of Health's efforts to ensure residents and families that nursing homes can provide safe, high-quality care," he said.
Hershey said consistent oversight is important when it comes to determining whether nursing facilities are providing high-quality care.
"Regulatory agencies must work collaboratively to ensure bad actors cannot operate unchecked and that residents receive safe, quality care," he said.

title: Towns need to balance pride in past with future
author: BRANDON WRIGHT
content:
Towns need to balance pride in past with future

 May 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BRANDON WRIGHT | Section: Columns 
 
 805
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Recently, I listened to a webinar about the challenges of planning, land use and economic development in rural areas. Communities frequently struggle to grow and still maintain their character. Balancing economic growth with the community's heritage is among the most significant challenges for elected officials because the two are often intertwined.An industry of consultants has grown up to help communities meet these challenges. Like the consultants, I believe a balance can be reached.
Maybe I am too much of an optimist, but I think opposing groups can find common ground if they are honest and transparent. I served as chief of staff in the Maryland Department of Planning nearly 10 years ago. I met with town council members, county commissioners and local business leaders, all vested in making their communities strong and vibrant. My confidence comes from listening to their hopes, dreams and goals for their communities.
I met with the consultants, too. Everyone wanted the same for the community — the absolute best.
Compromises that are in the best interests of all the various constituencies and stakeholders can be forged, even in rural Maryland like the Eastern Shore. There is no place like it. Its ecosystems and economies are different, even from other rural parts of the state. So much of the economy is dependent on the Chesapeake Bay and the rivers that feed into it. It is teeming with myriad species of animals on land and sea.
The motto of Federalsburg, my hometown in Caroline County, is "Pride in the Past, Faith in the Future." Unfortunately in towns like Federalsburg, more emphasis is placed on the past than the future. Local officials, sometimes pressured by citizens, have these gauzy memories of a better time and place in the community's past and yearn to get back to it.
However, in doing so, they strip decision-makers of any chance at finding the right balance between the past and future, choking off opportunities to attract large employers, employees and all the businesses that spring up to support them both.
As a young boy, I fished for bass and perch on the Marshyhope Creek, the northwest fork of the Nanticoke River. I heard the story that the DuPont Company was looking to build its new nylon factory in the area, and the Marshyhope Creek made Federalsburg an attractive site. Unfortunately, DuPont built its nylon plant on the Nanticoke River in Seaford, Delaware, less than 10 miles from Federalsburg. The plant was constructed outside the town, and Seaford quickly became a company town. The contrast between the two towns is dramatic.
Federalsburg missed out again, this time on AquaCon. An international salmon farming operation would have brought several hundred well-paying jobs, jobs with health care and all the other benefits that help smooth the rough edges of life. AquaCon would have increased revenue to the town, support for existing small businesses and all the different services that make a small town tick.
Town officials, under pressure from citizens, said no to this opportunity. Rather than work with the company to better understand the project and address concerns, the town leaders said no and now another community will benefit from these jobs and the economic development that comes with it.
According to state data, Caroline County is among the most economically depressed counties in Maryland. We can't lay all the blame at the feet of elected leaders for that. I know many of them, and each one cares deeply for the communities they serve; otherwise, they wouldn't do it. The blame, however, should be shared with the voters that elected them and the voters who pushed the elected leaders to say no to investments in the towns that would spur economic growth over fears of the unknown and fears of something different, a break from the past.
Because the citizens share the blame, they are responsible for turning their communities around.
Our rural communities are blessed with resources that other towns and cities envy. We have kind, friendly people who care for each other. We have the greatest renewable resource of all — an unending stream of smart and talented young men and women graduating from our high schools and colleges, prepared to make the world a better place. Let's do everything we can to keep them here.
Let our legacy be that we found that balance that everyone strives for and leave the next generation and the generations that follow a community poised for growth, good jobs and continued access to outstanding education. Let's be sure we live up to the motto, "Pride in the Past, Faith in the Future."
Brandon Wright grew up in Federalsburg and graduated from Colonel Richardson High School in 1997 and Salisbury University in 2001. He was the chief of staff at the Maryland Department of Planning from 2015 to 2017. He now lives in Annapolis, but his family still resides just outside of Federalsburg.

NEW HEIGHTS

 March 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports

 Words 

 Read News Document

 As March Madness is set to tip off, three of the most recognizable names in college basketball are in the women's tournament: Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers.Clark drew record crowds and ratings all season long. Reese has LSU in contention for a second straight national championship. Bueckers is finally healthy and doing things on the court for UConn reminiscent of her freshman season when she was the AP Player of the Year.
Throw in a few stellar freshmen like JuJu Watkins and Hannah Hidalgo and the game is reaching heights it's never seen.
"One thousand percent we've seen a shift in just the perception of women's college basketball in general," USC coach Lindsay Gottlieb said. "It doesn't have to be at the detriment of men's college basketball. The increased coverage and star power these players have; they are legitimate, popcorn-worthy type of players."
For countless seasons, the buzz around the NCAA tournaments have often been on the men's game. The one-and-done stars, the juggernaut blueblood programs, the buzzer beaters and athleticism all getting more attention. The women's game has pretty much all of that too, and the ratings and attendance this season suggest casual fans are fully engaged with a game that boasts star power and an increasingly high level of play.
It helps that the women's players stick around for three, four or even five years without the chance to leave early for the pros so fans get to know them and watch them grow. Three years ago, Clark said she thought women's players should be allowed to turn pro after their freshman year, like the men can.
Instead, she stuck around and had a record-setting year that grabbed the nation's attention.
"It's really, really evident that there's stars out there in this game," UConn coach Geno Auriemma said. "Whereas before I think they were there, but nobody wanted to acknowledge it and appreciate it as much. ... They're just really good. Everybody is going around telling everybody how good they are. They're all visible."
ESPN said it just saw the most watched women's college basketball regular season in more than 15 years, with viewership up 37% on its platforms from last season. That doesn't really even include the Clark effect as Iowa's star wasn't on the network much this season. Iowa's ratings on Fox Sports were the highest in a generation.
ESPN plans to show all of Iowa's games, including a few on ABC, as far as the No. 1 seed advances in the tourney.
"It's not just UConn and Tennessee on TV," Auriemma said. "Those kids are on TV a lot. They're in the limelight a lot. They know how to handle it because they're used to it now."
Clark, who broke the NCAA all-time scoring record this season, has helped six different networks reach all-time viewership marks for women's basketball over the past year, starting with last season's NCAA championship game that drew nearly 10 million viewers.
"I kind of get to be in the spotlight and I get to change people's viewpoint of how they see women's basketball," Clark said before the season. "The amount of people that have come up to me and said, 'I've never watched women's basketball before before you and your team ... .' Some people could take that as a negative. But to me that's a positive. We're finally getting them to turn on the TV and watch it, but not only watch it once. They're coming back for more."
People aren't just watching, they are also coming to games too. All five of the power conferences had huge crowds for their tournaments. The SEC and Big Ten had their best attendance ever. The Pac-12, ACC and Big 12 weren't far behind.
"The big names continue to put up big numbers and people are watching and the media is paying attention," Bueckers said. "The tournament will be great and will continue the rise of women's basketball."
Fans who pack the arenas are also sticking around afterward, hoping to get a coveted autograph. The importance of the moment isn't lost on the game's stars. Clark, Reese, Bueckers, Watkins and many others spend time postgame signing and taking pictures with not only young girls, but boys, too.
"There were 400 people in the stands before she got here and now we're selling out," Gottlieb said of Watkins. "We've got NBA players who want to see her, WNBA players, musicians and actors too. Regular fans also, it's a diversified crowd. Little boys and girls who ask me if I know JuJu. Could they meet Juju? Grown men you run into in downtown LA."
Even when Clark leaves for the WNBA after the NCAA Tournament, the future of women's basketball is still strong with Bueckers, Watkins, Hidalgo and many other up-and-coming players.
"It's going to get even better. So many kids coming out of high school are just unbelievably good," Auriemma said.

title: With some rules, a civil discussion is possible
author: DAVID REEL
content:
With some rules, a civil discussion is possible

 October 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: DAVID REEL | Section: Columns 
 
 587
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Last week, my wife and I hosted a visit from a longtime friend who I met before starting elementary school and have known ever since.Before he arrived, we agreed that because we have different opinions on issues in the political arena, we should avoid any discussion on politics while he was here.
We knew there are increasing numbers of family members, friends and acquaintances who are not on speaking terms due to strongly held and diametrically opposing political positions.
Instead of discussing politics, our time together was filled with talking about a wide range of other matters.
We talked about where he and I grew up, the schools we attended and all the changes that have occurred there.
We also discussed the challenges and opportunities we experienced with raising a family and long-distance relocations made necessary by job changes.
We talked about other childhood friends who died too soon and those who have recently died or are experiencing serious health problems.
Before his visit ended, we decided with some trepidation to discuss politics.
We did so with five rules:
Listen respectively to other points of view, even if we disagree strongly with them.Embrace the idea that listening is more than waiting for your turn to talk.End every discussion on strongly held differences of opinion with "you may be right."Not all discussions are a debate with a winner and a loser.Disagree without being disagreeable.
Following our rules was not always easy.
It was always worthwhile and meaningful.
For example, we discovered that we shared common ground with deep concerns over the steadily decreasing levels of civil discourse in our society.
As a result, shortly before my friend left to return home, we discussed Robert Putnam's book "Bowling Alone: The Collapse and Revival of American Community."
Written 25 years ago, "Bowling Alone" is still relevant today.
The book's unusual title is based on Putnam's research showing the number of people who bowl alone had increased, but those who bowl in leagues had decreased.
He suggested that when people bowl alone, they do not have opportunities to participate in the social interaction and civic discussions that might occur in a bowling league environment.
Putnam also wrote about the measurable declines in membership and participation in religious organizations, labor unions, parent–teacher associations, military veterans' organizations, fraternal organizations and community service organizations.
Putnam did acknowledge that some organizations and issue advocacy groups had increased their membership rolls, but they rarely focus on fostering face-to-face interactions that build what Putnam called social capital. Instead, they focus instead on fund raising, collecting dues, marketing services, lobbying and sending periodic news updates to their members.
Putnam also drew a distinction between two different but equally important types of social capital.
One type is "bonding" which occurs within a homogenous demographic group.
The other type is "bridging" which unites people from different groups.
Putnam concluded a lack of social capital undermines the active civic engagement that a strong democracy requires from its citizens.
I now know my friend's visit was more than a get-together to talk over old times, catch up on current times and ponder on the future.
In all our discussions, including those with civil discourse on politics, we built social capital.
It was unexpected opportunity to think about and evaluate what I can be and should be doing to help address the lack of civil discourse and to help increase social capital in our society.
The answer is clear.
Going forward, I must consistently strive to:
Respectively consider all points of view.Listen with more than waiting for my turn to talk.Say regularly "you may be right."Limit discussions as debates.Disagree without being disagreeable.Always look for opportunities to build social capital.

 QUEEN ANNE's COUNTY - This past weekend saw the Wreaths Across America truck convoy headed to Arlington National Cemetery with thousands of Christmas wreaths.Stopping over night Thursday. Dec. 7, for the 14th consecutive year, they were again hosted by Kent Island American Legion Post 278, in Stevensville, under direction of Past Post Commander and the 2023 Maryland State Legionnaire of the Year Nikki Randolph.
Randolph has earned a reputation for her passionate care for all veterans, making sure veteran grave sites are bestowed with American flags and Christmas wreaths at appropriate times of the year, every year.
The yearly tradition began when she was then commander of Post 278 and contacted Morrill and Karen Worcester of Maine, who had already begun the Wreaths Across America program - hauling Christmas wreaths from their state to the nation's capitol to place those wreaths on all veteran's grave sites at Arlington National Cemetery.
Randolph and Legion 278 volunteers provided three meals, dinner, breakfast and boxed lunches to the convoy before they made the final leg of their journey to Arlington.
This year, the Wreaths Across America sent out over 3,000,000 Christmas wreaths across the nation to more than 4,200 locations to be placed on those grave sites. Most were placed on Saturday, Dec. 9.
Eleven wreaths were also presented to families connected to Post 278, whose veterans chose to be cremated rather than buried in a cemetery.
One of those was to the wife of the late George Dashiell, who served during World War II in Germany.
Mrs. Wally Dashiell, now 100-years-old has been a widow for the past 17 years. She said, "I'm truly grateful that the Legion honored George in this way." The wreath was placed next to the urn that holds his ashes, the American flag presented during his memorial service, and a picture of George.
Friday morning the convoy departed from Legion 278 along Route 8, children from both Matapeake Elementary and Middle Schools cheering and waving small American flags. An emotional scene, it was clear the children were excited to participate.
Saturday at noon, American Legion Jeff Davis Post 18 in Centreville, hosted their annual Wreaths Across America ceremony at Chesterfield Cemetery. Approximately 200 people were present, many of them children and teens with their parents.

title: Meet the bikers who try – and fail – each year to erode Maryland’s helmet law
author: SAPNA BANSIL Capital News Service
content:
Meet the bikers who try – and fail – each year to erode Maryland’s helmet law

 March 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SAPNA BANSIL Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 945
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A group of bikers in leather vests and wispy beards greets lawmakers here each Monday of the legislative session, hoping this is the year they'll succeed in their galvanizing cause: gutting a Maryland law that requires them to wear helmets.The group, which calls itself A Brotherhood Against Totalitarian Enactments, has experienced decades of setbacks on the helmet issue. Its vociferous critics say ABATE's position is at a minimum, eccentric and at worst, dangerous.
But driven by a burning belief in personal freedom and a joy for riding, ABATE has used persistent, grassroots activism to keep the helmet issue alive in Maryland. It's why in nearly every legislative session since the state's mandatory helmet law took effect in 1992, the Maryland General Assembly has at least considered a bill that would make wearing a helmet optional for most riders.
"It's been 32 years this year to no avail," Bob Spanburgh, Maryland ABATE's board chairman, said. "But we keep introducing it. We have some pretty ardent supporters. We have a lot of people who think we're nuts, probably."
Like many of its previous incarnations over the last three decades, this year's bill would make wearing a helmet optional if a motorcyclist is at least 21 years old, has been licensed for a minimum of two years and has completed a safety course. It is named in honor of Gary "Pappy" Boward, a former ABATE executive director and motorcycle rights advocate who died in 2020 of health issues.
ABATE and other supporters insist that they aren't opposed to riders wearing helmets if they so choose. But they feel the current mandate abridges freedom of choice and represents government overreach.
"I firmly believe that we as government do better when we educate people, [rather] than legislating something," said Sen. Mike McKay (R-Allegany, Garrett, Washington), the bill's primary Senate sponsor and a friend of Boward's. "There are people that would like to have the choice [to not wear a helmet.] And I tend to believe that we should give people the choice but 100% support educating them about it."
Established in 1974, ABATE will mark 50 years of advocacy for motorcyclists' rights this June. Its animating issue has been eroding Maryland's helmet law, different iterations of which have been in place since 1968. Today, Maryland joins 16 other states and the District of Columbia in requiring all riders to wear protective headgear.
Spanburgh, a 66-year-old retired carpenter, only casually followed politics when he joined ABATE in the mid-1980s. Initially, he saw the group as a community of like-minded individuals, who shared his enthusiasm for bikes, firearms, the outdoors and rock and roll. But right away, ABATE turned Spanburgh into an unlikely activist.
"At the first meeting I went to, the thing they told me [was,] 'You got to register to vote. It's very important in this organization,'" Spanburgh recalled. "That was actually the first time I ever registered to vote in my life. I was 27 at the time."
Each legislative session, the helmet bill faces cockeyed glances and prodigious odds. Contending with a wealth of scientific evidence, which shows crashes involving non-helmeted motorcyclists are much more likely to result in severe head trauma and death, the measure almost always dies in committee.
But ABATE ensures the issue is revived and relitigated, year after year, by finding ways to get in front of elected officials, despite limited financial resources and dwindling numbers. In the past, the group used a tactic involving following lawmakers into the bathroom to gain an audience and get its message heard.
"They're diehards for what they believe in," Del. Jay Jacobs (R-Caroline, Cecil, Kent, Queen Anne's) said. "Thank God they do. They don't let go of this stuff. It's a tough fight over here to get that kind of legislation passed."
While Republicans are the most likely to sympathize with ABATE's cause, the group engages lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. This year's bill, cross-filed as HB639 and SB503, has bipartisan sponsors in both chambers.
"I don't agree with them that they shouldn't wear a helmet, but I do agree about the civil liberty issue," said Sen. Jill Carter (D-Baltimore city), one of the bill's Senate co-sponsors.
"They are adamant as dedicated motorcyclists that this is not something they want mandated to them," she added.
In a recent hearing of the House Environment and Transportation Committee, opponents included highway safety groups, medical associations and public health officials. They argued that a weaker helmet law would increase motorcyclists' risk of injury and death, impose an avoidable burden on taxpayers and encumber the healthcare system.
"A lot of people might say, 'Well, it's my free will to do whatever I want to do, no matter how stupid it is,'" Gene Ransom, CEO of MedChi, the Maryland State Medical Society, said in an interview. "The problem is, when it comes to healthcare … your decision then ends up costing the entire system a whole lot of money.
"Not only is it the right thing to do and the smart thing to do — logical people wear helmets when they ride a motorcycle or a bike or other things — it also is appropriate from a common good and cost point of view," Ransom added.
The bill is scheduled for a hearing before the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee later this week. Spanburgh hopes to see the measure make it out of committee and get a vote on the House or Senate floor. If unsuccessful, proponents vow they won't stop trying.
"If I don't do it, who else is going to do it?" said Ken Eaton, Maryland ABATE's executive director. "We try to get other people to help us as much as possible. But if I don't do it, how can I convince other people to do it?"

title: Always plenty to be thankful for in Maryland
author: Staff Writer
content:
Always plenty to be thankful for in Maryland

 November 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editorials 
 
 740
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It should be easy for most of us to be thankful in Maryland. Thanksgiving has just about arrived, that special day for reflection, for sharing our gratitude and for enjoying a splendidly large meal with those we love.We've mostly been spared the political rancor that marked much of the election season nationwide. The local campaigning leading up to filling out our ballots earlier this fall was mostly crisp and clean.
So as we prepare ourselves for the Thanksgiving holiday, let's hope that peace and civility will prevail, at least for a day. Let's hope that when extended families convene for the old familiar feast, debate won't rage between red and blue, but about whether dark meat is more delicious than white meat as the turkey is carved.
Thanksgiving is a legacy of early colonial America, when European settlers thanked God for the harvest that allowed people to survive under difficult conditions. These days, of course, only a dwindling portion of our population here still has lives so closely tied to the harvest. Most of us take comfortable shelter and an adequate food supply for granted every day.
Did you know that we have a president, a secretary of state and the author of "Mary Had A Little Lamb" to thank for Thanksgiving becoming a fully recognized holiday in the United States?
Editor and writer Sarah Josepha Hale launched her campaign in 1827 to see the annual Thanksgiving tradition dating back a couple hundred years become an official holiday. She started with President John Quincy Adams — son of Founding Father John Adams — and finally found success many years later with President Abraham Lincoln in 1863. Secretary of State William Seward penned Lincoln's proclamation, which came in "the midst of a civil war of unequalled magnitude and severity."
"I do, therefore, invite my fellow-citizens in every part of the United States, and also those who are at sea and those who are sojourning in foreign lands, to set apart and observe the last Thursday of November next as a Day of Thanksgiving and Praise to our beneficent Father who dwelleth in the heavens," Lincoln's proclamation reads.
Well, 2024 has certainly been a year, but we still have so much to be thankful for, each and everyone of us.
In a way, we're all accidents of birth, and ongoing accidents of geography. We could be anywhere else in the world — and plenty of those places have more than enough misery to go around. Gratitude for our peace, safety and security here at home would be in order.
We should also be thankful for the people in our community who will be required to postpone their feasts to help others in need. We can take comfort in knowing that police and hospital staff will be on the job, and volunteer firefighters and other first responders could be pressed into service at any time if there's an emergency.
Then there are those thoughtful souls who make sure that anyone who wants to come out can enjoy an absolutely free hot Thanksgiving family-style meal and fellowship. Food banks, soup kitchens and churches around the region help make sure that happens.
For sure, this holiday season that officially kicks off next week and runs all the way through New Year's Day can stretch time, money and sometimes patience particularly thin. But let's face it, most of us have plenty for which to be thankful. And we should have little reason not to feel blessed and grateful on Thanksgiving and every day.
Our community is strong. And through the works large and small of all our friends and neighbors, we will only continue to get stronger. And for that, too, we offer our thanks.
Even in our nation's darkest times, Lincoln and Seward found much to be celebrated: "The year that is drawing toward its close has been filled with the blessings of fruitful fields and healthful skies. To these bounties, which are so constantly enjoyed that we are prone to forget the source from which they come, others have been added, which are of so extraordinary a nature that they cannot fail to penetrate and even soften the heart which is habitually insensible to the ever-watchful providence of Almighty God."
We can all take their words to heart as we head into the holiday season. We can look to the good. We can focus on the positive. We can find our way forward with thankfulness and love in our hearts.
We wish you all a happy Thanksgiving.

title: Letter had no good reasoning
author: Staff Writer
content:
Letter had no good reasoning

 January 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 397
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Sometimes you publish letters to the editor that contain strong political views that are based on false information or bad logic or both.When a political view is based on good reasoning, I don't feel the need to respond. But I do feel the need to respond when a writer gets published with no good reasoning. Such is the case with Mr. Adrian's letter "Gone down a dark road," in Sunday's 14 January edition.
His letter is filled with false statements. For example, he claims that Democrats control elections to push some kind of agenda. There is no evidence for that. Quite the contrary. Mr. Adrian somehow completely missed the well-known information that Republicans are involved in managing elections. There are hundreds, if not thousands, of examples.
Even the head Republican, Donald Trump, knew that when he called the Republicans who control elections asking them to alter votes in 2020. As another example, Mr. Adrian seems to claim that harvesting crops in the fall leads to harvesting ballots. I don't think there is any evidence for that.
But what really gets me is the use of questions for arguments. This illogical method of argument is a tool of conspiracy theorists and despots for thousands of years. "When did you stop beating your spouse?" is the classic retort to that entire form of reasoning.
Mr. Adrian received a document about mail-in ballots and points out he could print it. "What could possibly go wrong?" he writes as if that question is a legitimate argument against the entire process. Without evidence, the question makes no sense, any more than me asking Mr. Adrian when he stopped beating people. Mr. Adrian should read about how the Arizona Republican Party spent millions of tax dollars on a month's-long audit of ballots that only showed Mr. Biden's votes were undercounted. Georgia audited their elections three times by hand counting ballots and found no fraud. These are just two facts out of hundreds of examples that belie the assumption underlying Mr. Adrian's question.
Mr. Adrian poses many other questions that assume evidence where none exists. And he ends his letter with the question, "Which political party controls the Board of Elections anyway?" as if that is a reason for everyone to doubt elections. It is not.
All available evidence is that elections in Maryland are fair and honest. People should appreciate that and take the time to vote.
MICHAEL DAVIS
Easton

 If someone is buying or selling this Spring, they may have noticed a few new ways of doing things since the last time they went through this process, noted Michelle Abplanalp, president of Mid-Shore Board of Realtors.There are several real estate changes that went into effect in August related to showing homes and compensation.
For buyers, a written buyer agreement is now required. Buyers and their Realtors will need to reach an agreement regarding how the agent will be paid for their services and put it in writing before seeing a home. "However, don't get hung up on signing this agreement," Abplanalp said. "This agreement can be specific. It can be to see one specific home, it can be for one day or one week, whatever you negotiate."
Before signing this agreement, buyers should ensure it reflects the terms they have negotiated with their Realtor and that they understand exactly what services will be provided and how much these services will cost, the Board of Realtors said.
The buyer agreement must include four items:
A specific and clear disclosure of the amount or rate of compensation the agent will receive or how this amount will be determined must be stated.
The compensation rate must be objective and stated as an amount, a flat fee, a percentage, or an hourly rate. The compensation cannot be open-ended.
The agreement prohibits the Realtor from receiving compensation for services from any source that exceeds the amount or rate agreed to by the buyer.
The agreement must note that the Realtor fees and commissions are fully negotiable and not set by law.
These written agreements apply to both in-person and live virtual home tours but do not apply to open houses or inquiries about services. The home seller may agree to offer compensation to their Realtor, or the seller can offer to assist with closing costs or home inspections.
For home sellers, the offers of compensation (when a seller or a seller's agent shares compensation with a buyer's agent) cannot be shared on Multiple Listing Services. MLSs are local marketplaces used by both buyer and seller agents to share information about homes for sale. Offers of compensation are still an option but are now communicated off the MLS should a home seller choose to pay the buyer's agent fee.
Sellers may consider doing this as a way of marketing their home or making their listing more attractive to buyers.
Per Abplanalp, whether buying or selling, the Realtors compensation or fees remain fully negotiable and are not set by law. Realtors have agreed to abide by the Realtor Code of Ethics and to provide clear and transparent discussions with their clients about compensation.
"What's important to know is these practice changes provide consumers on both sides of a residential transaction with additional choice and transparency," Abplanalp said. "It helps to have this discussion upfront so there are no misunderstandings. I have found that my clients appreciate knowing what I will do for them, what services I provide, and at what cost."
The Mid-Shore Board of Realtors mission is to advocate for its members and the public to preserve the right to own, transfer and utilize real property. For more information, visit midshoreboardofrealtors.com.

title: Student seeks to share Choptank River history
author: NIAMBI DAVIS Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Student seeks to share Choptank River history

 May 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: NIAMBI DAVIS Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Local News 
 
 967
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Kennedy Thomason grew up as an avid reader of historical fiction.Now, after working towards a degree in history, Thomason is sharing her historical interests with countless others, thanks to her family's river cruise business.
The 2019 graduate of Ridgely's North Caroline High School carried her love of history to Chesapeake College, where she graduated with an associate's degree in liberal arts, followed by a transfer to Washington College in Chestertown to major in American studies.
"It's the liberal arts version of a history major," she explained, pointing to the Washington College website description as "the exploration of U.S. culture and American national identity from cross-disciplinary perspectives in order to help students develop a rich understanding of the American experience."
"I chose this major because I'm particularly interested in how our history influences the society in which we live," she said. "Understanding the human experiences that have led us to this point is vital to figuring out where we go from here. The study of history is the key to solving the labyrinth of social, economic and political problems we face today."
At the Starr Center for the American Experience, Thomason works as a digital archiving intern under the supervision of Melissa P. Kemp, the center's digital archivist and historian.
She scans, archives and uploads content into the Chesapeake Heartland archive, which features local African American families and their personal collections of family photos, home videos, yearbooks and other mementos they've collected over the years.
"I've learned a lot about digital history and its importance, as well as how tedious it can be," Thomason said.
For Thomason, the rewards of her Starr Center experience are many. "It's the confidence boost and sense of community that comes from association with professors and students who are just as passionate as I am. At school I feel a sense of belonging and I'm exposed to opportunities that I never knew were available," she said.
She considers the most challenging aspect of student life as striking a balance between college, work and life. "I am a unique undergraduate, especially for a Washington College student, because I have a two year old daughter. Most of the students around me at school still live at home or in dorms and are accustomed to only being responsible for themselves and their studies. Commuting from about an hour away, having a little person depending on me, a household to keep up with, and finding time to work has added many struggles that most of my peers do not have to navigate. But I wouldn't change it for the world!"
As the oldest of the Thomason family's five children, Kennedy counts her parents as inspiration.
"I remember watching my mother wrangle five children. I learned a lot from my mom and I admire her and look up to her. She and my dad supported all five of us doing five different things. We have always been a very tight-knit family unit with parents who have provided immense support. I could not do what I do without them. They keep my daughter (whose name is Sailor) when I need them to. Our family has always functioned as a unit working towards whatever goal we have, that day, that week, whenever."
When her family purchased Denton's Ellen B from Captain Bill Behlke, it was a given that the River City Cruise Company would be a family affair. Thomason immediately planned to add history as part of the river tours.
"I love the Choptank River," she said.
Aware of the deep historical roots she was certain that many Eastern Shore residents knew of the area's history and wanted to learn more.
"I'm a huge proponent of accessibility to history, which means I'm always trying to think of ways to bring history to the public rather than waiting for the public to seek it out," she said. "The river tours are just one aspect of my advocacy."
The first year of the River City Cruise Company was a great success. "I had the time of my life on each trip," Thomason recalled.
Her favorite guests were the people who came along for the ride but found themselves fascinated by the stories of the Choptank's history and heritage.
"I also loved seeing people from our community learn more about the land. Although I love and appreciate the out-of-towners that come and enjoy everything the Choptank has to offer, seeing locals being able to connect their lives with the past is truly special. One thing that I tell each cruise is there's no reason that people, states or oceans away should know more about our land than us."
This year, she's revamping the script and expanding the talking points to make each cruise truly unique. "I never want someone to feel that they came once and can't come again. I always want people to take away something new, even if they've taken the tour ten times."
Recently, Thomason was awarded funds to complete her own Choptank River History project from the Gerda Blumenthal Grant through Washington College's chapter of Phi Beta Kappa.
Over the summer she'll publish a series of blog posts in conjunction with the Caroline County Historical Society's website that will focus on ways the Choptank has shaped the greater Caroline County community.
"My motto for the project has been that people tend to think of rivers as borders, but, historically, the Choptank has been the center," Thomason said. "What exactly this project will look like I am still trying to work out, but I am excited about it. I plan on having at least one public event and my research will lead to a more robust history tour."
This fall Thomason will graduate from Washington College. She's still trying to figure out what she wants to do post-graduation. Whatever she chooses, the study of history will benefit.
