title: Stroke of pen loses 75 years of science leadership
author: LENA GILL
content:
Stroke of pen loses 75 years of science leadership

 June 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LENA GILL | Section: Columns 
 
 713
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The U.S. higher educational system may in future years lose $38 billion a year. This is the estimated annual contribution by foreign students. In the school year 2023-2024 it was estimated that 1.1 million foreign students were studying at universities across the U.S., and they generally pay full fare or do work/study. They supported about 378,000 academic jobs.Now we risk driving them away.
On April 19, CNN reported that thousands of international students across the country were informed by email that their student visas were revoked. Six days later the Trump administration decided to restore 1,400 student visas. How many students did not have their visas restored is unknown. We do know that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had a list of about 300 students that he planned to expel. The National Immigration Project is challenging the visa cancellations in court.
Apart from the money that these foreign students bring in, why would we care? Because foreign students began many of the successful startups in Silicon Valley. We care because much research in science done at our universities has brought the U.S. to a revered leadership position in the world in medical science research.
With a stroke of the president's pen this may all disappear. The best brains in the world will not want to come here anymore. Research in advanced cancer treatments, drugs to treat Alzheimer, sudden crib deaths as well as CRISPRs use in treating genetic blood disorders by cutting out a person's faulty DNA will not continue without federal support. The U.S. inventors of CRISPR won the Nobel Prize in chemistry in 2020. We will be taking a giant step backward in the sciences.
In the 20th century up to World War II, Germany won about 30% of the Nobel Prizes in science. The second runner-up was Great Britain with 20% of the Nobel Prizes in science. The U.S. was way down the list with only 6% of the Nobel Prizes in science.
What turned the tide was Adolf Hitler who drove many of the best German scientists, artists and architects (some of them Jewish) to U.S. universities in the 1930s, where they were welcomed. The second German brain drain happened immediately after the war when U.S. intelligence invited physicists like Wernher von Braun (inventor of the German rockets) to the U.S. to work for the space program. The U.S. emerged from the war economically, technologically and militarily better than the rest of the world.
What really propelled the U.S. into today's leadership position was the futuristic vision of what could come, if the U.S. government funded basic research at universities small and large around the country with a promise to keep the government's hands off. The academic freedom and competition created by this decision attracted the best brains from around the world.
Since 2000, the U.S. has won 72 Nobel Prizes in science, of which about 30% were won by immigrants. Great Britain won 16, Germany 7, France 5, Japan 9, Israel 5. Canada, Australia.and Norway won three each.
This rosy picture will change fast if the Trump administration continues to threaten leading universities with withdrawal of funds and academic freedom. Harvard University, which so far has not backed down, was threatened with cancellation of its not-for-profit designation. $2 billion in research grants were withdrawn by the administration. Foreign students' and researchers' visas are being revoked. 27% of the students are from abroad. Attacking an elite university may appeal to the MAGA base, but it is still difficult to understand why President Trump wants to destroy the foremost academic institution in the US!
The Trump administration also is threatening withdrawal of funds from our other world-renowned science research facilities, the National Institutes of Health and the National Science Foundation. A science publication asked its readers if they were affected by government harassment and withdrawal of funds. If so, were they considering moving their research elsewhere? 75% of the 1,600 who responded said they were considering it.
With a stroke of the president's pen, we have lost 75 years of leadership in the sciences.
California, Texas, Illinois, Massachusetts and New York will see the most economic impact. Maryland also will suffer, as we are home to Johns Hopkins Hospital, the site of original cancer research and treatment, and the University of Maryland Medical Center with its world-renowned Shock Trauma Center.

title: Evergreen Fresh - Cawley Tree Farm offers variety of fresh trees, greens
author: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com
content:
Evergreen Fresh - Cawley Tree Farm offers variety of fresh trees, greens

 November 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly; cconnolly@chespub.com | Page: 15 | Section: News

 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - They've been farming west of Denton more than 100 years, and for over a quarter of that century, Cawley Family Farm has branched out to become the only Christmas tree farm in Caroline County.On the Saturday after Thanksgiving, a steady stream of families rolled up the lane of the farm, past the festively decorated John Deere combine, past the Cawley family home and past a huge pavilion housing cut evergreen trees from North Carolina."It's a beautiful day," said owner Charles Cawley." It's going good. We've got good trees. I got some beautiful trees - a little pricier than last year but still beautiful trees - got a lot on the lot, as you can see. The Canaans are going out of here like crazy." In addition to Canaan firs, Cawley grows Concolor and Douglas firs, blue spruce and white pine - all on about 15 acres of the farm."We can't grow Frasers, so we bring them in," Cawley said."But we're the only one that brings in a tree, recuts it and puts it in holding tanks. No one else does that. So we sell the freshest pre-cut trees you can buy." "They're very hard to get, but we've got some beautiful Frasers," he said.Cawley said it took him a while, but he "got to how to grow" Canaan firs about 15 years ago.He pampers them, irrigating, spoon-feeding and growing them in "real thick grass. It helps keep the roots cooler because it gets too hot here," he said.According to the National Christmas Tree Association, the Canaan fir is a "relative newcomer to the Christmas tree market, with many similarities to both Fraser and balsam firs." About 500 to 600 trees are brought in from North Carolina."We sold about 200 off the lot, so we're selling between 700 and 800 a year," Cawley said.Keeping the trees fresh is important to Cawley. "When we sell one of these (Frasers) they'll hold the needles as long as one of those out in the field," he said. "And these things drink a lot of water initially. I mean, we just got these the day before Thanksgiving, and I had to fill these tanks up a couple times, they soaked up that much water." Once the trees are rehydrated, they are shaken, drilled with a tapered bit, set up on a pin stand in a shallow steel basin and kept watered. The operation has two drilling machines, three shakers and plenty of water holding bins inside and outdoors.The 55-foot by 80-foot pavilion can be closed off when the wind whips up to keep the trees from dehydrating. "If we had to add a little heat, we can, but we haven't had to," he said.Cawley clearly takes pride in his product, and his family pitches in. Arriving at 7 a.m. was his 7-year-old grandson Bryant, ready to get started - and put in a 12-hour day.Cawley's eldest daughter, Amy, makes wreaths and wood-burned ornaments from slices of sawed off stumps. The focus is on customer service, so other family members, as well as employees, wait on customers, shake needles from trees, wrap net around them and tote them to cars.Cawley is vice president of the Maryland Christmas Tree Association. He said he started out as a farmer, "but I did a lot of things in the meantime," even working for "all three levels of government - county, state and federal. You don't build this by just farming. It takes something else," Cawley said, adding that his wife Jane is a retired school nurse.Several years of drought, along with root aphids in the Douglass firs and scale on some Canaans, have affected the growth and aesthetics of a few trees in the field, so Cawley has to be vigilant."There's a challenge every year," he said.Cawley Family Farm Christmas tree sales began Nov. 21.You can visit 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.Friday, Saturday and Sunday, and on Monday to Thursday by appointment. The farm is located at 24320 Willow Pond Road, Denton. For more information, call 410-479-4780 or 410-829-4781, or email info@cawley.farm. The website is www.cawleyfarms.com.

In 1865, Abraham Lincoln died after being shot by John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theater the previous evening; Andrew Johnson was sworn in as the 17th president hours later.
In 1947, Jackie Robinson, baseball's first Black major league player of the modern era, made his official debut with the Brooklyn Dodgers on opening day at Ebbets Field. (The Dodgers defeated the Boston Braves, 5-3.)
In 1955, Ray Kroc opened the first franchised McDonald's restaurant in Des Plaines, Illinois.
In 1974, members of the Symbionese Liberation Army held up a branch of the Hibernia Bank in San Francisco; a member of the group was SLA kidnap victim Patricia Hearst. (Hearst later said she had been forced to participate in the robbery.)
In 1989, a crush of soccer fans at Hillsborough Stadium in Sheffield, England, caused 97 deaths and over 760 injuries.
In 2013, two bombs made from pressure cookers exploded at the Boston Marathon finish line, killing two women and an 8-year-old boy and injuring more than 260.
In 2019, fire swept across the top of the Notre-Dame de Paris cathedral during renovation work on the landmark structure; the blaze collapsed the cathedral's spire and spread to one of its iconic rectangular towers. (The cathedral was restored and reopened to the public in December 2024.)

 Remember the excitement on Christmas morning when we were children - getting out of bed at 4 or 5 a.m. trying to come downstairs.The fun began and soon we had to dress and go to Grandmom and Grandpop's house to gather with the rest of the family to have a large country style breakfast.A lot of time was lost being away from our gifts at home those mornings until the later breakfast casserole was born.Christmas morning became perfect. Families would gather mid-morning (around 10 or 11 a.m.) bringing their favorite breakfast casseroles to share.The children of all ages got to enjoy their gifts before traveling. Some years, it would be at the grandparents' place but other members began taking turns also.Enjoy today's recipes to share with everyone and send some of your favorites to me at mmsavage21145@gmail.com so I can share with the readers.PANCAKE CASSEROLE Cooking spray, pancakes, 6 large eggs, 1.5 cups heavy cream, 1 cup whole milk, 25 cup granulated sugar, 1 tsp vanilla bean paste, .25 tsp kosher salt, unsalted butter and maple syrup (for serving).Lightly coat a 13-by 9-inch baking dish with cooking spray. Arrange pancakes in a baking dish in three rows, overlapping slightly, starting at a long end. Whisk together eggs, cream, milk, sugar, vanilla and salt in a bowl. Slowly pour mixture over pancakes.Cover and refrigerate for at least 8 hours or up to overnight. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees.Bake the casserole, covered, in a preheated oven for 25 minutes. Uncover and continue baking until the center is set, about 25 minutes. Let stand for 5 minutes. Dot with pats of butter; drizzle with syrup.CHEESY SAUSAGE, EGG AND HASH BROWN CASSEROLE 3 tbsps olive oil (divided), 8 ounces ground pork sausage, 1 sweet onion (diced), 1 poblano pepper (seeded and chopped), 1 red bell pepper (seeded and chopped), 1.5 tsps kosher salt (divided), 2 cups refrigerated diced potatoes, .75 tsp garlic powder, 4 ounces your favorite shredded cheese, 5 large eggs, .25 cup heavy whipping cream, 1 tbsp minced fresh chives. Preheat the oven to 425 degrees with an oven rack about 6 inches from heat. Heat 1 tbsp of the olive oil in a 10-inch cast-iron skillet over medium-high.Add sausage. Cook, breaking up sausage into pieces with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and just cooked through, about 4 minutes. Remove sausage to a medium bowl with a slotted spoon; set aside. Do not wipe the skillet clean. Add sweet onion, poblano chile, red bell pepper, and .5 tsp of the salt to the skillet. Cook over medium-high, stirring occasionally, until onion is tender and peppers have charred in spots, about 8 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon to bowl with sausage. Wipe the skillet clean.Heat the remaining 2 tbsps of olive oil in a skillet over medium-high.Add diced potatoes to the skillet in an even layer.Cook, undisturbed, until browned on bottom, about 5 minutes. Add ½ tsp of the salt. Continue cooking, stirring occasionally, until golden brown and crispy on most sides, about 5 minutes.Remove from heat.Return sausage and pepper mixture to skillet and add garlic powder. Stir to combine. Stir in ½ cup of the cheese until just combined.Whisk together eggs, cream, and remaining ½ tsp salt in a medium bowl. Pour over mixture in skillet, and tilt pan to allow eggs to distribute.Top with remaining ½ cup each of the cheeses. Bake in a preheated oven until eggs have set and cheeses have melted, about 8 minutes.Increase oven temperature to broil, and broil until cheeses have turned golden brown, 2 to 3 minutes. Remove; let stand for 5 minutes.Sprinkle with chives. Slice and serve immediately.BISCUITS AND GRAVY CASSEROLE 1 (1-lb.) pkg. ground pork sausage,1/2 cup chopped yellow onion (from 1 small onion),1/4 cup plus 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1/3 cup (about 1 1/2 oz.) all-purpose flour,3 cups whole milk,6 ounces pepper Jack cheese, shredded (about 1 1/2 cups),3/4 tsp kosher salt,1/2 tsp black pepper, Cooking spray,1 (25-oz.) pkg. frozen Southern-style biscuits (12 count) (such as Pillsbury Grands),2 tbsps minced fresh chives. Preheat the oven to 350°F.Place sausage and onion in a large skillet over medium, and cook, stirring often, until sausage crumbles and is no longer pink and onion is translucent, 6 to 8 minutes.Transfer mixture to a plate lined with paper towels to drain. Wipe the skillet clean. Reduce heat to low, and add 1/4 cup of the butter to the skillet; cook, whisking often, until melted. Whisk in flour until smooth. Cook, whisking constantly, 1 minute. Gradually whisk in milk; increase heat to medium, and cook, whisking constantly, until thickened and bubbly, 5 to 6 minutes. Whisk in shredded cheese, and cook, whisking often, until cheese is melted and mixture is smooth, 30 to 40 seconds. Stir in sausage mixture, salt, and pepper.Transfer mixture to a lightly greased (with cooking spray) 13-x 9-inch baking dish. Arrange biscuits on top of sausage mixture. Bake in a preheated oven until biscuits are golden brown and gravy is bubbly, 30 to 35 minutes. Microwave remaining 1 tbsp butter in a small microwavable bowl on HIGH until melted, about 20 seconds.Remove the casserole from the oven; brush biscuits with melted butter, and sprinkle with chives.Let stand for 10 minutes before serving.SLOW COOKER CINNAMON ROLL CASSEROLECooking spray,1/2 cup granulated sugar,1/2 cup packed light brown sugar,1 tsp ground cinnamon, 2 (16.3-oz.) cans refrigerated southern homestyle biscuits (such as Pillsbury Grands!Southern Homestyle), biscuits separated and cut into fourths (about 64 biscuit pieces total),1/2 cup (4 oz.) salted butter, melted, plus 2 Tbsp. butter, softened, divided,4 large eggs,1/4 tsp kosher salt,2/3 cup plus 2 to 3 Tbsp. half-and-half, divided,2 tsp vanilla extract, divided,1/2 cup chopped toasted pecans,1 (3-oz.) pkg. cream cheese, softened,2 1/4 cups (about 9 oz.) powdered sugar, divided. Line bottom and sides of a 6-quart slow cooker with aluminum foil; lightly coat foil with cooking spray. Stir together granulated sugar, brown sugar, and cinnamon in a small bowl. Toss together biscuit pieces and 1/2 cup melted butter in a large bowl until biscuits are coated. Working in batches, add biscuits to granulated sugar mixture, and toss to coat; transfer biscuits to prepared slow cooker. Sprinkle any remaining sugar mixture over biscuits in a slow cooker.Whisk together eggs, salt, 2/3 cup of the halfand-half, and 1 tsp of the vanilla in a bowl until well combined; pour over biscuits in a slow cooker.Sprinkle with pecans.Beat cream cheese and 2 tbsps softened butter with an electric mixer on medium speed until thoroughly combined, about 30 seconds. Add 1 cup of the powdered sugar and remaining 1 tsp vanilla; beat until smooth, about 1 minute. Gradually add remaining 1 1/4 cups powdered sugar to cream cheese mixture alternately with 2 tbsps of the half-and-half, beating on high speed until frosting is smooth, creamy, and a little loose, about 1 minute, adding remaining 1 tbsp half-and-half, 1 tsp at a time, if needed to reach desired consistency. Drizzle half of the frosting over the biscuit mixture in the slow cooker. (Cover remaining frosting and set aside until ready to serve.)Cover slow cooker; cook on low until center of casserole is set and biscuit bottoms are browned, 3.5 to 4 hours. Drizzle casserole with remaining frosting; serve warm.TEXAS TWO STEP CASSEROLLE11 oz canned mild chiles (drained), 8 corn tortillas (cut into strips), 12 oz bulk breakfast sausage (cooked and drained), 1 medium yellow onion (diced), 1.5 cups shredded pepper jack or cheddar cheese, 8 eggs, .5 cups heavy whipping cream, .5 tsp salt, .5 tsp freshly ground black pepper, .5 tsp garlic salt or powder, 1 tsp ground cumin, 2 small Roma tomatoes sliced, .5 tsp paprika, sour cream (optional), pico de gallo (optional). Lightly coat a 13-by 9-inch baking dish with non-stick spray.Spread half the amount of chiles in an even layer in the bottom of the dish.Add half of the tortilla strips. Add half of the sausage and onion. Add half of the cheese. Repeat a second time. In a medium bowl, whisk the eggs, cream, salt, pepper, garlic salt and cumin together until well combined.Pour over the casserole.Arrange the tomato slices on top. Sprinkle with paprika. Cover and refrigerate overnight. The next morning, heat the oven to 350 degrees. Uncover and bake the casserole 40 minutes or until the center has set and the edges are lightly browned. If desired, serve with sour cream and pico de gallo.

title: TODAY IN HISTORY/May 24
author: Staff Writer
content:
TODAY IN HISTORY/May 24

 May 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Columns 
 
 411
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On May 24, 1935, the first Major League Baseball game to be played at night took place at Cincinnati's Crosley Field as the Reds beat the Philadelphia Phillies, 2-1.On this date:
In 1844, Samuel F.B. Morse transmitted the message "What hath God wrought" from Washington to Baltimore as he formally opened America's first telegraph line.
In 1937, in a set of rulings, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the Social Security Act of 1935.
In 1941, the German battleship Bismarck sank the British battle cruiser HMS Hood in the North Atlantic, killing all but three of the 1,418 men on board.
In 1961, a group of Freedom Riders was arrested after arriving at a bus terminal in Jackson, Mississippi, charged with breaching the peace for entering white-designated areas. (They ended up serving 60 days in jail.)
In 1962, astronaut Scott Carpenter became the second American to orbit the Earth as he flew aboard Aurora 7.
In 1974, American jazz composer and bandleader Duke Ellington, 75, died in New York.
In 1976, Britain and France opened trans-Atlantic Concorde supersonic transport service to Washington.
In 1980, Iran rejected a call by the World Court in The Hague to release the American hostages.
In 1994, four Islamic fundamentalists convicted of bombing New York's World Trade Center in 1993 were each sentenced to 240 years in prison.
In 1995, former British Prime Minister Harold Wilson died in London at age 79.
In 2006, "An Inconvenient Truth," a documentary about former Vice President Al Gore's campaign against global warming, went into limited release.
In 2011, Oprah Winfrey taped the final episode of her long-running talk show.
In 2017, Ariana Grande suspended her Dangerous Woman world tour and canceled several European shows due to the deadly bombing at her concert in Manchester, England, two days earlier.
In 2018, Jerry Maren, the last surviving Munchkin from the 1939 film "The Wizard of Oz," died at a San Diego nursing home; he was 99.
In 2022, an 18-year-old gunman opened fire at an elementary school in Uvalde, Texas, killing 19 children and two teachers. The gunman, Salvador Ramos, a former student at the school, was also killed. It was the deadliest shooting at a U.S. grade school since the attack in Sandy Hook, Connecticut, almost a decade earlier.
In 2023, Tina Turner died at age 83. She teamed with husband Ike Turner for a dynamic run of hit records and live shows and survived her horrifying marriage to triumph in middle age with the chart-topping "What's Love Got to Do With It."

title: Exhibit to show charm and beauty of Delmarva
author: LISA J. GOTTO Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Exhibit to show charm and beauty of Delmarva

 June 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LISA J. GOTTO Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Arts 
 
 438
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — The "Science of Photography" as captured by the artist's eye will be on full display for those who appreciate what is revealed through the camera and life's lens when a new exhibit opens in Chestertown on Wednesday, July 3.The exhibition, which runs through Aug. 28 in the interior public areas of the Heron Point Retirement Community, will display the works of seven talented photographers who have a knack for chronicling the exquisite beauty and inherent charm associated with living in and among the environs and the inhabitants of what is known as the Delmarva.
Barbara Finneson, a representative of Heron Point's Art Interest Group, said she is personally very excited to view the work of this particular collective of artists. "This is a special group," she said, noting that it is based in Salisbury, and includes the works of Mike Morris, Libby Morris, Kenneth Jones, Tony Burton, Latoya Drummond, Samuel Everett and Seldon Dix.
This group of photographic professionals and friends has been known to do whatever it takes, whether that means chasing 3 a.m. sunrises, enduring bitter cold, or patiently waiting for just the right light and conditions to evolve, to get the perfect shot.
"These Delmarva artists," according to the statement provided by the Art Interest Group, "…are dedicated to capturing the unique beauty and essence of Delmarva through their lens. Their collection of work showcases the diverse landscapes, vibrant communities, and rich cultural heritage of the region, applying their individual perspectives and artistic styles. They create a fresh and innovative approach to documenting the natural wonders and human stories of Maryland's Eastern Shore."
Finneson, who is a 20-year resident of Heron Point, said her community always has the good fortune to have artistic works on display in its common areas by talented resident artists and others from the community at-large. Heron Point residents, she said, are oftentimes so inspired by what they see in these exhibitions, they have been known to start painting for the first time at the age of 80, and they particularly look forward to these special collections.
While the opening will take place on July 3 at 10 a.m., the artists themselves will be on-hand for a special gathering on the afternoon on Sunday, July 14 from 2 to 4 p.m. to speak to visitors about their creative process. The community is encouraged to come and participate in the discussion.
This exhibition will be open to the public daily from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. from June 3 through Aug. 28, with many works available for purchase. Heron Point of Chestertown is located at 501 East Campus Avenue, Chestertown. Call 410-778-7300 for more information.

title: Caroline Police Accountability Board reports progress
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Police Accountability Board reports progress

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 1030
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — The Caroline County Police Accountability Board shared its second annual report with the County Commissioners at their Feb. 6 meeting.The bottom line: Of the thousands of contacts people had with county and town law enforcement officers, a handful of complaints were made, and a fraction of those resulted in disciplinary action.
Presenting the report were Police Accountability Board Chairman John Bartlett and Board Administrator Kimberly Raeder.
Bartlett said he wanted to make one "very important" point: The Caroline County Sheriff's Office had over 26,000 calls for service in 2023, which generated only six complaints, he said.
"Five of those six were exonerated, meaning unfounded, and one was a very minor infraction, which led to a written reprimand," he said. "I think that speaks volumes with law enforcement here in Caroline County."
A state mandate
Raeder explained the purpose and scope of the three police oversight boards mandated by the Maryland Police Accountability Act of 2021, which became effective July 1, 2022.
The role of the county's Police Accountability Board "is to receive police complaints, recommend policy changes and identify any trends," Raeder said.
"The second board is the five-member Administrative Charging Committee, and their role is to look over and review completed complaint investigations and recommend discipline," she said. If the Charging Committee decides to administratively charge, they use the statewide police disciplinary matrix to "decide what kind of discipline would be necessary based on the complaint."
The five members of the Charging Committee were appointed and trained in April 2023 at the Fretterd Center by the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission.
The third board is the Trial Board comprised of retired Maryland Circuit Court Judge Owen Wise, a citizen and a police officer of the same rank, Raeder said. No complaints have been referred to this board.
"I'm proud to say that Caroline County is leading the way for other counties on the Eastern Shore who have reached out to us regarding using Judge Wise, if they need a judge for a trial board," she said.
Few complaints filed
Among the county's municipalities, 15 complaints were filed, including a pending complaint related to an April 7, 2023, incident in Denton that prompted millions of views on YouTube, Bartlett said.
A video of the incident shows Christopher Morgan threatening the residents and breaking the window of the storm door of a home while two Denton Police officers stand on the sidewalk watching.
The way the officers handled the call for service prompted Denton Police Chief George Bacorn to request the Talbot County Sheriff's Office to investigate the handling of the incident. Their findings were turned over to the Administrative Charging Committee.
There were no complaints from Ridgely or Greensboro. One was brought to the Police Accountability Board from Federalsburg, which was exonerated, Bartlett said.
The report breaks down the 15 complaints by percentages; numerically, four complaints are pending investigation, three were administratively charged, two were withdrawn by the complainant, four were exonerated and two were "not in the purview of the ACC (Administrative Charging Committee)."
The Accountability Board identified trends in the disciplinary process and didn't "recommend any changes at this time."
"A common identified trend, however, has been the lack of activation of body cameras when officers interact with the public," the report stated. "The ACC discovered this trend when reviewing completed complaint investigations which had no body camera footage for the ACC to review. The Board advised the municipal Police Departments and the Sheriff's Office to remind Officers to adhere to department policy and activate their cameras when encountering the public. The policy protects both the Officer and the Citizen if a complaint were to arise from the interaction."
Cost to the county
Bartlett thanked the commissioners for their "financial support of the committee for legal decisions when needed."
The boards' complying with the state mandates has incurred expenses for the county, although some have been covered by the Police Accountability, Community, and Transparency Grant program.
Of the $105,272 in grant funds received, the Accountability Board has spent $49,545, which includes the purchase of IAPro software for filing complaints, annual computer licensing for all board members, and pay for the Board's administrator.
The Police Accountability Board is asking the state to continue offering these grants, as well as other police-oriented grant programs for local police departments to be able to purchase "the required technology, resources, and tools to comply with the law," including software and a change in the vendor for body cameras, so that every law enforcement agency in the county has the same system.
Other costs included outside legal counsel, with expenses the County Commissioners agreed to fund to the tune of nearly $8,000.
Questions arose requiring legal clarification for both the Police Accountability Board and Administrative Charging Committee, and the county commissioners "agreed to bear the expense of hiring outside legal counsel" to represent both. "Legal Counsel attends each quarterly meeting and provides interpretation of the Maryland Police Accountability Act of 2021 as needed," the report stated.
The legal expenses for the Police Accountability Board were $3,650, while those of the Administrative Charging Committee amounted to $4,300.
PAB recommendations
The Accountability Board recommends "changing ACC training from all in-person training to online meeting based or pre-recorded online training. With one member of our ACC board resigning this past July, we have firsthand knowledge of the burden imposed on the newly appointed volunteer Board member. As terms end or resignations occur, the pool of applicants will continue to shrink when advised that members must undergo uncompensated training prior to serving."
Another unanticipated result of the law has been the withdrawing of multiple complaints, which created a legal conundrum for the Accountability Board and is currently being resolved with the Office of the Attorney General.
The report also suggested amending the law by mandating only complaints of "matters of public concern," that is, "police misconduct, such as abuse of power, false arrest, police brutality, or criminal activity" be referred to the Charging Committee, thus alleviating pressure on municipal police departments. "Rude and discourteous" behavior towards a citizen would be handled at the department or agency level, as suggested by the Accountability Board.
To read the full report, which includes rosters of members of the PAB and ACC boards, visit carolinemd.org/DocumentCenter/View/8606/2023-Annual-Report-PAB?bidId=. The last page provides links to other documents and resources provided by the PAB.

title: Larry L. O'Ferrall
content:
Larry L. O'Ferrall

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: B7 | Section: Obituaries 
 
 284
 Words 

 Read News Document

 LANHAM - Larry Lee O'Ferrall passed away on December 5, 2023 at the age of 84 with his family by his side. He was born near East New Market in 1939, to the late Margaret and William O'Ferrall. Larry had three brothers Franklin, William, and Daniel O'Ferrall. He attended North Dorchester High School and graduated in 1957.Larry married Helen Hurlock on August 7, 1960 in Hurlock, MD. They moved to the suburbs of Washington, DC and in 1966, they had a son, Larry Allen O'Ferrall. Larry Lee has two grandchildren, Steven and Shannon O'Ferrall.
Larry worked in the computer field for the Central Intelligence Agency from 1960 to 2005. After retiring he briefly worked for the US Army as a contractor.
Larry was an avid sports fan who played baseball and football in High School as well as softball and football with the CIA. For over a decade he played softball on the same team with his son.
He was an avid reader and interested in history.
He enjoyed crabbing and fishing in the rivers on the Eastern Shore as a youth. He was a devoted family man and a proud grandparent. He was always in attendance at his grandchildren's events and games.
Besides his wife Helen, Larry is survived by Larry Allen O'Ferrall, his daughter-in-law Elizabeth O'Ferrall, his grandchildren Steven and Shannon O'Ferrall, his sister-in-law Barbara O'Ferrall and several nieces and nephews. He is preceded in death by his parents and brothers.
A viewing and funeral service will be held at the Zeller Funeral Home in East New Market, MD on Sunday, December 17th. The viewing will be at 1 pm and service at 2 pm. The burial will follow immediately at the Unity Washington Cemetery in Hurlock.

title: Lakeside wastewater treatment plant is complete
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Lakeside wastewater treatment plant is complete

 June 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 1257
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TRAPPE — The Lakeside wastewater treatment plant is built, running and ready for the next step in the Lakeside development plan, which is transferring ownership to the town of Trappe.Two Lakeside transfer agreements were presented during a recent Trappe Council meeting. These agreements are the first steps in eventually passing over ownership of the wastewater treatment plant to the Town of Trappe.
This controversial project has faced lawsuits, petitions and an array of public outcry over environmental concerns, but it is an essential step in moving forward with the Lakeside development.
First proposed over 20 years ago, the planned 2,501-unit Lakeside at Trappe development spans more than 850 acres off of U.S. Route 50. The development is slated to include a mix of single-family homes, townhouses and apartments, and commercial and retail spaces.
Trappe's existing plant has the capacity to take on wastewater from the development's first 120 homes. That flow will eventually be diverted to the new wastewater treatment plant serving the development, a plan approved by county legislation and via an MDE wastewater discharge permit.
Spray irrigation systemThe new plant, set with enriched nutrient removal technology, uses a spray irrigation system to discharge treated wastewater onto nearby fields.
According to the Pennsylvania Water Science Center, the sprayed wastewater either evaporates into the air, soaks into the soil or percolates through the soil and recharges the groundwater.
Robert Rauch, president of Rauch Inc., a project management and civil engineering firm for Lakeside, said spray irrigation has been recognized for years by states and the federal government as a preferred method of treated wastewater disposal.
"It is an exceptional re-use method of disposal that recharges groundwater and can provide needed nutrients to agricultural ground covers," he said. "Generally, spray irrigation does not require the highest levels of treatment, so valuable nutrients are available for plants to reduce farmers' costs for additional commercial fertilizer."
Raunch said this is based on Lakeside's developer's voluntary election to provide enhanced nutrient removal level treatment to avoid groundwater nutrient increases. The MDE discharge permit establishes strict limitations on the discharge of treated wastewater, which results in the application of a fraction of the nutrient uptake requirements of the grass planted in the irrigation field.
Raunch said that due to the high quality of the Lakeside wastewater effluent and the nutrient needs of the ground cover, there is no practical scenario in which the spray irrigation of treated effluent will negatively impact surface or groundwater.
"Ironically, the nutrient levels of the treated effluent will be so low that the farmer will have to apply fertilizer to the spray irrigation field to maintain a vigorous and healthy crop cover," he said.
Alan Girard, advocacy director of the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, argued that nutrients absorbed into groundwater could eventually discharge into nearby impaired rivers and streams like the Choptank River.
"I don't think people understand that the state is claiming that there will be zero discharge of nutrients to groundwater," Girard said. "The state has already demonstrated that there's a link between groundwater and surface water and surface letters that are tarred right near the discharge. So the state needs to be accountable for that issue."
The Chesapeake Bay Foundation and ShoreRivers filed separate petitions for judicial review of the permit in, citing concerns about the spray irrigation of treated wastewater and specifics of a nutrient management plan not being made available during the permit's public comment period in 2020.
Matt Pluta, Choptank riverkeeper and director of riverkeeper programs for ShoreRivers, said that the wastewater issue has been a concern for ShoreRivers due to the existing Trappe plant and how poorly it has been functioning and treating the wastewater before discharging it into Trappe Creek.
According to Pluta, the Lakeside Plant is making noticeable improvements that were not seen in the old Trappe Wastewater Plant.
"I'll go on and say that one thing that's very clear and obvious is that there will be more treatment from this new plant," Pluta said. "The wastewater will be treated to a cleaner standard. That's what we want to see. We support that. The thing that concerns us with the new plan is just the method of discharge. That's where they'll be spraying the treated wastewater onto nearby farm fields."
Pluta said the way the state permits spraying the treated wastewater onto nearby farm fields is under what he calls "legal fiction or false assumptions." When someone is spraying wastewater on a farm field, that wastewater gets taken up by the plants.
Through studying agricultural practices, Pluta has learned of the impacts of runoff and pollution on groundwater. He said there are different incentives for someone operating a wastewater treatment plant compared to farmers caring for local crops.
Pluta stated that no farmer is applying nutrients to their crops every day throughout the whole growing season. There is an incentive for wastewater treatment operators to focus on controlling their volume and not so much on a healthy crop, which Pluta said is concerning for the sake of adding too much pollution to these fields.
Each farm that receives spraying from the plant needs a nutrient management plan on how many nutrients can be put on the fields. Those plans were not public information, but because it was part of the treatment process, ShoreRiver argued to make that information public.
It was through the 2020 filed lawsuit that the permit was remanded to the Maryland Department of the Environment, which issued a new permit with fewer homes and less wastewater.
A separate lawsuit was filed against MDE by concerned residents in May 2022 asking to revoke the permit and suspend any work with a sewage system as inconsistent with the county's comprehensive plan. Though the suits was ultimately dismissed last June, MDE issued a revised discharge permit for Lakeside, approving a significantly smaller wastewater treatment plant.
The revised permit allows for an average flow of 100,000 gallons per day. A vast decrease from the 540,000 gallons per day initially requested by the developer.
OversightIn part due to the outcry and lawsuits made by residents and environmental organizations, a wave of resolutions were brought forward to better address concerns involving the Wastewater Treatment Plant.
One that stood out to many was Resolution 338, which amended Talbot County's Comprehensive Water and Sewer Plan. It requires an amendment to the comprehensive plan for any future expansion of the new Lakeside wastewater treatment plant.
Though this was deemed favorable to the environmental organizations, there were many, including members of Trappe's council, that opposed the Lakeside resolutions.
During a public hearing before the vote of Resolution 338, Brian Schmidt, Trappe Town Council president, commented opposing the resolution and stated that the county was treating Trappe differently than other towns, hurting the municipality's growth.
"We did not ask this council to intervene," Schmidt said. "MDE is the controlling authority in matters of wastewater discharge, not the county. Disguising growth legislation as wastewater discharge is not proper procedure is only impeding the town's authority to control its own growth."
Next stepsDuring the June 5 Trappe Town Council meeting, two Lakeside transfer agreements were presented. These agreements are the first steps in eventually passing over ownership of the wastewater treatment plant to the Town of Trappe.
According to Showalter, Once the initial phase of the wastewater treatment plant is complete and turned over to the town, the developer remains responsible for any deficiencies between the costs of operation and maintenance and the sewer revenues collected by the Town from Lakeside residents. Additionally, the developer remains responsible for the incremental expansion of the wastewater treatment plant as the capacity is utilized.
Further discussion on the transfer agreements will be discussed and reviewed during the Town Council's next executive session.

 January 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 The application process for the 2025-2026 Talbot County liquor licensing period is now available to the public.Businesses and individuals interested in applying for a new license, or renewing current licenses, can access the application on the board's webpage at talbotcountymd.gov/liquorboard.
All applications must be completed and submitted by March 31. Applicants are encouraged to review the application requirements and guidelines thoroughly to ensure compliance with local and state regulations.
In addition, in accordance with Talbot County Code, Article 2 — Alcoholic Beverages, "Renewal licenses shall be administratively approved without a hearing before the Board, unless a protest signed by not less than ten (10) residents or property owners in the voting district in which the place of business is located has been filed against the granting of a renewal license at least thirty (30) days before the expiration of the license for which renewal is sought." All 2024-2025 alcoholic beverage licenses expire on April 30. The new license must be posted in the business by May 1.
"Our goal is to provide a streamlined and transparent process for applicants," said Victoria Bradley, secretary for the Talbot County Liquor Board. "We're here to assist individuals and businesses in navigating the application process successfully."
For questions or additional assistance, applicants can contact the Talbot County Liquor Board office at 410-770-8019 or via email at vbradley@talbotcountymd.gov. The office is open from 8 a.m. to noon and 1 to 4 p.m. Monday through Friday.

title: ‘It’s certainly over’ for aid-in-dying bill this year
author: SAPNA BANSIL Capital News Service
content:
‘It’s certainly over’ for aid-in-dying bill this year

 March 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SAPNA BANSIL Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 577
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ANNAPOLIS — Lawmakers have tabled a fiercely debated bill that would have granted terminally ill Maryland residents the right to end their lives, a setback to supporters who hoped it would finally pass this year.Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) said in a press conference Friday that the measure had not won enough support among the 11 members of the Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee to move forward this term. Ferguson indicated he was unwilling to bring the bill for a vote if it was likely to fail.
"For this year, it's certainly over," said Senate Judicial Proceedings Committee Chair Will Smith (D-Montgomery), noting the bill would have fallen one or two votes shy of passing his committee.
Although Democratic leaders — from Gov. Wes Moore to Ferguson and Smith — all previously expressed support for the bill, they said there would be no last-ditch efforts to change lawmakers' minds on an issue that is deeply sensitive for both supporters and opponents.
"I told every member of this committee that on issues like this, it's a vote of conscience," Smith said. "It's so personal. It's such a tough issue … In order to come to me and say, 'Hey, look, I'm expressing unreadiness, I cannot vote for this bill,' I would honor that."
This bill, known as the End-of-Life Option Act, sought to make Maryland the 12th jurisdiction to legalize medical aid in dying, which provides patients with incurable illnesses the option to die by self-administering lethal medication. Patients would have been eligible if they had less than six months to live, were of sound mind and made a series of oral and written requests.
As the Senate and House considered companion bills over the past few weeks, the issue became the subject of contentious debate and hours of testimony. Proponents said aid in dying was a matter of dignity and bodily autonomy, while opponents expressed religious, ethical and moral concerns.
The bill's failure elicited strong emotions from its supporters on Friday, many of whom have experienced years of setbacks on the issue.
"It's gut wrenching," said Sen. Ariana Kelly (D-Montgomery), a member of the Judicial Proceedings Committee and a bill co-sponsor. "The proponents of this bill have come before the legislature, year after year, explaining why it's necessary. I have a broad community of constituents back at home and friends and colleagues who I see in Annapolis who are gutted … People feel this very personally."
Among those who testified in support of the bill was Diane Kraus, a 59-year-old Baltimore woman living with metastatic breast cancer. She said she wanted to have the option of medical aid in dying in the event her condition became terminal.
"I'm really disappointed," Kraus said in a phone interview. "I don't want to have to move out of state in order to be able to use this."
But one opponent said the bill's demise was the right outcome.
"I'm actually very pleased," said Sen. Mike McKay (R-Allegany, Garrett, Washington). "I know that it's a very, very personal piece of legislation that affects each of us much differently than (Republicans) to (Democrats) or rural to suburban … There's just people (who) weren't comfortable moving forward."
While the bill has met its end for this session, lawmakers said they anticipate reintroducing aid-in-dying legislation in upcoming terms.
"This is one that in time, maybe things will change with more education and more discussion," Ferguson said. "And so it's best to just know that it's just not happening this year."
Angelique Gingras contributed reporting for this story.

title: ‘Hello Girl’ from Maryland may soon win a medal for her WWI service
author: ROBERT STEWART Capital News Service
content:
‘Hello Girl’ from Maryland may soon win a medal for her WWI service

 December 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ROBERT STEWART Capital News Service | Section: News 
 
 955
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Marie Edmee LeRoux has been buried at the Fort Lincoln Cemetery here for 79 years, but she may soon win a gold medal for her service in World War I.LeRoux was one of 223 bilingual women deployed to France as telephone operators, often under combat conditions, as part of the U.S. Army Signal Corps. They were the country's first women soldiers, popularly known as the "Hello Girls."
They've been long overlooked for their service. But now the U.S. Congress has approved a special congressional gold medal as part of the National Defense Authorization Act for the coming year. The measure now goes to President Joe Biden for consideration.
"It's a story that's been forgotten and needs to be told," LeRoux's granddaughter, Catherine Bourgin of McLean, Va., said. "With the passage of the Congressional gold medal, that's what I want."
Women like LeRoux braved German submarines on the transport to the war front and disease and bombardment to serve in the signal corps under the American Expeditionary Forces. Their service helped set a precedent for women's service in the U.S. military and influenced support for the 19th amendment, guaranteeing women the right to vote.
Gen. John Pershing requested that bilingual women operators deploy to France. They were more skilled and experienced at operating the new telephone systems of the time, and the AEF needed bilingual people to communicate with the French forces.
LeRoux had those skills. She was born in Montreal and grew up speaking French and English before moving to the U.S. at age 10, according to Bourgin. She was a passionate singer but, according to Bourgin, LeRoux abandoned her music career to answer the call.
LeRoux traveled to France in 1918, operating the switchboards that connected military commanders with the front lines and their French counterparts. She stayed in France after the war to restart her music studies. When war threatened France again in 1939, LeRoux fled the country with her 4-year-old daughter in tow. She eventually came to live near family in Prince George's County.
She passed away in 1945 and was interred in an unmarked grave here, according to her granddaughter. She did not receive a military headstone because she was not considered a veteran.
Many women who served in the U.S. Army signal corps found out they weren't considered "soldiers" when they applied for benefits after the war. They received no veteran medical care and no federally funded rehabilitation training.
This was only remedied in 1977 when Congress acknowledged them as veterans, following decades of petitioning by Hello Girls like Merle Egan Anderson. Most had already passed away by then.
While Bourgin was researching her grandmother's history, she discovered LeRoux was a member of the Hello Girls. She also learned that a congressional commission had recommended these female veterans receive a Congressional Gold Medal collectively.
So, in 2023, Bourgin began working with others to help her grandmother and the other Hello Girls get that medal.
Bourgin refers to the advocacy group as the "Hello Girls Family," and she joined them to bring their story to Capitol Hill. Elizabeth Cobbs' 2017 book also helped reintroduce the women operators' war contribution into the mainstream.
"The telephone," Cobbs said, "was the only way that they could rapidly communicate with troops who were facing mechanized onslaughts of the most destructive machinery ever devised by humans."
Women could operate the war switchboards faster than their male counterparts, she said. They couldn't even vote at the time, nor serve on juries in most states.
Chris Christopher led the advocacy charge.
As a former staffer on the World War I Centennial Commission that recommended in 2018 that the Hello Girls receive the award as part of the country's formal efforts to commemorate the war, Christopher thought getting the award across the finish line was important. In 2023, with no bill passed, Christopher decided to tackle the issue head-on.
"I sat down," Christopher said, "and wrote a letter to every single senator who was not already a co-sponsor."
If a senator was not a co-sponsor, Christopher said, he researched and included World War I registration documents of a relative or ancestor of that senator to personalize the letters. He then made sure those were hand-delivered to the senators.
Volunteering in his free time, he also coordinated the network of history buffs and Hello Girl descendants and supporters for virtual meetings and lobbying on the Hill.
Catherine Bourgin had just discovered her grandmother's unmarked grave in Fort Lincoln Cemetery, in a plot next to her great-grandmother's. She also connected with Christopher at the same time.
Bourgin said her grandmother's grave was symbolic of what happened to the Hello Girls. LeRoux was in an unmarked grave, Bourgin said, just miles from the nation's capital but nevertheless lost to history.
While lobbying on Capitol Hill a few months later, Bourgin said, she told other advocates about the unmarked grave. The group got fired up, she said, and decided to change that.
They procured the grave marker and arranged for a military honors ceremony at the cemetery.
"The folks that did what they did for my grandmother," Bourgin said, "they truly made an indelible mark on my family's history."
Bourgin thinks the ceremony drew attention to the gold-medal cause. They made sure members of Congress were invited.
Now it seems the advocacy may have worked. Senators are expected to take up the defense act in the coming days.
Both Bourgin and Christopher hope that the award will bring attention to the untold stories of the country's first female soldiers, and ensure that all of them have veteran's grave markers.
"There are so many stories out there like this," Bourgin said, "and we just have to discover them."
"Hopefully once we get past all this, this is going to be something that will generate an ongoing effort," Christopher said. He wants "to get all of the Hello Girls their appropriate grave marker."

title: One proves enough for Easton
author: Bill Haufe
content:
One proves enough for Easton

 October 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 568
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Both coaches obviously wanted victory, and after 80 minutes of heated, physical play in the latest installment of the Easton-St. Michaels High soccer rivalry, Warrior head coach Avery Brice breathed a sigh of relief as his team continued its late-season surge."Good game. One-oh. Got the result," Brice said after Rodrigo Fresco's goal in the fifth minute Wednesday night proved enough for a 1-0 Easton victory over the Saints.
And though St. Michaels suffered its fourth loss in five games, Saints head coach Pat Hambleton may have gotten something he was looking for as well — momentum.
"We've had a hard stretch," Hambleton said after his team's third one-goal loss in 10 days, which included a 3-2 double-overtime defeat to two-time defending North Bayside champion Queen Anne's County. "I asked them, 'Just give us momentum. Create momentum so we can move forward. Win, lose, draw, figure out a way to play well. Work hard. Find something to carry on for tomorrow (a 9-0 victory Thursday over Cambridge-South Dorchester) and then carry on into the playoffs.'"
The Saints (6-4-1 overall, 2-4-1 North Bayside) may have found that momentum, playing the game's last 35 minutes, 54 seconds a man down after one of its players received a red card while an Easton player was given a yellow.
"I thought down (to) 10 men, I felt like we had the upper hand, and I felt like we were the man up," said Hambleton, who argued Easton should have also received a red.
"Couldn't be more proud," Hambleton added of his team. "We took them out of their game. They were sitting six guys in the back for the last 20 minutes terrified of our attack and our pressure. And I thought the second half was a completely different game than the first half."
With 4:28 elapsed in the first half, Fresco got a ball on the right side and parked it past Saints keeper Lucas Greenwood for the game's lone goal and a 1-0 Warrior lead.
The remainder of the game featured a string of highlight-reel saves by Greenwood (10 saves) and Easton goalie Sam Hutchison (eight saves).
Greenwood leaped to punch a ball away with 26:10 remaining in the first half. Hutchison stopped St. Michaels' Abel Delgaudio just 50 seconds later. Greenwood lunged left to foil Luke Stanco a little over 5 minutes later. St. Michaels' Connor Wheeler then struck a direct kick that Hutchison reached before colliding with Delgaudio. Greenwood made another stop a moment later, and Hutchsion responded with another save before a second collision 5 minutes later, leaving Brice pleading with his team, "You need to wake up."
The game was mostly played between the 18s in the second half, though both keepers continued to come up big. Easton had a chance to pad its lead 9 minutes into the half, but Emmet Fox drove a shot off the left post. Hutchison picked up another save, when he knocked away a ball on a Saints corner. Greenwood maintained the one-goal difference, smothering a ball off a wild scramble with an Easton player leaping over him.
"We just need to be consistent in the back and then take care of the ball a little bit better," said Brice, his team 6-5, 6-2 after its fourth win in five games.
For Hambleton, it was a familiar theme.
"The story of the second half of our season is we're winning games off the scoreboard," Hambleton said. "And that doesn't count."

 Sitting around a lunch table at Harrison's Harbour Lights on Wednesday, pioneers of Talbot County's advanced life support program told me about their vision for comprehensive cardiac response efforts.Some surely saw it as a far-fetched goal back in 1985, as people were accustomed to sometimes 20-minute wait times for first responders, even during serious cardiac emergencies.

title: Planners not sold on 365-unit development near new Easton hospital
author: Konner Metz
content:
Planners not sold on 365-unit development near new Easton hospital

 June 26, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 739
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — An application for a 365-unit residential development near the in-construction regional medical center in Easton has been submitted to the town's Planning Commission for review, though it's drawing criticism from some town and county officials.The project, Fox Chase Estates, is proposed on 112 acres of land off of Airport Road nestled within the Easton Technology Center. Developers are seeking town approval through Easton's planned unit development process, which would allow the homes to be built on the commercial-zoned land.
The developers are Easton Sunrise Partners LLC and Scott Wagner, a Talbot County businessman and a former Republican member of the Pennsylvania State Senate. They previously aimed to build warehouses on the site, but in recent years plans shifted to residential — an effort that Shore Regional Health President and CEO Ken Kozel supports, according to Wagner's attorney, Lawrence Scott.
"We are trying to build a residential community that meets the need of the hospital," Scott said Tuesday, noting that Wagner and Kozel have met to discuss the project.
In a statement Wednesday, Kozel said affordable housing availability is "essential" to recruit and retain health care workers in a rural community like Easton. The hospital is not legally or financially involved with the proposed development, Scott said.
At an hours long meeting Tuesday, Planning Commission members were nowhere near ready to provide a positive recommendation on the proposal.
"It feels like we're being the Planning Commission for the hospital and not for the town," said member William Ryall. "And that gives me a lot of concern."
Victoria McAndrews said the plans are "overwhelmingly suburban." Michael Ports, the commission's vice chair, said a lack of connectivity from the proposed development — which sits at the northernmost part of town limits — to Easton's core is a "non-starter."
Philip Toussaint, commission chair, said parts of the plan significantly fall short of meeting Easton's comprehensive plan, which sets the framework for how the town facilitates growth. That comprehensive plan is undergoing an update currently, and McAndrews said such a large project should wait for that update.
Scott said Tuesday that developers have met individually with Town Council members and Mayor Megan Cook multiple times and that the 365-unit project meets affordable housing needs that the town and its residents are asking for.
THE UNITS
Application documents show that developers are planning for a variety of units, including single-family homes, three-story townhomes and multifamily buildings, along with two commercial buildings.
The 365 units are broken down as follows: 108 single-family detached homes, 137 three-story townhomes and 120 multifamily units, the latter of which are contained in four four-story buildings.
The density is well below the maximum permitted by the town's planned unit development standards. According to developers, 185 of the 365 units would be affordably priced.
"We're doing that without even the statutory forcing of us to do it," Scott said, adding that developers have a "bidding war" from home building companies to take on the project. "The market is working on its own."
APPROVAL PROCESS
Fox Chase Estates still has a handful of steps before it is approved by Easton officials. With significant pushback already, it's likely to be a lengthy process.
In staff analysis of the application, concerns were raised about the site plan, which only includes one main vehicle access point to the 365-unit development. An emergency exit stretching west to Goldsborough Neck Road did not satisfy town staff. Scott said developers would prefer not to add that as a main access point but will consider it.
"We really want two access points to any project like this," said Town Engineer Rick Van Emburgh.
Talbot County Engineer Ray Clarke criticized the project and the lack of communication between developers and the county. Clarke said it'll put an undue stress on Airport and Goldsborough Neck Roads and added concerns that the homes will be in the runway protection zone for Easton Airport.
"We need to be very, very careful when we're looking at these types of development," Clarke said. "This was general commercial as originally planned. We were told three or four years ago it was going to be warehouses."
On Tuesday, the Planning Commission opted to place a pin in the matter and revisit it on July 17. Commission members may then provide a recommendation.
Once the commission makes its recommendation, council members will consider the application and hold a public hearing before any decision. While the council may take the commission's decision into account, the five council members have the final say, with a majority required for approval.

title: A single candlelight can chase darkness away
author: Ken George; Ridgely Church of the Brethren
content:
A single candlelight can chase darkness away

 September 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ken George; Ridgely Church of the Brethren | Page: B8 | Section: News 
 
 265
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The book of Lamentations, attributed to the prophet Jeremiah, is a sad book that expresses sorrow and regret over the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, over the people turning away from God and over the desolation of their country at the hands of the Babylonians.The definition of the word "lament", according to the Mirriam-Webster dictionary, is "to mourn aloud, to express sorrow" or to "regret strongly".There are five chapters in Lamentations; and, yet, in the middle chapter, amid all this sadness and regret, there lays a ray of hope. We read in Chapter 3, verse 21-23, "But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: the steadfast love of the Lord never ceases, His mercies never come to an end.They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!" We often find ourselves lamenting the state of the world today.Injustices against minorities, human trafficking, mass shootings and other heartbreaking occurrences seem to dominate the headlines of the news. Even so, amid all our trials, troubles and tribulations, we are reminded that the sun peeks out from the clouds, and a single candlelight can chase the night away.In John 8:12, Jesus tells us that He is "the light of the world", and those who follow Him "will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life." With God's word, and with Jesus as the light of the world that we follow, we have the hope that the "steadfast love of the Lord never ceases. His mercies never come to an end." In the end, it will be all right.

title: White House OKs Maryland wind energy project
author: KATHARINE WILSON Capital News Service
content:
White House OKs Maryland wind energy project

 September 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KATHARINE WILSON Capital News Service | Section: State News 
 
 959
 Words 

 Read News Document

 WASHINGTON — Offshore wind energy is coming to Maryland, and with it, union jobs.The Biden administration on Thursday approved Baltimore-based US Wind's project to build offshore wind turbines about 10 miles off the coast of Ocean City, Maryland.
The offshore wind farm could generate over two gigawatts of wind energy and power over 718,000 homes, according to the Department of the Interior.
President Joe Biden said in a statement that the wind energy industry had been "struggling to gain a foothold" in the years before he came into office.
"From manufacturing and shipbuilding to port operations and construction, this industry will support tens of thousands of good-paying and union jobs, provide reliable clean power to homes and businesses, strengthen our power grid against outages, and help reduce pollution — all while protecting biodiversity and marine ecosystems," the president said.
Maryland Energy Administration Director Paul Pinsky called the Biden administration's action "an important step forward in the effort to bring clean, renewable energy production to Maryland's coast."
"Today's announcement underscores the careful, comprehensive and collaborative environmental analysis that has gone into these projects," Pinsky said in a statement.
The Maryland project is the tenth commercial-scale offshore wind energy project approved by the Biden administration. Combined, the projects are projected to generate 15 gigawatts of clean energy, half of Biden's goal of 30 gigawatts of offshore wind-produced energy by 2030.
The Maryland project includes up to 114 wind turbines, four offshore substation platforms and a meteorological tower. There will be three phases to the US Wind project, two of which — called MarWin and Momentum Wind — have already received offshore renewable energy certificates from the state.
Energy is set to start flowing in December 2028 from the first phase of the project. The final project is expected to be completed in late 2027 or early 2028, according to the plan submitted by US Wind.
The approval is a win for Maryland environmental groups and the state government, which have been working for offshore wind power in the state for around 10 years.
Starting in 2013, the Maryland legislature passed a series of bills to set offshore wind energy projects in motion.
The state set a goal in 2023, through the Promoting Offshore Wind Energy Resources Act, to generate 8.5 gigawatts of power from offshore wind by 2031.
This goal has hit some road bumps along the way, including the withdrawal of Denmark-based Ørsted's planned offshore wind projects in January.
US Wind won the competitive lease sale of the 46,970 acres of federal ocean waters in 2014.
"By moving away from reliance on dirty fossil fuel energy and building renewable energy, Marylanders will be able to breathe cleaner air and benefit from new clean energy jobs," Maryland Sierra Club Chapter Director Josh Tulkin said in a statement Thursday.
Jamie DeMarco, the federal campaigns coordinator for the Chesapeake Climate Action Network, said in an interview with Capital News Service that the Maryland wind farm is a milestone in moving offshore energy generation forward in Maryland.
"This is a huge undertaking to build an entire machine to deploy offshore wind, but once that machine is built, it'll be able to hum and crank out new domestic energy, and clean energy that's going to help us clean the air and meet our climate goals," DeMarco said.
Offshore wind turbines have been coming online across the East Coast, DeMarco said, but this will be the first operational offshore wind facility in Maryland.
Environmental advocates aren't the only celebrating parties. Union officials are touting the jobs set to be created by the wind farm.
Almost 2,680 jobs annually over seven years could be created during the development and construction phase of the wind farm, according to the Interior Department.
US Wind's planned permanent offshore wind components production facility, called Sparrows Point Steel in Sparrows Point, Baltimore — the former home of Bethlehem Steel — is forecast to generate jobs for steelworkers.
The Baltimore Bethlehem Steel mill, which closed in 2012, was once the largest steel producer in the world. Sparrows Point Steel will bring steelworker jobs back to Maryland, DeMarco said, in a way that hasn't been seen since the closure of Bethlehem.
Jim Strong, the offshore wind sector assistant for the United Steelworkers International Union, told CNS Thursday that the facility is expected to bring in over 500 jobs. The project will help not only steelworkers, Strong said, but other union trades as well.
"It's about addressing our climate crisis, about creating new green energy jobs — these will be high paid union jobs," Strong said.
Strong has served as a liaison between the union and US Wind. He said that the Sparrows Point facility has the opportunity to become a "central hub" for monopile production on the Atlantic Ocean. Monopiles, steel cylinders, are used for wind turbines, bridges and other projects, he said.
US Wind is a subsidiary of Italian company Renexia SpA.
The project has some detractors, like Rep. Andy Harris (R-Maryland), who represents the Eastern Shore.
"Offshore wind industrialization comes at a heavy cost to our marine life and environment, and is an incredibly expensive way to generate electricity," Harris said on X in July. "We should never allow foreign owned companies to control our energy supply — much less harm our environment while doing it."
The federal Bureau of Ocean Energy Management's director, Elizabeth Klein, said in a statement that the Maryland project "reflects the best available science and invaluable insights from Tribes, government agencies, local communities, industry leaders, ocean users, and environmental groups gathered during our extensive environmental review process."
"As we continue to support the undeniable momentum we see along our coasts, our focus remains on fostering responsible energy development, while protecting marine life and ecosystems," she said.
Democrats in the state, including Gov. Wes Moore, have been supportive of the project. Moore signed a memorandum of understanding with the federal government in June supporting offshore wind production.

title: Talbot school board dives into test score trends
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot school board dives into test score trends

 September 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 695
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Talbot school officials took a deeper look at state test scores last week, indicating upward trends in math and English for some grades and dips in others.At a work session on Sept. 15, Helga Einhorn, assistant superintendent of school leadership and student success, presented to Talbot Board of Education members breakdowns of 2024-2025 Maryland Comprehensive Assessment Program scores by grade and student group.
The presentation showed increases from the previous year in English proficiency for third and fourth grades, but drops for fifth and eighth grades. Math proficiency spiked year-to-year for fourth, sixth and seventh grades, but the number of students proficient algebra significantly fell.
The deeper dive came after the state released test score data for the 2024-2025 school year last month. While proficiency rates increased statewide, Talbot County students saw mixed results. English proficiency dropped to 45.4%, 16th in the state and the largest year-to-year decrease (1.9%) of all districts.
In math, 18.9% of students were proficient, 18th in the state and nearly even with the previous year's mark. Other counties, such as Dorchester, saw notable gains, rising spots in the statewide rankings.
Two days after the Sept. 15 work session, Talbot Board of Ed Member Deborah Bridges said at a monthly meeting that the district's results kept her up at night.
"After our work session on Monday night, I couldn't sleep," Bridges said. "Our scores, it upset me so much. And I wondered, what are we missing? What is going on in our schools?"
Board members largely agreed that the results aren't a matter of pointing fingers at teachers or staff. Instead, they are focused finding solutions to fix some of the problem areas.
Board President Emily Jackson said at the work session that she hopes school officials can begin to pinpoint some reasons behind the data trends.
"If I look at us, and we're going down, whereas a neighboring county who has a similar population of kids and they're going up, I want to know why," Jackson said.
Einhorn said while the state tests are an "important measure," it's one of many ways to assess academic achievement and growth.
"This is one assessment given at a single period of time, which does not always accurately reflect what students know and what they're able to do overall," Einhorn said.
ENGLISH
Fifth and tenth grades suffered the largest proficiency drops of 5.6% and 10%, respectively. But fourth grade proficiency rose to 50% in the most recent results. And while third grade proficiency dipped from last year's 47.9% mark, it's still at 43.6%, an improvement over a 35% rate two years ago.
"This really speaks to the work that this board has invested in early literacy, and starting to see that trend move up," Einhorn said at the work session.
Meanwhile, most student groups followed the district's overall trend of slightly decreasing in English proficiency. Asian students fell from 68.9% to 51.2%, while Talbot's multilingual learners dropped from 8.7% to 5.1%.
MATH
One of the sharpest drops came in Algebra II proficiency: 32.8% of students passed the state test in 2023-2024; only 7.1% passed in 2024-2025.
Einhorn acknowledged that as an "area of need." She noted that new math standards for K-8 will go into effect next school year. And in two years, the district will begin integrated algebra courses, infusing geometry concepts, she said.
Fourth grade rose nearly six percentage points to 32% proficiency this past year, while seventh grade had a similar hike from 11% to 17%.
By student group, one result stood out: Black students in the district remain under 5% proficient in math. Einhorn admitted the shortcoming.
"The less than 5% is indicating that we are still underserving our Black students and that we still need to continue looking at strategies that better prepare them to show what they know and are able to do in mathematics," Einhorn said.
Board Member Dyshekia Strawberry said she'd like to see the district work with community partners to specifically tackle the gap in math proficiency for Black students.
Board members thanked Einhorn for presenting the detailed trends, acknowledging that there's work to be done to get some of the numbers going in a positive direction.
"We have to do better, and we're open to hear how we're going to do that," Jackson said.

title: Contractor bringing Oxford's Strand project up to specifications
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Contractor bringing Oxford's Strand project up to specifications

 April 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 318
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Efforts to complete the first phase of the Strand Beach project are underway this week after it was determined the project was not finished to the specifications originally presented to the town.During a Commissioners of Oxford meeting March 25, Oxford Town Manager Holly Wahl said work to complete the project would begin the week of March 31.
In order to finish the first phase of the project, the contractor, Underwood and Associates, will lower the islands on the beach, remove temporary access to the islands, purchase and install native plantings and install a grassy strip along the roadway to prevent sand from flowing into the roadway, Wahl said. All of these items are to be completed to match the approved permit and site plan.
Wahl said Underwood and Associates is required to complete this phase of the project by April 19.
In December, the Commissioners of Oxford announced that although the Strand Beach project was signed off on in June by previous Town Manager Cheryl Lewis, the project had not been completed to the specifications that Underwood and Associates had originally presented.
The plan for the project was to create a berm, place hooks along the east and west areas of the Strand to bring in sand, create small islands in the water to reduce waves coming onto the beach and plant low marsh grasses on those islands. During the commissioners meeting in December, Commissioner Katrina Greer said not all the grasses had been planted on the islands and the islands were two feet higher in elevation than they were supposed to be.
That month, Greer brought together the Maryland Department of the Environment, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Underwood and Associates and the organizations that funded the project to ensure Underwood and Associates would bring down the elevation of the islands and take out the sand that goes out to the headlands at no cost to the town.
