title: Julia Child's kitchen at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
Julia Child's kitchen at the library

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 696
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Monday, March 3, at 6 p.m., in the Easton branch of the Talbot County Free Library, it will be my honor to interview Paula Johnson about her newest book, "Julia Child's Kitchen: The Design, Tools, Stories, and Legacy of an Iconic Space."Full disclosure: Johnson is a lifelong friend of mine. She is also a distinguished curator at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. Among her many curatorial triumphs, it was Johnson and co-curator Rayna Green that brought Julia Child's kitchen to the museum in 2001. Almost a quarter of a century later, it remains one of that institution's most popular exhibits.
I was one of the lucky fellows who received a copy of Johnson's new book when it came out in October.
Initially, truth be told, I wasn't sure what I would think of a book about a kitchen, fool that I am. Anyone who knows Julia Child, read her books or watched her television shows, knows that a book about Julia Child's kitchen is a book about Julia Child.
It's been a long time since I've had so much fun reading a book.
And the word "fun" is apt. Again and again in the book, as people recall cooking with Child in her kitchen or a meal they shared there, the word they use to describe both their host and the place is "fun."
Which is not to say that serious labor did not take place in that kitchen.
The book makes it clear that Child and her husband Paul were both workhorses. In the early television shows, the sponsoring public television station, WGBH Boston, couldn't afford retakes or editing. Julia had to begin upon a complicated recipe, carry it through, instructing all along, and arrive at a finished product that she could take a bite out of in just 28 minutes flat. The cameras shut off at 28 minutes, and there was no going back.
To accomplish this feat of legerdemain, she and Paul would practice for hours at home before a show, choosing which elements of a recipe to demonstrate, deciding how to demonstrate those elements and carefully working out the language to use in explaining them.
The whole thing was choreographed from beginning to end and different stages of the cooking prepared in advance so that, "through the magic of TV," they could be displayed at the proper time as if just pulled from the oven.
Yet somehow, Julia always came across as relaxed and enjoying herself. And it wasn't a guise.
One of the things I found most endearing about "Julia Child's Kitchen" is the way sections on subjects such as the kitchen's organizing principles inevitably end up revealing the love Paul Child felt for his wife, the care he took in setting up that kitchen and showcasing her art. In letters to his brother, Paul sometimes referred to his wife as "Julie."
Julia called her kitchen "the soul of the house," and her nephew, Alex Prud'homme, called the table where meals were served in that kitchen "the center of the universe."
Unsurprisingly for that time and a family of their class, the Childs had a formal dining room, but Julia's preferred place to serve friends a meal was the kitchen. Julia's unpretentious attitude toward entertaining (and herself) is made clear in her explanation for the placement of that kitchen table, "I want the dining table in the middle of the room because, like a sheepdog, I need to be right there in the midst of everyone."
That statement is so characteristic of the woman we meet in Johnson's book. Julia Child never fails to charm, yet somehow she never seems to patronize or fawn.
The book itself is like a party at Julia's house. You meet fascinating people, hear terrific stories, experience a magical place, and, at the very least, get to imagine yourself enjoying extraordinary meals.
Speaking of stories, I can tell you from long experience that the author of "Julia Child's Kitchen" is a great storyteller in person as well as in her writing. And so I ask the pleasure of your company on March 3 at 6 p.m. for an evening in Julia Child's kitchen, courtesy of the Smithsonian's Paula Johnson. Trust me, you're in for a real treat.

title: Caroline Commissioners pass bills, approve roads projects
author: Connie Connolly
content:
Caroline Commissioners pass bills, approve roads projects

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Connie Connolly | Section: Local News 
 
 532
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Road paving projects, legislative picks and pans, and zoning decisions formed the bulk of the Caroline County Commission meeting at 9 a.m. Tuesday, Feb. 13, in Denton.After a lengthy discussion with Deputy County Administrator Daniel Fox and Roads Superintendent Bryan North, the commissioners settled on beginning paving projects for two county roads.
Wolf Road near Henderson and a short dirt section of Jones Corner Road at Concord will be paved with tar and chip, and paid for with leftover American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 funding.
Two roads affected by flooding are awaiting better weather and materials. Fox said he will be getting a purchase order to the commissioners next week for $122,000 to buy the precast concrete needed to improve the River Road site. Unusually high tides have prevented work on Gilpin Point Road, although the replacement pipes are on hand.
Legislative actionsThe commissioners introduced legislation to change zoning requirements for solar energy systems in the R-Rural District, repealing subsections in Section 175 of the county code, and "reenacting the same with amendments." The legislation is Bill 2024-003.
Originally proposed in October 2023, public comment prompted the county Planning Commission to recommend changes. Screening requirements, including working with a licensed landscape architect and providing for a variety of buffers were not changed.
Also unchanged was the restriction on placing commercial solar on the portion of acreage that was used for transfer development rights. Road right-of-way setbacks were increased.
The second reading and public hearing for Bill 2024-003 is set for Feb. 20 at the County Commission meeting. The third reading is scheduled for March 12, with an anticipated effective date of April 26.
Two other pieces of legislation were read for the third time and enacted unanimously. Legislative Bill 2024-001, authorizes additional projects to be funded from the proceedings of the Consolidated Public Improvement and Refunding Bonds of 2019.
The projects are roof replacements for Federalsburg Elementary School, North Caroline High School and Preston Elementary School, as well as a new HVAC system for the Fretterd Center in Denton.
The bond proceeds were reallocated since the commissioners are not pursuing the renovations of the county detention center, anticipating the eventual construction of a regional detention center.
Legislative Bill 2024-002 revised stream buffer requirements for both perennial and intermittent streams, increasing them from 25 to 50 feet.
State legislation
Commission Vice President Larry Porter and Public Information Officer Jennifer Reibly have attended Maryland General Assembly legislative session updates with various groups.
The commissioners will send letters of opposition and directives to the lobbyists to oppose bills that "take away local autonomy" such as House Bill 1407, which would preempt a county's authority to decide if and where to place solar arrays, Porter said.
Porter recommended opposing a statewide school emergency response bill, consulting with the Recreation and Parks Department regarding legislation that would require counties to replace certain playground surface materials and opposing funding cuts to community colleges.
Because the county "has been a catalyst" for lithium battery safety, Porter recommended supporting House Bill 468/Senate Bill 530.
The commissioners discussed other pending legislation. To view the meeting of the commissioners, watch the video posted on the commissioners' website, usually within 48 hours of the meeting.
Agendas, videos and transcripts of commission meetings are posted at carolinemd.org.

title: rest of mike's story
author: Staff Writer
content:
rest of mike's story

 September 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Rest Of Mikes Story 
 
 710
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FOCUS ON THE BASERyan Waite, a veteran campaign consultant and vice president of public affairs with northern California-based consulting firm Think Big, said the political parties and most campaigns are focused on ginning up and turning out their voter bases and don't tend to engage with low-propensity voters."They put resources where it is going to make the most difference. Typically, you are looking at people who have previously voted, who are kind in that soft middle," said Waite, who has mostly worked on Republican campaigns.
Waite said while social media can help engage more voters and could help engage nonvoters, especially young ones, the medium presents challenges.
"You are competing with everything else. The slice of time you get in front of them is very very small," he said of the social media content streams.
Negative campaigning, coarse social discourse and misinformation on key issues have also magnified on social media leaving voters and nonvoters distrustful of content and disparate and sometimes ideological information sources.
"It's hard for average voters to figure out what's going on," said Waite.
In an Aug. 26 letter to the House Judiciary Committee, META Platforms chairman and CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the Biden-Harris administration "repeatedly pressured" Facebook and Instagram to censor dissenting content (including humor and satire) related to COVID-19.
The White House defended those actions as helping protect public health from misinformation.
Recent surveys show low levels of trust in politics, the media and government, as well as plenty of economic stress stemming from the post-pandemic inflation wave.
A June survey by financial firm Credit Karma and research firm Qualtrics found 68% of Americans don't believe official economic data touting job gains and easing inflation after post-pandemic spikes in prices.
Another recent poll by Gallup and the Walton Foundation shows Gen Zers (ages 12 to 27) have little trust in the media, government and politics. But they showed strong turnout in 2020 and are expected to also show up in November, said Craig Snyder, campaign director for Haley Voters for Harris (a group that hopes to get GOP supporters of former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley to eschew Trump).
NEW ENERGY?Snyder said Harris' campaign should energize younger voters more than the matchup between Trump and President Joe Biden.
"They weren't excited about a race between two 80-year-old men," said Snyder, noting that Democratic enthusiasm for Harris will also generate GOP energy for Trump.
Harris was installed at the top of the Democratic ticket after Biden, 81, was pressured to quit the race by donors and party power players over concerns about his age.
Snyder said voting groups such as suburban women, Black and Hispanic men, along with voters on both sides of Israel's war in Gaza against Hamas could tip the race in battlegrounds such as Michigan, Wisconsin, North Carolina and Pennsylvania.
Independent presidential candidate Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s endorsement of Trump could also shift his voters, many of whom are disaffected by COVID policies (including vaccines), in key states.
Snyder also sees another contingent of nonvoters beyond the disaffected and those with logistical barriers.
"There's a third group," he said. "They just don't connect politics to their lives."
GOTV EFFORTSPolitical organizations on both sides do have get-out-the-vote (GOTV) efforts across the country, including some aimed at first-time and nonvoters.
Conservative groups — such as Christians United for Israel — hope to turn out evangelicals for Trump and Republicans. That includes working with churches across the country on support for Israel and voter mobilization.
Democrats look to college campuses, as well as Native Americans, Blacks and Hispanics in key races.
In Montana, Nick Marroletti, coordinated campaign director for the state Democratic Party, said grassroots turn-out efforts have included knocking on 100,000 doors and making 97,000 phone calls supporting U.S. Sen. Jon Tester, who faces a tough challenge from Republican Tim Sheehy.
'LACK OF FAITH'Mara Ostfeld, a research scientist at the University of Michigan, analyzed voting sentiments in Detroit and found Latino voters, in particular, have lower turnout propensities.
Ostfeld agrees that nonvoters, especially lower-income ones, don't see the outcome of elections impacting their daily lives.
"There is a disconnect," Ostfeld said. But she also said that doesn't mean nonvoters are not engaged or connected to their communities in other ways and don't follow politics.
"It's not like they are disinterested or disengaged," Ostfeld said. "There is just a lack of faith in the political system in particular."

title: Five counties unite for recovery awareness event at Church Hill Park
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Five counties unite for recovery awareness event at Church Hill Park

 September 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 534
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHURCH HILL — Standing united as one community in support of recovery and awareness across the area, Mid Shore Behavioral Health, Inc. hosted its annual five county collaborative Going Purple Together at Church Hill Park Sept. 27.Organizations and agencies from neighboring counties of Queen Anne's, Talbot, Kent Caroline, and Dorchester came together to show the community all the resources available for substance recovery, mental health, addiction, and support.
Annually supporting recovery across the Mid-Shore region, the 2025 Going Purple Together event offered a blend of, fun, education and community engagement, with local vendors, activities, and the message of continually learning about substance abuse, overdose, recovery, peer support, and prevention.
Highlighting important community resources in a fun, casual environment, festivities were complete with DJ, food trucks, giveaways, family fun activities and performances by Hula Hoop Love.
Building awareness through engagement
Recognizing substance abuse awareness and prevention is more nuanced than "Just Say No" community engagement is the first step in addressing issues.
By building awareness in a fun environment, the community can be proactive and not reactive, said Queen Anne's County Circuit Court Judge Lynn Knight, a founder of the Queen Anne's County Circuit Court Assisted Recovery and Treatment program.
Ten years ago substance abuse resources did not exist in the county like they do today, and the growth in support is tremendous, she said.
Personal stories of recovery
Showcasing the possibilities of recovery straight from those who have lived it first hand, peer support specialists shared their personal experiences to help inspire and encourage those in need.
One such peer, Kaylee Whitby, of Federalsburg, noted for the longest time her personal story was a continual cycle riddled with active addiction, treatment, jail, and legal issues.
Finally after an attempt on her own life, Whitby fought to give herself a new way of living because "it was obvious my way was not working."
Through continual effort and the support of peers, Whitby was able to join in recovery services that finally made a lasting impact on her recovery journey and ultimately her life.
Whitby voiced gratitude for the opportunities offered through supportive recovery houses, including security, accountability, growth, and networking connections still part of her life today.
"Recovery saved my life," she said. Because of recovery Whitby learned to surrender and make amends to rebuild relationships. Whitby was able to be the mother that her children deserved and be the person she wanted to be.
Knowing there were others out in the community with their own similar experiences helped shape Whitby and she was eager to pay that forward to inspire others and be part of that journey.
"Today I chose to live," Whitby said.
Comprehensive support services
Understanding the many avenues that go hand in hand with recovery, organizations connected the community with the tools for support including behavioral and mental health, social services, gambling help, out and inpatient services, as well as resources for loved ones of those facing diseases of addiction.
Mid Shore Behavioral Health, is proud to continually work closely with community and county health departments and administration to erase stigma and further advocacy said Alisha Saulsbury, forensic mental health program manager.
Seeing people smile proud of themselves on their recovery journey makes it all worthwhile, Saulsbury said.
More information about Mid Shore Behavioral Health can be found at midshorebehavioralhealth.org.

title: CBMM launches new construction buyboat
author: Contributed
content:
CBMM launches new construction buyboat

 October 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 10 | Section: News 
 
 496
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Bay Maritime Museum's Shipyard has completed its latest project with the launch of the 36-foot Chesapeake Bay buyboat Mr. Dickie.The Shipyard team began work on the new construction build last fall after finishing up its build ofMary-land Dove and worked over the past year under the direction of Shipyard Foreman Jeff Reed to bring the vessel to life.A contract build for owners Grigg and Cindy Mullen of Lexington, Va., Mr. Dickie will be on display later this month at the Sultana Downrigging Festival in Chestertown before returning to dock at CBMM."Grigg provided the opportunity for us to have our Shipyard team do a complete build from start to finish, creating a unique object in a way that realizes Grigg and our dream of a comprehensive construction that allows for public and Shipwright education," said Vice President of Shipyard Operations Christian Cabral. "It's been an incredible experience."The construction of the unique vessel in CBMM's Shipyard offered a glimpse into the past while highlighting the future for a historic style ofvessel vital to the story of the Chesapeake Bay.Buyboats are cross-planked workboats that were traditionally used for hauling oysters from skipjacks to market in season and anything else that needed transporting the rest of the year.Today, there are estimated to be fewer than 30 buyboats that continue to ply the Bay's waters.Mr. Dickie pays homage to the 60-foot buyboat Mundy Point, designed to bring the buyboat look to a scaled-down 36-foot version. It was constructed from heart pine, white oak, Atlantic cedar and western red cedar, and outfitted with a restored late-1930s Buda diesel engine.A retired engineering professor, Grigg Mullen maintained a hands-on role throughout the yearlong construction, working alongside CBMM's Shipyard crew whenever his schedule allowed.He and Cindy were on hand for a CBMM Member Night on Oct. 12 celebrating Mr. Dickie and the Oct. 20 launch for the new buyboat that is named in honor of the late Dickie Whaley, Mullen's neighbor growing up in Queen Anne's County."It's been a wonderful year building Mr. Dickie and working with the Shipyard folks," Mullen said. "Every time there was a decision to make, it was always - if we do it this way, it's going to be better. It's turned out wonderfully."With Mr. Dickie completed, CBMM's Shipyard will stay busy with a variety of projects heading into the winter months, including ongoing work on a pair of buyboats in its historic floating fleet.Winnie Estelle, CBMM's passenger-carrying 1920 buyboat, is amidst a refit that includes the removal, fabrication, and replacement of its structural timbers. 1938 buyboat Choptank is undergoing a final fit out, which involves building out the interior with cabins and heads for expedition-style overnight trips and outfitting it with modern safety equipment and a new rig.Findmore information about CBMM's Shipyard and itsprojects at cbmm.org/ship-yard.

title: Hawaiian outrigger canoes making waves in the Chesapeake
author: JEREMY COX Bay Journal
content:
Hawaiian outrigger canoes making waves in the Chesapeake

 February 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JEREMY COX Bay Journal | Section: Local News 
 
 631
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Skipjacks, deadrises, log canoes, tall ships, bugeyes — the Chesapeake Bay has no shortage of iconic boats. But if a core group of devotees has anything to do with it, a vessel closely associated with the South Pacific could be next.The outrigger canoe is practically synonymous with Polynesian and Hawaiian cultures. Many Americans of a certain age, though, likely received their notions about outriggers from the closing credits of the original version of the TV crime drama Hawaii Five-O, which showed a sequence of muscly men vigorously paddling through waves.
That depiction — of brute strength and more than a whiff of masculinity — continues to loom over the sport of outrigger racing in the popular imagination. But the brand practiced by Maryland's Kent Island Outrigger Canoe Club tends, by intention, toward inclusivity and working in harmony.
"People of all ages and abilities can do this," said Bill Key, 72, a longtime member. "You can't screw it up. We're thrilled to have you out here no matter what."
To that end, during routine club practices, members are often found welcoming newcomers who want to try their hands at the ancient sport. This spring, they hosted a series of outings explicitly geared toward coaxing novices onto the water, with the hope of boosting membership.
So, there I was on a Sunday morning in April, standing with a strange-looking paddle in my hands and absolutely no idea what I was getting myself into.
The first thing you notice about an outrigger canoe is how long and narrow it is. Single and tandem versions are available. But, like the one in the Hawaii Five-O outro, the craft I boarded could comfortably seat six adults. Most outriggers in this class measure more than 40 feet from stern to bow, roughly the length of a school bus, but the main hull might be a mere 16 inches across.
This is where the "outrigger" part comes into play. Two arms (iakos in Hawaiian) project from one side of the canoe. These connect to a float (the "outrigger" or, in Hawaiian, the ama). Without these second hulls, the vessels would be highly unstable in the open seas.
Now, let's turn to the paddle. The shaft isn't straight like a traditional canoe oar or kayak paddle; it's slightly bowed, and the blade is angled back a bit to compensate for the bend. At the opposite end of the paddle is a t-shaped handle. Your palm wraps around it, kind of like a bicycle handlebar. Your lower hand should be gripping the shaft just above the blade. It feels more like digging into the water than sweeping through it.
The outrigger club here traces its history back 25 years, when John Fulton, who had recently returned to Maryland after a few years living in Hawaii, raised enough money to purchase a communal outrigger canoe.
"It's the state sport of Hawaii," he said. "Just about everybody does it."
The sport has long since migrated to the mainland United States, but its presence on the East Coast remains limited. The nationwide parent organization for outrigger canoe racing chapters lists 70 clubs operating in the three continental states that border the Pacific Ocean. The East Coast boasts a mere 17 clubs.
The Kent Island club, the only outrigger group with a Maryland address, counts about three dozen active members. They compete in races up and down the East Coast and host their own event over Labor Day weekend, a 35-mile relay race in which paddlers circumnavigate Kent Island.
From what I could gather, outrigger canoe racing tends to attract experienced standup paddleboarders or kayakers looking for a team environment.
"This is a great way (to) get out on the water with people who become your friends," said longtime member Nancy Wallace. "I think I knew one person when I first started. It becomes a family."

title: Dorchester County ballot questions will not take effect due to 'administrative error'
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Dorchester County ballot questions will not take effect due to 'administrative error'

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 454
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Although Dorchester County voters who took to the polls in November voted on whether changes should be made to the county charter, those changes will not be made this year.During a Dorchester County Council meeting on March 4, Council President Lenny Pfeffer announced the county had made an "administrative error" by not advertising the referendum questions for five consecutive weeks after the council approved them.
"With it not being advertised correctly per state law, it would not make those referendum questions valid to change the charter," Pfeffer said.
The error in advertising was an accident, Pfeffer said, and he apologized to county residents.
"As far as blame for this, this entire (council) and Dorchester County takes general responsibility for this mistake," he said.
Pfeffer said the error was discovered in the process of reclaiming the county's sanitary district. He said that during the bond review process, legal counsel for the bond review discovered the oversight.
Pfeffer said the county waited for additional legal review before telling the public.
In an interview with the Star Democrat March 5, Pfeffer said the council was notified of the error a little over a month ago. He said the county had previously been trying to have the amendments made to the charter by spring.
In November, county residents voted to amend four parts of the county charter. The changes amended the charter to:
Have the review of administrative structure be conducted within the first fiscal year of each Dorchester County Council term. Currently, the charter says a review of administrative structure should take place at least every four years, but it does not state when in that four years it should take place.Push back budget-related due dates 15 days.Clarify responsibilities of the county manager, including day-to-day operations, and establish procedures for certain vacancies. Currently, the charter has procedures in place for council member and treasurer vacancies, as well as certain board and commission vacancies.Include language to ensure transparency of governmental functions as well as access to open meetings and public records.
Pfeffer said although these amendments cannot be made to the charter now, they could be voted on again in future elections.
"So it will be up to the wishes of the Charter Review Commission and the council before the next election on if any one, all of, or whatever list of referendum questions could get placed on the ballot next time," he said.
Dorchester County Attorney Chip MacLeod said the county is looking into whether the ballot questions that were approved by voters could be addressed through county code or policy changes.
MacLeod called the situation "unfortunate," but made it clear other opportunities might exist.
"One way or another, the county's going to be impacted by those charter amendments, even though they're not technically valid," he said.

title: QAC achieves significant milestone in reducing marine industry plastic waste
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
QAC achieves significant milestone in reducing marine industry plastic waste

 July 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 440
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Queen Anne's County has achieved a remarkable success in its ongoing efforts to reduce plastic waste generated by the marine industry. The county's recent initiative to recycle single-use boat shrink wrap has resulted in a significant increase in the amount of plastic diverted from landfills.In the second year of the program, the Queen Anne's County government, in partnership with Plastic Free QAC and the Marine Trades Association of Maryland, has seen a 370% increase in the amount of recycled shrink wrap compared to last year.
This year, a total of six tons pounds of plastic shrink wrap was collected and recycled, a substantial increase from the 1.62 tons collected in 2023.
Queen Anne's County Commissioner Phil Dumenil expressed his enthusiasm, stating, "This significant increase in our recycling efforts underscores the dedication and commitment of our residents and businesses to protect our county. By expanding the availability of MTAM recycle bags and increasing the public awareness, we have made it easier for everyone to participate in this important initiative."
Key highlights of this year's success include:
Increased participation from individual boat owner with a notable rise in the number of individual boat owners participating in the recycling program, showcasing the community's growing environmental consciousness.Expansion of recycling bag pickup locations; the program expanded from one to four convenient pickup locations for MTAM recycle bags, including:West Marine in Chester, Rommel's Ace Hardware in Stevensville, Centreville Town Hall and Refill Goodness in Stevensville.Commitment from local marinas and boat companies. Several local businesses committed to responsible disposal of shrink wrap, among them: Bay Bridge Marina, Bosun's Marine, Atlantic Yacht Services and Pocket Yacht Company
The MTAM recycle bags, sponsored by the County Commissioners, were provided free of charge and made available at multiple locations. The dedicated MTAM shrink wrap dumpster at the Grasonville Transfer Station facilitated easy and eco-friendly disposal for boat owners from early April to June.
This initiative is part of Queen Anne's County's broader commitment to environmental stewardship and sustainability. By continuing to work together, the county aims to set an example for other communities across Maryland and beyond.
Plastic Free QAC started in 2018 with the mission to reduce single-use plastic usage in general and places focus on education and building public awareness, according to Sara Shelley, president of Plastic Free QAC.
"We are really thrilled with the community response," she said.
Understanding that old habits with single-use plastics can be hard to shake, Plastic Free QAC looks to continually build involvement by connecting with individual boat owners and hosting community-wide clean ups, Shelley said.
For more information about the recycling program, including where to pick up MTAM recycle bags and drop off cleaned shrink wrap, visit https://lnk.bio/RecycleBoatShrinkwrap.

 On Jan. 24, 1984, Apple Computer began selling its first Macintosh model, which boasted a built-in 9-inch monochrome display, a clock rate of 8 megahertz and 128k of RAM.On this date:
In 1848, James W. Marshall discovered a gold nugget at Sutter's Mill in northern California, a discovery that led to the gold rush of '49.
In 1943, President Franklin D. Roosevelt and British Prime Minister Winston Churchill concluded a wartime conference in Casablanca, Morocco.
In 1945, Associated Press war correspondent Joseph Morton was among a group of captives executed by the Germans at the Mauthausen-Gusen concentration camp in Austria.
In 1965, Winston Churchill died in London at age 90.
In 1978, a nuclear-powered Soviet satellite, Cosmos 954, plunged through Earth's atmosphere and disintegrated, scattering radioactive debris over parts of northern Canada.
In 1985, the space shuttle Discovery was launched from Cape Canaveral on the first secret, all-military shuttle mission.
In 1989, confessed serial killer Theodore Bundy was executed in Florida's electric chair.
In 2003, former Pennsylvania Gov. Tom Ridge was sworn as the first secretary of the new Department of Homeland Security.
In 2011, a suicide bomber attacked Moscow's busiest airport, killing 37 people; Chechen separatists claimed responsibility.
In 2013, President Barack Obama's Defense Secretary Leon Panetta announced the lifting of a ban on women serving in combat.
In 2018, former sports doctor Larry Nassar, who had admitted molesting some of the nation's top gymnasts for years under the guise of medical treatment, was sentenced to 40 to 175 years in prison.
In 2023, the sci-fi indie hit "Everything Everywhere All at Once" led Oscar nominations with 11. (It would go on to win seven, including best picture.)

In an interview with the Star Democrat, Dorchester County Council President Lenny Pfeffer said Powell resigned from the CWDI board over a year ago when he took on the role of interim county manager.

title: Men For Change recognizes volunteers' service
author: Tom McCall
content:
Men For Change recognizes volunteers' service

 July 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 532
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — On July 20, about 80 people gathered at the Federalsburg Volunteer Fire Company banquet hall to recognize Men For Change's People of the Year.The Federalsburg nonprofit's slogan is "changing our community through service." They are geared toward mentoring youth and trying to help them make productive choices. This was the 14th year of the recognition awards.
There were six people honored for their work: Federalsburg's District One Councilman Brandy James, Principal of Federalsburg Elementary School Stephanie Brohawn, coach and volunteer William Eric Smith, community activist Cynthia Fletcher, Haitian community liaison Cederick Turner and Roberta Butler of the NAACP.
Betty Jarman, the media spokesperson for Men For Change, said, "The keynote speaker for this event was Vaughn Evans Sr. He was the principal of the North Dorchester Middle School in Hurlock.
She said, "The Men For Change theme this year was 'Let's Get Busy,'" which featured heavily in Evans' address.
In his speech, Evans urged the audience to get busy doing productive, positive things to support youth with the resources they need to become successful.
"They are our future leaders and enterprising entrepreneurs," he said.
He said that the essence of his message aligns with Colossians 3:23-24, which encourages community service and giving back. The bible verse starts, "And whatever you do, do it heartily, as to the Lord and not to men."
James, whose son was in the program years ago, said she is something of a "behind the scenes person" for the nonprofit.
"I am just part of a puzzle, and it takes more than me to push the wheel. It is a community effort," she said. "It was exciting to be acknowledged, but it was more exciting and more rewarding to see the others who were acknowledged.
"So much greatness being acknowledged — magnificent work. It is because of those individuals that so much goodness is happening in Federalsburg," James said.
Recognizing these volunteers is part of MFC's mission. They want the community to know what is happening.
"This is important because we want the broader community to know the people that are doing outstanding volunteer, work without any fanfare. These people are not looking for recognition. We want them to know that we appreciate the work that they are doing," Jarman said.
State Sen. Johnny Mautz (R-Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Wicomico) made citations for all the honorees, though he was unable to attend the event in person.
A recent graduate who participated in the program was also honored Saturday evening. 2024 Colonel Richardson High School graduate Elson Davis was presented with a certificate.
Jarman said, "The event was well attended by young people, young Black men. I thought that was a wonderful thing that they were there to support the honorees."
Jarman also took the opportunity to highlight an upcoming partnership between Men for Change and another local organization, the Federalsburg Activity Center.
"We are also partnering with the Federalsburg Activity Center and their after school mentoring program and other activities going on at the center," Jarman said. "It is still in construction, but we hope it will be open by September."
This project, still under construction, is repurposing the Dollar General in Federalsburg. Men For Change is still open to receiving donations.
"Once the center is open, we will need more volunteers," Jarman said.

 EASTON - Angie Webb wasn't sure what she did.But Saints Peter and Paul High's freshman knew the way her field hockey teammates were celebrating it must have been something good.It also proved to be the difference Tuesday, as Webb ripped the game's lone goal into the right side of the cage with 3:50 remaining in the first quarter, helping the Sabres to a 1-0 victory over Easton."It was a beautiful goal," Sts. Peter & Paul head coach Debbie McQuaid said after the Sabres improved to 10-2 with their fourth straight victory, the last three by shutout.Webb gained possession of the ball from about 25 yards away from Easton's cage near the 4-minute mark of the first period. She circled left, then moved right before unloading a hard drive from the left side that got past Warrior goalie Alli Newman before banging into the far right corner of the cage."My teammates basically helped us all get up the field," Webb said. "I just took it and I don't know what really happened.I was just really determined to get that goal. I knew I had to get off a shot real quickly. I just hit it and it went in. I was really shocked." Easton (5-4) earned two of its nine penalty corners in the final 1:15 of the first quarter, getting one shot off that was wide of the mark. Both teams each picked up one corner in the second quarter, but could not capitalize.The game remained even through the third, as the Warriors picked up three more corners, with Easton's Bis Johnson firing wide left.Sts. Peter & Paul had one corner in the third, with Gennie Webb shooting wide right."They came out and they scored on us, and it was a beautiful goal," said Easton head coach Kim Neff, whose team lost its second straight by shutout. "I do feel like the rest of the game we picked up our pace, we had good passing.I felt like our defense and middies played a really great game."They just struck first and we just couldn't capitalize on our opportunities," Neff continued."We had plenty of corners. We had plenty of shots. We just couldn't put it in today." The Sabres earned their fourth and final corner with 11 minutes remaining but didn't managed anything on goal. Easton had two more corner chances, the last with a minute remaining but could not get the equalizer."We really had the determination to win," Sts. Peter & Paul's Jules Stepp said. "They're our friends, and even though they're our friends, we like to have our friendly competition with them."I really think we communicated well and we looked up and we passed to each other," Stepp continued. "And we played a little bit of short and long ball together. And our defense, every time they got the opportunity to get the ball they cleared it out to the side and they recovered. They were on their 'A' game today." But McQuaid thought it took a little while for that 'A' game to materialize."Defense held solid," said McQuaid after goalie Maddie Maloney and company registered their sixth shutout of the season. "They were a little befuddled in the first half and not marking the way they were supposed to. It took them until the second half to start marking the way they were supposed to.Both teams played hard. Lot of skill on both sides.K. ISLAND 3, POCOMOKE 0POCOMOKE CITY - Willow Yost had a pair of goals and Brynja Petursson made nine saves Monday, as the Buccaneers won for the fourth time in five games.Audrey Fleshman scored a goal for Kent Island (4-4) and Sadie Latchaw had two assists.BOYS' SOCCERQUEEN ANNE's 5 NORTH DORCHESTER 0CENTREVILLE - Adan Canales scored twice Monday, and Nicolas Esper added a goal and one assist as the Lions extended their unbeaten streak to four.Ryan Lee and Ryf Eubanks each scored a goal for Queen Anne's (7-1-1, 6-0). William Nagle picked up an assist.NORTH CAROLINE 6ST. MICHAELS 0ST. MICHAELS - Josh Huster, Heremi Capistran Mejia, Omar Marroquin, Austin Lynn, Kevin Godinez and Yossin Roblero had one goal apiece Monday, leading the Bulldogs to their fourth victory in five games.Goalie Gavin O'Brien made three saves for North Caroline (6-3, 5-1).GUNSTON 4DELMARVA CHRISTIAN 0GEORGETOWN, Del. - Senior Jordan Mahaffey scored twice Tuesday as the Herons raised their record to 6-2 with a shutout of Delmarva Christian.GIRLS' SOCCERQUEEN ANNE's 1 STEPHEN DECATUR 1BERLIN - Shannon Rath had a goal and keeper Bea Holthaus made seven saves as the Lions dualed the Seahawks to a double-overtime stalemate Monday.GUNSTON 7SALISBURY SCHOOL 2CENTREVILLE - Freshman Abby Philippon had a hat trick as the Herons improved to 7-1-1.

title: Homemade cleaning solutions save money
author: Mary Hunt
content:
Homemade cleaning solutions save money

 I pretty much hate to buy things I know I can make for less money and in a fraction of the time it takes to find them in a store.Take cleaning products, for example.Knowing I can make specific cleaners for pennies that cost dollars in a store just makes me happy. It's a no-brainer.Here are my top handy recipes to help you get started saving all that money you've been spending on cleaners:EYEGLASSES CLEANING SOLUTIONFill a spray bottle of any size 3/4 full with 70 percent isopropyl rubbing alcohol (91 or 99 percent are fine to use but more costly and not necessary).Add 2 small drops of mild dishwashing liquid (Blue Dawn is ideal), and fill the rest of the bottle with distilled water (see note).Add the spray top, and gently shake the bottle by rolling it between your hands or on a countertop, so as to not create a lot of bubbles. To use: Spray both sides of your lenses, and gently rub them clean with a clean microfiber cloth.WINDSHIELD WASHER FLUIDPour 3 cups rubbing alcohol, 1 tablespoon Blue Dawn and 10 cups distilled water into a 1-gallon plastic jug. Shake thoroughly to mix. Pour into your car windshield washer reservoir in place of commercial windshield washer fluid. Always shake prior to adding to the reservoir.The alcohol speeds the drying time and prevents the windows from freezing or cracking in the winter.Mary Hunt invites you to visit her at Everyday-Cheapskate.com, where this column is archived complete with links and resources for all recommended products and services. title: An Italian seafood Christmas feast
author: Marie Savage; Country Cooking
content:
An Italian seafood Christmas feast

 December 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marie Savage; Country Cooking | Page: A5 | Section: News 
 
 1407
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Recently I attended a luncheon that featured mainly Italian dishes, and I was very impressed with both the number of dishes featured and that you could tell they were a labor of love. Especially my favorite - spaghetti and meatballs!My memory went back to my late Italian friend who served Italian Christmas dinners each year in honor of her Italian ancestry. So, I decided to do an Italian dinner this year in memory of my late friend.
In future columns I will feature others. One of the traditions my old friend's family always celebrated was The Feast of Seven Fishes or, Festa dei Sette Pesci.
A southern Italian tradition known as the "Vigilia di Natale" commemorates the wait for the midnight birth of the baby Jesus. Italian-American families around Christmas time gather together to celebrate Christmas with a huge dinner made up of seven different fish and seafood dishes coming in all different types of forms.
Italian-American immigrants - homesick for the land they left behind - combined classic Italian dishes with seafood. The sea was a representation of the connection between their home country and the new one.
The number seven stems from the biblical importance of the number and its lucky connotation. While many of these symbols are taken from Catholicism and Italian tradition, the Feast of the Seven Fishes is virtually unheard of in Italy and instead is considered an Italian-American tradition.
Baked Clams, Baccala, Mussels, Calamari and Lobster are some of the dishes you'll see being served. Here on the Eastern Shore of Maryland, we have oysters, rock fish and so many other forms of seafood native to our bays and Atlantic coast.
For a holiday so widely celebrated, the traditions surrounding Christmas are as unique as the ornaments that decorate your tree.
From decor, songs, stories and gifts, Christmas looks a little bit different in every home across the world, but the "reason for the season" never changes.
Whether you're having any of the below recipes or baking a chicken or turkey or prime rib with potatoes, the time you are spending with family and friends is the most important.
CLAMS WITH LINGUINE
Kosher salt, 12 oz linguine, 4 tbsp unsalted butter, 4 cloves garlic finely chopped, 2 tbsp chopped fresh parsley, pinch of crushed red pepper flakes, 2 dozen littleneck clams (scrubbed), 1/2 cups dry white wine, juice of 1 lemon plus wedges for serving, freshly ground black pepper.
In a large pot of boiling salted water, cook pasta, stirring occasionally, until al dente according to package directions. Drain, reserving 3/4 cup pasta cooking liquid. Meanwhile, in another large pot over medium heat, melt butter.
Add garlic, parsley and red pepper and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add clams and wine. Cover pot with a tight-fitting lid and cook until clam shells open, 7 to 10 minutes. (Discard any unopened clams.) Add lemon juice, linguine and 1/4 cup pasta water, tossing frequently and adding more pasta water if needed, until glossy and warmed through, about 2 minutes; season with salt and black pepper. Divide pasta among bowls. Serve with lemon wedges alongside.
BACON WRAPPED SCALLOPS
1 lb. dry sea scallops (about 14), Kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 8 oz bacon (about 7 strips, not thick-cut), 2 tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 clove garlic (smashed), 1 tbsp. fresh thyme leaves, lemon wedges for serving.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Line a rimmed baking sheet with foil. Pat scallops dry with paper towels; season with 1/2 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon pepper. Cut bacon slices in half crosswise so you get 3-to 4-inch long strips. Wrap bacon around scallops and secure with a toothpick. Arrange scallops on a prepared sheet. In a small skillet over medium heat, melt butter. Add garlic and thyme leaves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute. Spoon butter and thyme over scallops, leaving garlic in the pan. Roast scallops until bacon is crisp and scallops are cooked through, 15 to 20 minutes. Remove toothpicks.
Transfer scallops to a platter and serve warm with lemon wedges alongside.
MUSSELS WITH TOMATO AND GARLIC
2 tbsp. butter, 1 onion chopped, 3 cloves garlic minced, 1 15-oz. can diced tomatoes, 1/2 cup dry white wine, 2 tbsp. freshly chopped parsley, kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 2 lb. mussels (scrubbed and debearded).
In a pot over medium-low heat, melt butter. Add onion and cook until fragrant and soft, 5 minutes, then add garlic and cook until fragrant, 1 minute more. Add diced tomatoes, wine and parsley and stir until combined. Season with salt and pepper. Add mussels and simmer until all shells are open. Discard any shells that aren't open.
Garnish with more parsley and serve with a hard bread such as sour dough.
OYSTERS ROCKEFELLER
2 cloves garlic, 1 cup tightly packed fresh spinach, 1/2 cup roughly chopped green onions, 1/2 cup roughly chopped parsley, leaves and stems, 2 tsp. lemon juice, 1/2 cup (1 stick) butter softened, 3/4 cup Panko bread crumbs, 1/4 cup freshly grated Parmesan, 1 tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 1 lb. coarse salt, 24 fresh oysters (shucked, shells reserved), lemon wedges for serving. Position rack in top third of oven and preheat to 450 degrees. Add garlic, spinach, green onions, parsley, lemon juice, butter and Pernod to a food processor and pulse until finely chopped. In a medium bowl combine, panko, Parmesan and oil. Sprinkle coarse salt over a large baking sheet to a depth of 1/2".
Arrange oysters in half shells in salt. Divide spinach mixture among oysters and sprinkle with Parmesan mixture. Bake until the spinach mixture is bubbling and the Panko is deeply golden, about 8 minutes. Serve with lemon wedges alongside.
GARLIC LEMON MAHI MAHI
3 tbsp. unsalted butter divided, 2 tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil divided, 4 (4-oz.) mahi mahi fillets, kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 1 lb. asparagus trimmed, 3 cloves garlic finely chopped, 1/4 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 2 lemons (1 sliced, 1 zested and juiced), 1 tbsp. chopped fresh parsley plus more for serving. In a large skillet over medium heat, heat 1 tablespoon butter and 1 tablespoon oil until butter is melted. Add mahi mahi; season with salt and black pepper. Cook, turning occasionally, until golden on both sides, 4 to 5 minutes per side. Transfer to a plate. In the same skillet over medium-high heat, heat the remaining 1 tablespoon oil. Add asparagus and cook, tossing occasionally, until tender, 2 to 4 minutes; season with salt and black pepper. Transfer to a plate with fish. SteIn same skillet over medium heat, melt remaining 2 tablespoons butter. Add garlic and red pepper flakes and cook, stirring occasionally, until fragrant, about 1 minute, then stir in lemon slices, zest, and juice, and parsley.
Remove from heat. Return mahi mahi and asparagus to the skillet and spoon sauce over. Top with parsley before serving.
BAKED COD
4 cod filets (about 1" thick), Kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 4 tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 1 cup cherry tomatoes, 1 lemon, 2 garlic cloves (smashed but not peeled), 2 sprigs thyme, 2 tbsp. freshly chopped parsley. Preheat the oven to 400 degrees and pat cod filets with a paper towel until dry. Season all over with salt and pepper. Combine olive oil, cherry tomatoes, lemon slices, garlic, and thyme in a 9 by 13 inch baking dish.
Toss to coat and spread into an even layer. Nestle cod pieces into a baking dish.
Bake until fish is opaque and flakes easily with a fork, 15 to 20 minutes, depending on thickness of filets. Serve garnished with parsley, more lemon juice, and pan sauce.
GARLIC PARMESAN FLOUNDER
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 fillets flounder, Kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 1/2 cup freshly grated parmesan, 1/4 cup bread crumbs, 4 cloves garlic (minced), juice and zest of 1 lemon, fresh chopped parsley for garnish. Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Drizzle 2 tablespoons of oil on a large baking sheet. Season flounder with salt and pepper.
On a large plate, combine parmesan, bread crumbs, garlic and lemon zest. Season with salt and pepper.
Dredge fish in bread crumb mixture, pressing to coat.
Place fish on a prepared baking sheet and drizzle with remaining 2 tablespoons of oil and lemon juice. Bake until golden and fish flakes easily with a fork, 20 minutes. Squeeze a bit more lemon on top and garnish with chopped parsley.
I wish each and every one of you a safe, warm and blessed holiday with family and friends.

title: Dems score coup with McCarthy ouster
author: David Harsanyi
content:
Dems score coup with McCarthy ouster

 October 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: David Harsanyi | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 640
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Kevin McCarthy has become the first House speaker to ever be successfully ousted in a motion to vacate vote. One day, you can tell your grandchildren you were alive to witness this completely pointless bit of history.Rep. Matt Gaetz's (R-Fla.) self-aggrandizing political stunt makes no sense and changes nothing - other than perhaps his fundraising totals.And other than some platitudinous blathering about "the establishment" and "the uniparty," I still haven't seen anyone offer a coherent reason - not even retroactively - for how any of this is the "best way to advance the conservative agenda." It would be one thing, perhaps an admirable thing, if Gaetz had gone on this crusade for a coherent ideological or principled reason. But his post-ousting demagoguery and grandstanding about issues completely unrelated to McCarthy's job performance proved it was a personal matter."I don't think voting against Kevin McCarthy is chaos," Gaetz explained."I think $33 trillion in debt is chaos. I think that facing a $2.2 trillion annual deficit is chaos." Now, there are numerous people to blame for the impending fiscal disaster, but McCarthy is no more guilty than most.One of the least convincing claims by Gaetz's defenders is that McCarthy was punished for ignoring the base. "The base," of course, is a popular euphemism for the most vociferous populist faction of the GOP.This faction enjoys blowing things up - mostly their own party's prospects. In this case, the "base" was represented by eight Republicans and the entire Democratic Party.And among these principled eight GOPers who were fighting for the honor of the base - what The New York Times called the "far-right GOP faction" - were Reps.Nancy Mace (who said Gaetz was a "fraud" the last time he tried to knock off McCarthy) and Ken Buck (who we last heard was reportedly looking for a CNN gig). I'm going to go out on a limb and say that the future of conservatism was not the motivating factor for their votes.Most Trump-endorsed candidates didn't even participate in McCarthy's removal. Donald Trump himself tepidly supported the speaker because, as he noted, the man had said "very great things" about him. And, really, what's more important? Though, I bet McCarthy was expecting a far more energetic defense after pathetically ingratiating himself to the former president a couple of weeks ago.Even if Gaetz had excellent reasons, Republicans did not eject McCarthy.Eight Republicans can't do anything by themselves. No, 208 Democrats ousted McCarthy with the help of some petulant backbenchers nursing personal vendettas. It is a political coup for the Dems.Gaetz, who only yesterday was going on about McCarthy's "secret deal" with Democrats, had no qualms sitting on the opposition side of the House plotting to oust a speaker who holds a rickety nine-seat majority. If there was actually a brewing House rebellion, Gaetz would have been able to corral far more votes.But Gaetz wanted to "break the fever" of D.C., so he teamed up with minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, "the squad," Adam Schiff and so on. Jeffries claimed he was supporting Gaetz's efforts because Republicans have shown an "unwillingness to break from MAGA extremism in an authentic and comprehensive manner." The notion that Democrats are backing a leading MAGA loyalist because they want to temper the "extremism" of Republicans makes about as much sense as Jamaal Bowman's fire alarm story. Democrats keep pretending they yearn for a more responsible GOP and stable political environment, then keep supporting every fringe effort and candidate to undermine both.Of course, no one is owed anything.McCarthy isn't the only person available in D.C. to serve as a middling speaker of the House. And, frankly, if he'd been more talented at the job, he might have headed off this challenge more effectively. But it's doubtful anyone is going to perform better with a slender majority and the Senate and presidency in Democrats' hands.But then again, none of that matters when you're having a tantrum.

title: Country Cooking: Shrimp, an Eastern Shore tradition
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Shrimp, an Eastern Shore tradition

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1529
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Growing up on the farm, surrounded by the Atlantic Ocean and Chesapeake Bay as well as the many rivers, we ate many types of seafood, but shrimp was not my favorite dish.Shrimp has a long history in the Delmarva region, particularly in the Chesapeake Bay and its estuaries. While not typically fished with a large-scale commercial harvest due to gear restrictions like the beam trawl ban, shrimp populations have been present and studied for decades. Recent observations suggest increasing shrimp populations in the area, possibly due to factors like warming waters.
Shrimp have always been found around the Chesapeake Bay, which is replete with the marshy, muddy habitat they love. Shrimp like to bury in sediment and can be found in both the Bay and its river estuaries, from shallow to deep water. Around the last week of October each year, a sudden drop in temperature drives the shrimp to funnel out of the Bay and into the southern Atlantic, where the water is a little warmer.
The shrimping industry is most popular in the Gulf states of Louisiana, Alabama, Florida and Texas. In the last five years, shrimp sales volume increased from 275 million pounds to 415 million. The percentage of households buying fish has also increased from 44.2% to 48.6%. This growth is seen in all areas of the country.
Shrimp is an excellent, affordable meal option for families. Shrimp can be enjoyed as an appetizer, snack, main course or side dish. Shrimp is a great addition to many popular favorites as it's easy to toss some shrimp into a creamy pasta or grill up some prawns to top your preferred cut of steak.
In later years, I discovered shrimp and became a "shrimp lover." My parents really didn't care for shrimp, so therefore when I became a cook in my own kitchen, I ventured into exploring many different foods. The same happens generation after generation, introductions to different foods.
JUMBO STEAMED SHRIMP
1/2 cup vinegar, 1 tbsp Old Bay seasoning, 3/4 cup water, 1 tsp salt, 1 1/2 lbs jumbo shrimp.
In a medium sized saucepan combine vinegar, Old Bay, water and salt. Bring these ingredients to a boil. Add shrimp. Stir gently to coat the shrimp in the liquid. Cover and steam for 5 to 6 minutes or until tender. Drain and serve.
SHRIMP AND RICE
1/4 cup butter, 1/4 cup chopped onion, 1/4 cup chopped green pepper, 3 tbsps flour, small can tomato sauce, 1 cup water, 1/2 tsp hot sauce, 1 1.2 lbs pre-cooked shrimp, rice.
Melt butter, add onion and green pepper, mix well with the butter. Mix in flour, stirring until bubbly. Add tomato sauce, water and hot sauce. Cook slowly for about 10 minutes. Add shrimp and cook slowly for another 10-15 minutes. Serve over cooked rice.
SHRIMP SCAMPI
1 1/2 cups olive oil, 1/4 cup lemon juice, 4 crushed garlic cloves, 1 tsp salt, 1 tsp black pepper, 4 lbs raw shrimp (shelled and deveined).
In a large skillet, place olive oil, lemon juice, garlic cloves, salt, and pepper. Heat thoroughly and add shrimp. Stir well and cook until the shrimp are pink. Serve with rice.
SHRIMP STIR FRY
2 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil, 1 lb shrimp (peeled and deveined), Kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 1 tbsp sesame oil, 1 small head of broccoli (cut into small florets), 1 red bell pepper (seeds and ribs removed, thinly sliced), 8 oz sugar snap peas, 3 garlic cloves (minced), 1 tbsp finely chopped peeled ginger, 1/2 cup reduced-sodium soy sauce, juice of 1 lime, 2 tbsps light brown sugar, 1 tbsp cornstarch, pinch of crushed red pepper flakes.
In a large wok or skillet over medium heat, heat olive oil. Add shrimp; season with salt and black pepper. Cook, turning halfway through, until pink, 2 to 3 minutes. Transfer shrimp to a plate. In the same skillet over medium heat, heat sesame oil. Add broccoli, bell pepper, and peas and cook, stirring and adding a splash of water if browning too quickly, until softened, about 7 minutes. Add garlic and ginger and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute more.In a small bowl, whisk soy sauce, lime juice, brown sugar, cornstarch, and red pepper flakes. Add to the skillet and toss to coat. Add shrimp and cook, tossing frequently, until heated through, about 2 minutes.
OLD BAY SHRIMP BURRITOS
For Old Bay aioli: 1/3 cup mayonnaise, 1 1/2 tsp Sriracha, 3/4 tsp fresh lime juice, 1/2 tsp Old Bay seasoning (plus more for serving), Kosher salt. For shrimp filling: 1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, 1/2 yellow onion (finely chopped), 1 small green bell pepper (diced), 2 cloves garlic (thinly sliced), 1 lb small shrimp (peeled and deveined, tails removed), 1/4 tsp ground cumin, 1/4 tsp paprika, Kosher salt, freshly ground pepper. For assembling burrito: 4 large flour tortillas (warmed), 1 cup cooked long-grain white rice, 1 cup cooked black beans (rinsed and drained), 3/4 cup shredded Mexican cheese, 1 cup shredded lettuce, 1 cup pico de gallo (drained), 1 avocado (thinly sliced), 2 tbsps chopped chives (plus more for serving).
Make aioli: Whisk together mayo, Sriracha, lime juice, Old Bay, and 1 teaspoon water. Season with salt, if desired. Make shrimp filling: In a large skillet over medium-high heat, add oil, onion, bell pepper, and garlic. Cook, stirring occasionally, until lightly golden, about 2 minutes. Stir in shrimp, cumin, and paprika. Season with salt and pepper. Cook, stirring occasionally, until opaque and just cooked through, about 4 minutes. Assemble burritos: Lay a tortilla on a serving plate. Add 1/4 cup each of the rice and beans. Top with ¼ each of the shrimp filling, cheese, lettuce, pico de gallo, and avocado slices. Sprinkle with chives and drizzle with aioli. Roll the burrito tightly and repeat with remaining tortillas and ingredients. Slice each burrito in half and serve with more aioli, Old Bay and chives.
SWEET CORN, SHRIMP & RICE SKILLET
1/2 cup basmati rice, 1 bunch scallions (divided), 1 medium red bell pepper (chopped), 6 garlic cloves (5 roughly chopped, 1 minced), 4 tbsps white miso, 1-inch piece ginger (thinly sliced), 1 1/4 tsp turmeric powder (divided), 1 tsp Kosher salt (plus more for seasoning), 1 tsp granulated sugar (optional), 1/4 tsp ground cayenne pepper (optional), 4 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil (divided), 1/2 lb medium shrimp (peeled and cleaned), freshly ground black pepper, 3/4 cup water, 1 cup frozen corn (rinsed in warm water and drained), lime wedges for serving.
Rinse rice well, until water runs clear, then transfer to a medium bowl and cover with water. Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Cook 5 roughly chopped garlic cloves and ginger in a pan for around 1 minute. Remove roots and ends from 4 green onions and roughly chop into pieces. Add chopped scallions to blender or food processor, along with the bell pepper, garlic cloves, miso, ginger, 1 teaspoon turmeric, salt, and sugar and cayenne if using. Blend until all ingredients are finely chopped and thoroughly mixed, then slowly drizzle in 3 tablespoons olive oil while running the food processor or blender. Blend until mixture is smooth. Pat shrimp dry and transfer to a medium bowl. Add remaining turmeric and minced garlic clove, and season with salt and pepper. Heat remaining tablespoon of oil in a 12-inch oven safe skillet over medium heat. Add shrimp and cook until opaque, 2 to 3 minutes per side. Remove cooked shrimp into a bowl just big enough to fit and cover with a plate to keep warm. Return the skillet to heat and add prepared puree. Cook on medium-high heat, stirring frequently, until the liquid has cooked out and paste has darkened, 8 to 10 minutes. (You'll know it's done when the oil starts to separate from the paste! Reduce heat to medium and whisk in water until smooth. Strain rice, and add rice and corn. Drain any cooking juices from the shrimp into the skillet, using the plate to keep the shrimp from falling in. (Be sure to keep shrimp covered. Stir to incorporate everything, then bring mixture up to a simmer. Place in a preheated oven and cover tightly with a lid or sheet pan. Bake until all liquid is absorbed and rice is tender, about 23 to 25 minutes. Meanwhile, thinly slice remaining green onions for garnish. Fluff rice with a fork, then scoop into serving dishes. Top with cooked shrimp and green onions and serve with lime wedges on the side.
SHEET PAN SHRIMP
1 lb. baby red potatoes (quartered), 1 1/2 lb raw medium shrimp (peeled and deveined), 2 ears of corn (cut crosswise into 4 pieces each), 2 links smoked andouille sausage (thinly sliced), 2 lemons (sliced), 1 tsp garlic powder, 1 tbsp Old Bay seasoning, 2 tbsps melted butter, 2 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil, Kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 2 tbsps freshly chopped parsley for garnish.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. In a large pot of salted boiling water, cook potatoes until just tender, about 10 minutes. Drain. In a large bowl, combine cooked potatoes, shrimp, corn, sausage, lemons, garlic powder, Old Bay, melted butter, and oil and season with salt and pepper. Toss until combined, then divide between two large baking sheets. Bake until shrimp is cooked through and corn is tender, 13 to 15 minutes.

author: Konner Metz
content:
16-year-old charged with attempted murder for incident in Federalsburg

 May 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Caroline 
 
 223
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — A 16-year-old is being charged with attempted murder after allegedly stabbing a woman in a Federalsburg parking lot, according to police.The incident occurred just before noon on Monday, the Caroline County Sheriff's Office said in a press release. The juvenile allegedly stabbed the woman multiple times during an altercation.
The 16-year-old suspect, who was not publicly named, is charged as an adult with attempted first- and second-degree murder, first- and second-degree assault, reckless endangerment, and possession of a dangerous weapon with intent to injure.
Police also arrested Franky Florestal, 29, and charged him with two counts of accessory after the fact to attempted first-degree murder.
Florestal, a Federalsburg resident, posted $5,000 unsecured bond following a bail review Thursday, according to court records. A preliminary hearing is scheduled for June 16.
The juvenile is being held without bond at the Caroline County Detention Center, police said.
The woman, 20, sustained life-threatening injuries but is now in stable condition, police said.
According to the Sheriff's Office, police in Seaford, Delaware responded to a local hospital where the woman was dropped off with multiple stab wounds. Per investigators, Florestal and the 16-year-old "transported the victim to the hospital before fleeing the scene."
The Caroline County Sheriff's Office, at the request of the Federalsburg Police Department, is actively investigating the incident. Anyone with information is asked to contact 410-479-2515 or info@carolinesheriff.net.

title: Project Healing Waters Brings Veterans To The Bay
author: Doug Bishop
content:
Project Healing Waters Brings Veterans To The Bay

 September 4, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Doug Bishop | Page: 4 | Section: News

 CHESTER - Fishing along the Bay was the theme of the 11th Stars & Stripers fly-fishing event last month for veterans resumed at the Kent Island Yacht Club in Chester. A record 63 veterans participated.The event, sponsored by Project Healing Waters Fly-Fishing, Inc.(PHWFF), headquartered in La Plata, had not been held since 2019, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.Concerns for the health of everyone, especially veterans still recovering for wounds, was the main reason for delaying the resumption of the event.A record number of privately owned boats, 36, were provided by qualified boat captain "guides" to take the veterans out fly-fishing at different locations around the Chesapeake Bay. The boats, veterans and guides departed early Saturday, Aug. 19, all going out by 7 a.m., fishing until 11 a.m.Founded in 2005 by Navy veteran Ed Nicholson of southern Maryland, PHWFF was founded especially for wounded veterans returning from Iraq and Afghanistan. PHWFF hosts over 200 such events nationally, from coast to coast; 85% of all donations to the foundation go directly to support these events.The first Stars & Stripers began as part of PHWFF in 2009, led by veteran Roger Carlson, of Edgewater, with only five veterans and five fishing guides. Carlson eventually turned over leadership of this local event to the late Vietnam veteran, U.S. Army Major (retired) Dr. Ed Fulton, who became a successful orthopedic surgeon in civilian life. Fulton hosted the event at Dominion Marina for seven years, until his unexpected death in May 2017. With his marina sold, the event was relocated to the Kent Island Yacht Club.Fly-fishing enthusiast Mark Eustis, of Davidsonville, has managed the event since 2017. Pulling together the support of local businesses and the immediate fraternal community to continue a first-class fishing experience for these veterans, Eustis recognized the aid received from the Kent Island American Legion, Centreville Post 18, Queenstown Post 296, Grasonville VFW Post 2576 and the Kent Island Elks, Lodge 2576, in Stevensville.Under the leadership of Elks member Lorraine Sincavage, the organization provided 11 volunteers to serve a wonderful luncheon for the veterans, their families and boat guides following the morning of fishing.Local businesses, Fisherman's Crab Deck and Harris Seafood, Inc., provided steamed crabs, and the Yacht Club provided pulled pork with all the side dishes.For the third time, Hardee's, under the Cato family's franchise ownership, using its "Stars for Heroes" program, collected donations for this event from their 23 locations around on the Eastern Shore of Maryland and Delaware. Hardee's presented a check toward next year's Stars & Stripers event for $9,375. The restaurant also provided breakfast sandwiches to the attendees.Eustis had high praise for the continued support from the community. He had hoped back in 2019 to "continue to grow the event", having more veterans participate, pushing that number to 60-65. That was achieved this year.If interested in more information about Project Healing Waters Fly-Fishing, either as a participant or volunteer, visit their site projecthealingwaters.org.

title: GOP not there yet with articles of impeachment
author: Byron York
content:
GOP not there yet with articles of impeachment

 August 24, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Byron York | Page: A6 | Section: News 
 
 782
 Words 

 Read News Document

 There's a lot of talk among House Republicans about impeaching President Joe Biden. But GOP members disagree on whether there is enough evidence to go forward.On one hand, Republican investigators have made enormous progress in the past few weeks. The testimony of former Hunter Biden business partner Devon Archer demolished Joe Biden's claim that he didn't talk to his son about Hunter's shady foreign business deals.GOP lawmakers are also finding increasing evidence that foreign money flowed to multiple members of the Biden family close to Joe Biden himself."We have caught Joe Biden in so many lies," House Oversight Committee chairman James Comer told Fox News recently. "I can't even count the number of lies now. So we have put together a case that I think would stand up in any court of law in America." Of course, no one is talking about criminal charges against the sitting president of the United States. Rather, if Republicans were to take action against Biden, it would be through impeachment.GOP House members have filed several resolutions of impeachment against Biden. Now there is a new one, the first since the Archer testimony, from a member of the House Judiciary Committee, Florida Republican Rep. Greg Steube. The resolution, containing four articles of impeachment, shows why the effort to impeach Biden is just not there yet.Article One attempts to link Joe Biden to Hunter Biden's, and brother James Biden's, influence peddling operations.The article says Hunter and James Biden "sold access" to then Vice President Joe Biden and then "sold promised access" to Joe Biden before he became president.Joe Biden himself "assisted by making appearances, phone calls, meeting with business partners, and knowingly allowing his family members to promise access to him and actions by him in furtherance of these schemes." The Biden family, the article says, benefited financially from that; Joe Biden's role was an "abuse of power" and a violation of federal law.Article Two accuses Joe Biden of obstruction of justice, charging that the Biden Justice Department interfered with investigations into Hunter Biden's activities. The accusations are taken from two IRS whistleblowers who have outlined in detail how DOJ dragged its feet and actually blocked IRS investigators from looking into what appeared to be clear tax evasion by Hunter Biden."These acts constitute an abuse of power as well as obstruction of justice," the article says.Article Three accuses Joe Biden of fraud for a matter in which James Biden allegedly deceived investors in a health care company. "Access to Joe Biden and indications that Joe Biden supported these schemes were used to lure investors into the schemes," the article says.Finally, Article Four accuses Joe Biden of "financial involvement in drug and prostitution activities." The article says Joe Biden and Hunter Biden "have a long history of comingled and intertwined finances." During the 2010s, Hunter Biden was famously blowing millions of dollars on drugs and prostitutes, both of which are illegal."Given the intermingled finances of Joe Biden and Hunter Biden, Joe Biden financially supported and should have been aware of these drug transactions and prostitution transactions," the article says. "Many of these transactions would have occurred using accounts with a nexus to Joe Biden." So that is the current case against Joe Biden. The obvious weakness in all the articles is that they are based on an effort to tie Joe Biden to Hunter Biden's, or James Biden's, allegedly illegal activities. Republicans have made great progress in beginning to discover such links. They have shown that Joe Biden lied about his knowledge of Hunter's activities, which is an important breakthrough. There appears to be much left to be discovered.In addition, Republican have convincingly established that the Biden administration improperly interfered with investigation of Hunter Biden's activities. That is an important breakthrough, too, although there is much more to learn.So as far as the first two articles are concerned, there is good reason for Republicans to push forward with their investigation. The third article, about James Biden, is very iffy, and the fourth article, about Joe Biden's knowledge of Hunter's drugging and whoring, will never go anywhere.And that is the current state of efforts to impeach Joe Biden. Republicans do not yet have a convincing case for impeachment. Maybe they will get there, and maybe they won't. As far as exercising general restraint against taking the extreme measure of impeachment is concerned - well, that sort of restraint went out with Nancy Pelosi's leadership of the House. If Republicans do eventually gather enough evidence against Biden, they'll use it. But they don't have it yet.Byron York is chief political correspondent for The Washington Examiner.COPYRIGHT 2023BYRON YORKDISTRIBUTED BY ANDREWS MCMEELSYNDICA TION

 I had to smile when I saw your cartoon in the Wednesday Aug. 16 paper and the apoplectic reaction of some of your readers.Most people can see the irony in the cartoon when it is the Republican party that has dragged Christianity into the public square and wrapped itself in it. These sensitivities are rich. You don't own Christ's image. And you can't use the political process to impose your brand of Christian beliefs on the public and expect others not to see it as fair game for cartoonists.As a born-again Christian, I felt called to run for state Senate in 2018. Matthew 25 was my platform where Jesus says whatever you do for the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, those needing clothes, the sick and those in prison you do for Me.I was at my beautiful church, New St. John's in Wittman, and was called up at the last minute to read the new testament scripture and the lectionary reading happened to include that portion of Matthew 25.That settled the debate in my head about whether to run.Before I moved to the Eastern Shore in 2010, a friend and I had a nursing home ministry where we would visit six nursing homes to conduct worship and prayer services.Since coming here, I had a worship service in the Alzheimer's unit at the Pines for four years. I studied a year of clinical pastoral education and served as an on-call chaplain at the Easton Hospital.Today I visit the women in the Talbot County Detention Center.The shame today, of course, is that one party has been wrapping itself in the cloak of Christianity for the past decade, insisting our pluralistic country is a Christian country and promoting policies that exclude the LGBTQ+ community.They even insisted that restricting gatherings including church attendance during the early days of the pandemic was anti-Christian.Their efforts to impose an abortion ban is organized around certain faith-based communities.Our beautiful country is a pluralistic one.Churches, synagogues and mosques are simply human institutions and churches in particular have shrinking attendance.
